#3499. Soccer Player Receives 12-Game Suspension After Fatal Match Collision

FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono has been suspended for his involvement in the now-fatal game collision that led to opponent Jesús de Miguel’s death.

The Spanish football federation’s disciplinary committee announced on Friday, November 13, that Owono, 25, would be benched for 12 games.

“[Owono] was sent off for ‘violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play,’” a statement read, per the BBC. “The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesús de Miguel Alameda, is public knowledge.”

The committee found that Owono’s conduct and “the accompanying circumstances” of de Miguel’s death justified the significant suspension time.

Owono tackled de Miguel during a November 2 soccer game and was immediately issued a red card for the remainder of the match. De Miguel was subsequently transported to a local hospital, where he was ultimately pronounced dead. He was 30.

“Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true,” de Miguel’s team, CD Tenerife said in a statement at the time. “There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today.”

The Tenerife team’s president also issued a statement after de Miguel’s death.

“We are all feeling vulnerable and deeply saddened right now. It’s hard to even believe what has happened,” Felipe Minambres told reporters after de Miguel died. “We know, especially the players and the players’ partners, that we will need support. We’ve already begun receiving offers of help today, and that support will continue. We will need professional assistance, but we also need the support of all our fans, because they are likely feeling the same way we are today.”

Owono’s team, for their part, shared their condolences to de Miguel’s family.

“We are deeply affected by what has happened and we share the pain that the club is experiencing,” a statement read. “From the very beginning we have maintained contact with them and we are at their disposal for anything they may need. What has happened has had a huge emotional impact on our players, the coaching staff and everyone at FC Andorra. These are particularly difficult times for everyone and we want to make sure that no one has to face them alone.”

#3498. The Best Early Black Friday Deals on DeWalt, Milwaukee, and Ryobi Cordless Power Tools

Becca Lewis is home maintenance writer who aims to foster confidence in and inspire DIY enthusiasts at all skill levels.

Becca attended Southern Connecticut State University, where she studied technical theater and design. She has a background in carpentry and fabrication and has worked in specialty shops, using a wide variety of tools and materials, for more than 20 years.

Becca has also written for Angi, where she specializes in creating guides for DIY, home maintenance, and renovations, and she indulges her love of sci-fi and fantasy by writing about entertainment and science for Giant Freakin Robot. She serves on the board of the Good Junk Sanctuary in Portland, Oregon, focusing on community engagement in the DIY and reuse space.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. This is an excellent addition to your emergency roadside tool set because you can use it to inflate a car tire with the charged 18-volt batteries.

The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $324, 38% off its regular price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales on tools to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. If you already have a cordless tool set and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something else they can use, a single tool deal might make more sense.

Disneyland will always be a magical place, but there is something particularly magical during the holiday season. The lights, the fake snow (because this is Southern California), the trees, the food, and the music all make it extra special this time of year. I have been to Disneyland more times than I can count, but there is one ride I have avoided for over a decade: It's a Small World.

It's not that I don't like the ride. It's just that if I hear that earworm-inducing song, even just the first note, I will have it stuck in my head for days, maybe even weeks. However, this was my first time experiencing the ride during the holiday season, and it had me singing a different tune.

First of all, the ride has definitely had a glow-up since the last time I stepped onto the boat. From adding inclusive dolls in wheelchairs and new characters like Coco's Miguel and his alebrije dog, Dante, to adding a third and final verse to the song, there was a lot for me to see and hear. However, the holiday version takes things a whole step further.

If you have never been on this attraction, let me tell you, you are in for a treat. And yes, there is another song that may be just as hard to get out of your head as the original. The holiday version of this ride incorporates none other than "Jingle Bells." Disney knew what they were doing, and surprisingly, I am here for it.

As I took that first bend into the tunnel, with rain coming down on my head, I was greeted by a bright "Happy Holidays" sign before entering the magical, doll-filled world, complete with all the twinkling lights of the season. There are garlands hanging everywhere, toys, presents, floating Christmas trees, and signs in all different languages wishing you happy holidays and a merry Christmas.

I had a chance to chat with one of Disneyland's cast members, Alexa Garcia, about why she loves It's a Small World this time of year. She told us:

Inside, you've got the beautiful music heard in different languages, and it's just such a beautiful message during this time of the year.

I found myself connecting with the music in a way I haven't in quite some time, and I even got a little choked up. Honestly, I think having "Jingle Bells" mixed in with the iconic song throughout really helps.

And then there is the final room, which is truly a showstopper. As the boat takes its final turn, you enter a white winter wonderland with everyone singing "Deck the Halls." It is elaborate, decadent, beautiful, and above all, just really, really cute.

This ride really won me over, and I am so glad I gave it another chance. Otherwise, I would have missed out on all the holiday joy this little boat ride gave me. And with the combination of songs, you actually end up leaving without either of them stuck in your head. At least, that is what happened to me.

While I may not be in a hurry to ride It's A Small World again without its holiday makeover, I encourage everyone visiting Disneyland for the holidays to give it a chance. The holiday celebration runs through January 6, 2027. I guess I'll just have to wait until next Christmas to willingly get back on board.

#3496. Lady Eliza and Lady Amelia Spencer Support Cousin Prince William In Style

Lady Eliza and Lady Amelia Spencer stepped out in style at the 2026 Tusk Conservation Awards on Wednesday. The annual awards ceremony recognizes and celebrates the leaders, researchers, and rangers working on the front lines to protect wildlife and ecosystems in Africa.

It’s a cause close to the sisters’ hearts, as they have spent much of their lives in South Africa. It is no surprise, then, that they attended the London event and showed their support for their cousin, Prince William, who has supported the charity for many years.

For the occasion, the twin sisters pulled two of the most dazzling dresses from their collection and, in true sisterly fashion, opted for the same designer: Oscar de la Renta.

Lady Eliza Spencer chose a strapless silver-toned midi dress with cutout details designed to create a sophisticated play of see-through effects. The shimmering texture makes it the perfect dress for the holidays, while the floral pattern, with its sculpted leaves, lends the whole look a romantic flair. In short, a harmonious blend of inspirations.

To amplify the outfit’s radiance, a handbag studded with cubic crystals—a true crystal box also by Oscar de la Renta—and a pair of elegant nude-toned, satin-finish pumps by Roger Vivier. The precious touch? A pair of bling-bling comet-shaped earrings to illuminate the face.

Her sister Amelia, by contrast, went all out in gold. She wore a refined ankle-length dress studded with sequins and fringes at the hem, giving the whole look a 1920s flair. The elegant, sophisticated look was completed with a gold clutch and a pair of pumps, also by Roger Vivier, featuring a precious buckle.

For jewelry, Amelia opted for a pair of diamond hoop earrings to sparkle in the light.

Charles Spencer’s daughters were not the only cousins supporting Prince William on this prestigious evening. Zara Tindall—daughter of Princess Anne—also attended. For the occasion, she wore a midnight-blue dress with short puff sleeves by Rebecca Wallace, featuring an exquisite collar and equally striking buttons, as if they were brooches borrowed from the royal jewelry box.

#3495. The Chosen’s Jonathan Roumie Wants More Celebrities to Discuss Their Faith

The Chosen star Jonathan Roumie is calling on more celebrities to openly discuss their personal relationships with religion.

“People in the public eye — for better and sometimes for worse — carry a lot of impact and a lot of weight in the culture, and when we’re talking about promoting things like prayer in the culture at a time in this world when everything seems kind of crazy and noisy and chaotic — we need people whose voices are recognizable and whose voices are trusted,” Roumie, 52, exclusively told Us on Thursday, November 12, while discussing Hallow’s Advent Pray25 Challenge for 2026, launching on Monday, November 30.

“As a celebrity, that’s a responsibility,” the actor continued. “People are watching the things you do and following you and following your story and taking notes. I think as responsible artists, when we are doing things like praying on the Hallow app and praying with this Advent challenge for days at a time … Next thing you know, their hearts are opened and their spirits are, for many, just set on fire with what it means to have a relationship with Jesus and kind of get this grounding from a life of prayer that, sadly, so many people today are missing.”

Like Roumie, a slew of Hollywood celebrities — Chris Pratt, Gwen Stefani and Mark Wahlberg, among others — have used and promoted Hallow, a Christian-based prayer app that offers guided meditations and prayers for users looking to grow in their faith.

While the rise of white Christian nationalism has come under scrutiny as of late — experts believe a rise in the movement coupled with the erosion of separation of church and state is one of the biggest threats to U.S. democracy — studies suggest more people, in particular young people, are turning to organized religion as a way to better understand themselves and the world.

According to the annual PRRI Censure of American Religion, 66 percent of Americans identify as Christians, while roughly 28 percent do not consider themselves to be religiously unaffiliated. According to the Barna research group, most Gen Z teens are interested in learning more about the Christian Jesus, while their younger counterparts are leading the way in the growth of new religious commitments.

“We need hope right now,” Roumie told Us on Thursday of people’s draw to organized religion. “Being able to lead prayer on the Hallow app, for me, is something that I’ve derived so much hope from myself.”

While Roumie believes more celebrities should speak openly about their faith journeys, he sees the trends and realizes that more people are also hungry for faith-based entertainment that honors their personal beliefs.

“I think it’s much more in the mainstream now than it ever has been,” Roumie says of Christian programming. “I think that is a direct response to what people are searching for, to what people are seeking. … I think people for a long time have been sort of starved of this kind of entertainment, and for me, I never thought I would be working in entertainment that functions on a spiritual level before.”

He added, “But I knew that if I was going to do it, the most important thing that I had to be sure of was that there was a level of quality to it — like, artistically the bar has to be set high. It has to be as high as anything that’s made in Hollywood or anywhere else for that matter. So it’s really up to us to be able to set that bar and shape the way things are seen and viewed and experienced, and offer people something more.”

Wicker might not get any Oscar recognition (although that would be a pleasant surprise), but I'd argue it's one of the best theater-going experiences of any film released on the 2026 movie schedule. Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård’s unconventional rom-com turned out to be much more than a smutty romance about a perfect man built of wicker. Audiences were won over not only by Skarsgård’s wicker abs, but also his character’s pure heart, leaving many hungry for more, Skarsgård included. And I laughed out loud when I heard the “sequel” he’s been pitching.

Alexander Skarsgård has never been one to take himself too seriously, especially while doing press tours. I can’t say I blame him, doing the same interviews over and over would get pretty old otherwise. However, his effortless deadpan and jesting tendencies make it difficult to sometimes tell if he’s being serious or not, like with this recent pitch to Entertainment Weekly about a Wicker follow-up:

It’s called Corduroy. We tried to find financing for it, but, for some reason, it’s been hard, but we’re pitching it around Hollywood this week.

At this point, I can’t tell if this is a serious pitch or not, but the idea is genuinely hilarious. Skarsgård added that this corduroy character would be “delicate and soft,” as well as an “attentive lover.” I’ve got to be honest, that doesn’t sound as sexy as a sturdily built wicker man, but I get the sense this concept is in very early stages of development. Forget splinters, we’d be wondering about carpet burn.

Seriously, I’m going to need someone to ask the A-lister about this again, because I really need some clarification. Skarsgård is known to joke with the media, even tot he point of teasing a “smear” campaign against his father, Stellan Skarsgård (Sentimental Value) during awards season. However, I wouldn’t put it past him to actually try and get this wild sequel made.

I’m just not fully sold on “Corduroy” for another reason. If your mind went to the same place as mine upon hearing this pitch, you understand why. Yes, I’m talking about the children’s story “Corduroy,” in which a corduroy teddy bear comes to life in a department store. Given Wicker’s salacious content and marketing, it feels really weird to relate the two, and therefore I fear it might be difficult to get that sequel pitch off the ground. However, the Legend of Tarzan actor has been persistent in the idea of a Wicker sequel, and I’m curious to see what that might look like.

This isn’t the first time the Northman actor has pitched a sequel to his latest movie. During the press tour, Skarsgård expressed interest in continuing the Wicker Husband’s story, following questions about what happens at the end of Wicker when the unconventional family of three leaves their village behind.

Clearly, Skarsgård enjoyed playing the wicker sex symbol that has taken the internet by storm, but that’s not surprising. If 2025’s kinky Pillion taught us anything, it’s that Skarsgård isn’t afraid to get a lil freaky (in the best ways) and Wicker seems to have opened a whole new realm of possibilities in his mind.

However, between the wicker husband’s kind heart and the fairytale-like setting that allows this somewhat raunchy, yet overall heartwarming love story to take place, I’m just not sure the same effect would work with a “corduroy husband” or any other textile husband for that matter. I’ll be quite surprised if something along these lines pops up on the 2027 movie schedule, but you can bet I’ll still buy a ticket. In the meantime, check out Wicker in theaters now.

I love them all, but I really want this couple to win now.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At the very start of Dancing with the Stars' 35th season, I thought Harry Shum Jr. was the ultimate frontrunner. However, I quickly came to love Ezra Frech. His story is remarkable and empowering. Plus, he’s so naturally talented, and he's partnered with one of my favorite pros, Daniella Karagach. So, as the weeks have passed on the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve wanted him to win. However, as each episode has gone by and that appreciation for Frech has stayed consistent, my love for Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov just keeps growing stronger and stronger.

While I always thought Amber was one to watch, she’s proven time and time again that she and her partner are helping set the gold standard for this season. Then, the figure skater went on the Zach Sang Show to talk about her experience on DWTS, and she said something about winning that really made her the frontrunner in my mind. When asked what it’d mean to get Pasha his first mirrorball, the Olympian said:

That would mean the world, because, I’ve said this before, is that I came into this competition, of course, who doesn’t want to win. But it wasn’t like, ‘I need this because I’ve worked my entire life for it.’ Like, I’ve been dancing for two months. Yes, it has been a very intense, very passionate two months of working, but it has been his whole life that he has been dancing. And he’s been on the show for, I believe, nine seasons. And every single year, he has put his everything into every single celeb he’s had.

Pasha has been on the show for eight seasons, and with each year, I love him and his wife, Daniella, even more. Seriously, season after season, I find myself more invested in the pros than the stars. That’s because they’re there year after year, and I get to know them all quite well through the show and social media. So, while I adore them all, and my love for Daniella is very strong, I have wanted Pasha to get his flowers really, really badly.

In his eight seasons, the highest place he’s ever gotten is third, and he deserves a win. Amber is the perfect person to help him do it. As she explained, he wanted to have an athlete as a partner, and she has “the stamina and the physical capabilities” to do tougher dances. She also complimented her partner’s ability to teach, and ended up saying:

There’s no reason that we shouldn’t be able to make this happen besides me limiting myself.

Her drive to do this for her partner is so endearing, and it’s now a big reason why I want her to win. Along with that, the Olympian went on to detail how much work the pros have to do for this show. While it looks hard for the stars, the pros have to do twice as much, and she wants Pasha to get recognized for it, explaining:

He has been putting everything into this, and I really want for everyone to see him succeed. Because it is technically, you know, every year it’s the celeb, but it’s also about the pros. Like, he is putting – imagine how much work I’m putting into it; he’s doing twice the amount. He has to choreograph; he has to do so many visual selections. Like, there’s so much that the pro does for every single show that people don’t see. So, yes, it’s about the celebrity and who wins, but it is also about the pro.

Of course, all the pros have to do this, and I'm sure their stars would praise them the same way Amber praised Pasha. However, her passion is infectious, and that, paired with their fun and high-quality dances, makes them my No. 1 couple.

Plus, of the vets still on the show who have been there for over seven seasons, Mark Ballas, Jenna Johnson, and Daniella have won before; Pasha has not.

So, yes, while I’ll be happy if Ezra and Daniella win, because they are amazing, right now, I’m rooting harder for Amber and Pasha. They are killing it week after week, and Amber’s drive to win for her pro and get him his first mirrorball is making me even more motivated to text “Amber” to 21523 as many times as I possibly can.

Now, to see who takes home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, make sure to tune in to the last few weeks of Dancing with the Stars on Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET either on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription.

#3492. Beto O’Rourke Says He’d “Do Anything” for James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa—Including Work for Them

After the shocking Democratic victories in Texas last week, it was hard not to look over the shoulders of James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa and see the shadow of Beto O’Rourke, whose losses for Senate in 2018 and governor in 2022 had become cautionary tales of Democratic hopelessness in Texas. And perhaps proof that nice guys couldn’t win. But in the years after those failed runs, O’Rourke never really went away. He launched a voter-registration group called Powered by People, punched out missives on Substack, livestreamed his thoughts, and quietly advised his party from the background.

“Should I have talked to Joe Hagan when he was on my front porch in 2019?” O’Rourke says now, looking back at the cover story I wrote, in which he proclaimed he was “just born to be in it,” a premature declaration that almost immediately sank his prospects. “I’m glad I did. I’m grateful for everything that’s happened, because look where we are. It’s a beautiful new day in America.”

O'Rourke taks the stage during the Fight the Trump Takeover rally at the Texas Capitol in August 2025.

Like Stacey Abrams in Georgia, who lost her own race for governor but used her visibility to build a stronger coalition, O’Rourke can claim some credit for setting the table for Democratic success in Texas. Talarico won his first race, for a Republican-held state House seat, on O’Rourke’s 2018 wave. And as it turns out, O’Rourke himself weighed another Senate run this year. When Talarico asked whether he’d run, O’Rourke said only if Talarico ran for governor instead, eventually stepping aside after concluding that the moment called for “something and someone new.” When he launched his Senate campaign, Talarico said he wanted to replicate O’Rourke’s “energy.”

O’Rourke, meanwhile, became a behind-the-scenes player: Powered by People was one of four partners in the Texas Democrats’ $30 million coordinated campaign, and it says it reached more than 110,000 new and young voters in Texas this cycle. Ken Paxton noticed and tried to put O’Rourke “behind bars” for funding the Democrats who fled the state to block its Donald Trump–backed redistricting.

O’Rourke says the wave cascaded so far down the ballot in Texas that a candidate who tried backing out of her campaign before Election Day ended up winning. “At that point it was too late to take her name off the ballot,” he says. “She didn’t campaign, just won her election. That speaks to the magnitude of the wave, but also to the value of having a fighter on every front. Somebody said to me, ‘A wave’s great, even better if you have a surfboard.’”

Over an hour-long conversation, O’Rourke parses the political revolution in his home state, suggests how Democrats can hold on to their land grab, and, perhaps unsurprisingly, looks ahead to another run for office.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: The conventional wisdom is that this was a revolt against Trump, and that the candidates and the Democratic strategy were secondary. What’s your read?

Beto O’Rourke: So much of this election was a rejection of Trump and Trumpism: the corruption, the wars, the cruelty. But after 2024, people were anxious that we didn’t have a unifying national leader. [Joe] Biden was not going to be it. Kamala Harris turned out not to be it. President Obama, I think wisely, held back…. Chuck Schumer was persona non grata in any gathering of Democrats. The DNC was in the red.

What it did was allow for candidates in different parts of the country to really establish themselves in their own right and by their own merits, never having to fear being under the shadow of a larger figure. It’s really a blessing. That’s how you get Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, Mary Peltola, all these extraordinary candidates who are extraordinarily different from each other. In Texas, for the first time in half a century, Democrats fielded a fighter on every front: 150 state House candidates, 38 congressional candidates, 16 state Senate candidates. You had to have a historically terrible, corrupt president. But you also had to have this historically beaten-down Democratic Party; that the Democrats don’t have a message, they don’t have a leader. That all turned out to be a great thing.

Read Party Animals: A letter from the back rooms, barstools, and bacchanals of Washington, DC—with exclusive reporting, interviews, and analysis.

A year ago you convened Talarico, Colin Allred, and Joaquin Castro to think about a statewide slate. Talarico went his own way. You warned him he’d “want friends on that ticket.” What did you mean?

I just wanted to win, and I put that before anything else. James and I had many conversations before he officially announced. He asked me, “Are you interested? Would you run?” And I told him, “The only condition on which I would run is if you were to run for governor, or somebody else who could draw that kind of attention and resources, and if we had the ticket rounded out by strong contenders for every position on the ballot.”

My advice to him was: “Look, I’ve done this before. No matter how talented you are, no matter how much you can raise, this state is so big, the Republicans are so entrenched, you need a fighter on every front.” And ultimately, that’s what happened. Gina really hit her stride at the right time. Her strength as a candidate a year ago compared to how she finished is worlds apart, and that is a testament to what an exceptional leader she is.

Clearly, it was the right call for James to be there. He is just an extraordinarily talented communicator. He was a phenomenally focused candidate. He was absolutely the right guy for the moment. I also think it was the right call for Jasmine Crockett to run too. I know from being on college campuses how electrifying she is, how many young people she brought into the electorate this time. They stayed in even after Jasmine was defeated in the primary.

The Atlantic reported that you told Hinojosa, “Not one person can win Texas. It has to be two.” Is that what you said?

I definitely spoke to Gina before she made the decision to run, and then after. To be honest with you, I can’t remember if I said “two.” What I said consistently to everybody who was thinking about it—Colin, Joaquin, Gina, Jasmine [Crockett], James—was that you need a fighter on every front and the strongest possible ticket. That was based on the last run I had, in 2022, and even the ’18 run. If Joaquin or Julián Castro had run for governor when I was running for Senate, who knows? Of course, at that time, we didn’t know the size of the wave that was about to crash.

I definitely did. I could have run…. You’d have to ask James, but I think he probably would have supported that if I had. We have an amazing organization in waiting, volunteers who’ve been with me, the ability to raise money. But was that the right thing to do? No. I had been before Texas twice before, and the moment demanded something different and, I would argue, something better.

You can’t discount a politician’s ambition and ego. I had to find a way to get past that. It helped having conversations with my wife. It helped having conversations with our kids. It helped having conversations with people who’d been on these runs with me before. Also, I spent a lot of time traveling Texas. My love language is a town hall meeting, where it’s just a free-for-all and anybody can step to the mic and ask any questions. At the end of that, I really felt this moment called for something and someone new. I don’t know that Texas could have produced a stronger—I was going to say candidate, but really a one-two punch. It was James and Gina. They’re both exceptional individually. Together, they transcended what had happened in politics for as long as I’ve been alive.

Honestly, my own doubt about whether Texas could be won was based on you. We’d seen this story before.

I wouldn’t have done this work as a volunteer for the last four years if I didn’t believe in Texas. I know in my heart and in my bones that we are so much better than the people in power. It’s the obscene abortion ban that has cost the lives of girls and women, the $7.25-an-hour minimum wage, the fact that we’re the least insured state in the country. Four years after Uvalde, and no one in power has done a single thing. It’s insane having Texas Republicans say, if you’re Muslim, regardless of whether you’re an immigrant, you should be deported from this country. That’s just not who we are.

O'Rourke speaks during the Fight the Trump Takeover rally, where 5,000 people attended. Attendees protested proposed redistricting, immigration enforcement, and other Trump-backed legislation and proposed changes.

When I ran for governor, 9 million registered voters didn’t cast a ballot. It’s not because they don’t care; it’s not that they’re lazy. This state makes it harder than any other to participate, so we’ve got to try that much harder. I knew it was a matter of time and effort. The greater the effort, the shorter the time. But did I know it would be 2026? Did I know it would be every statewide office and the state House? Fuck no, man. Nobody knew that.

Ken Paxton called you a “repeat loser” and tried to prosecute your PAC. He lost by 12 points.

We’ve spent more than $600,000; we have Powered by People defending our organization, defending me. He accused me of bribery. He tried to remove the license for Powered by People to do voter-registration work in the state of Texas. He promised to lock me up, to put me behind bars. The 15th Court of Appeals [judges], all of whom were appointed by Greg Abbott, so none of them friends of mine, have ruled against Paxton for attacking somebody for exercising their First Amendment rights. Do I think that I’m going to get that money back? I don’t know.

Couldn’t have happened to a better person.

Did Talarico and Hinojosa acknowledge your role, or did they keep their distance?

You’d have to ask them. I got a really nice message from James on election night, and I had a chance to campaign with Gina in the closing days of the election. That’s not an easy choice for Gina, right? Both of them did an exceptional job of being themselves and not seeming to be beholden to anybody. They invited nobody in from outside of Texas, and we all understood: This is their show. So getting to campaign with Gina here at the University of Texas at El Paso, at the University of Houston, it was really nice to hear her acknowledge the work that so many of us have been doing, especially all these volunteers who’ve been out there, whose names most people will never know.

I’ve known them both for a decade. James and I were on the campaign trail together in 2017 and 2018, when he was running his first race for state House in Williamson County. Somebody just sent me a picture of the two of us at an event in Williamson in 2017. These are really fucking good human beings, and they’re also really good at understanding power and how to win it. It is so rare that those two things come together.

O'Rourke speaks during a "Fighting Oligarchy" event in Houston, Texas on Oct. 20, 2026.

Are Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries the right leaders for this moment?

Chuck Schumer absolutely is not. Early 2025, [Elon] Musk is running wild with DOGE, Trump is steamrolling every center of power. They’re all bending the knee—the Ivy Leagues, the big law firms, the media companies. Hakeem marshaled every Democratic vote in the House but one to stop Trump, DOGE, and Musk, and the deal with Schumer was going to do the same. Then, inexplicably, Schumer bent the knee as well. In that moment, it was absolutely over for me.

Schumer deserves so much credit and praise for his work over the decades. But he doesn’t deserve to be majority leader at this major turning point for the country, not when you have James Talarico, Abdul El-Sayed, or Jon Ossoff. We have an embarrassment of talent in the Senate right now, and we should use it. The age when any American cares what the majority leader reads on the Senate floor is over. I don’t even know what his message is, and that says something.

Hakeem Jeffries hasn’t had the chance to lead as Speaker. We were elected in the same class in 2012, and I’m grateful that he stood strong early in the Trump administration. I wish he could communicate more effectively than he has so far. Maybe there’s a scenario where he’s Speaker, but he taps the far better communicators in his caucus, like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, to do more of that work, and he’s focused on getting the legislative results.

Eleven House Democrats missed the vote to impeach [Pete] Hegseth, enough to have changed the outcome. What happened there?

Eleven is a big number. That certainly invites some conspiracy thinking, or, maybe just as bad, the idea that these folks aren’t up to the job. It’s really important that the Democratic leadership in the House address this directly, explain what happened, and take ownership and responsibility for it.

You’ve said Democrats wasted their power in 2009 and 2021, and that next time they should “drive that car like we stole it.” What happens in the first 100 days?

Right off the bat, you have to make our lives better in a way that we can feel. In Texas, that’s not hard, because we are in such a fucking hole. Raise the minimum wage from $7.25. Expand Medicaid when the federal government’s paying 90 cents on the dollar. Stop this voucher thing that is draining tax dollars from local schools, and pay teachers so they don’t have to work a second or third job.

Nationally, you have to do the same. The response to this from many is that Trump has the power of the pen and will veto that. Make him veto that. I don’t like anything about him, but I don’t know that there’s a more successful political operator than Trump. I don’t think there’s someone who reads power better than he does. Maybe there are deals to be had. Maybe you force the veto, and you set up a clear contrast going into 2028. At a minimum, you have to get caught trying.

The huge issues that Democrats have absolutely failed to lead on, we have to lead on now, so that would include immigration and that would include democracy. Immigration was arguably the issue that voters made their decisions on in 2016 and 2024, and if we continue to hope that it’s just going to solve itself, instead of making tough choices and using political capital on this, then it’s going to be our demise in future elections as well. [On democracy], there’s no democracy to restore or save. There is a democracy you can build anew. Getting corporations out of politics; what just passed in Montana is potentially a wonderful precedent from which we could build. Getting a voting rights act passed again. [Pushing] the popular-vote compact; I think we have enough trifectas now. I’m probably in the minority in the Democratic Party, but I’m a big believer in term limits. People give a speech and are like, “We’ve got to overturn Citizens United,” or, “We’ve got to do away with the Electoral College.” That’s a great applause line, but when is that ever going to happen?

O'Rourke spoke in October 2026 as the fight for the Senate came down to the wire.

The big dig on Democrats is: You talked a great game on immigration, then you won the White House; you had the House and the Senate. You didn’t do anything. You talked a great game about voting rights. You had the trifecta, and you didn’t do anything. Now we have the power. We’d better deliver, or watch out.

I’m surprised I’m not hearing more from you about prosecutions and subpoenas. You spent the last two years warning about fascism and calling for accountability.

That’s got to be part of it too. The law is king in this country; no one’s above it, no one’s below it. We’ve allowed the precedent, through the Epstein crimes, that you can be rich enough and well-connected enough to rape and traffic girls and women with complete impunity. I spent a lot of time with young people doing this voter-registration work, and that is probably the number one thing I hear from them for why they don’t vote: This shit doesn’t work. Ghislaine Maxwell [went to jail], but no man who actually did this has gone to prison or even faced trial.

Then there’s the corruption that flows from the president through his family, through his Cabinet officials, through the oligarchs [with whom] he surrounds himself. If we let this stand, much the way that we let stand his crimes against this country on January 6, 2021, that sets the most dangerous precedent. Look at the Roman Republic. It wasn’t Caesar crossing the Rubicon. It was Sulla turning his armies against Rome, and there was never a consequence or accountability for that, so the precedent was set and Caesar picked that up. [Editor’s note: O’Rourke is an avid fan of the podcast The Rest Is History.] There will be a more capable, powerful demagogue than Trump—he or she may be a Democrat; he or she may be a Republican—who will use that precedent unless that door is closed. I know this is an unpopular thing to talk about within our party, because folks want to turn the page. But that keeps biting us in the ass. Everyone who went to prison for [January 6] was pardoned by this president.

But if you spend the next two years investigating him and prices stay high, Democrats are cooked.

That’s exactly right. That’s why I said you’ve got to deliver for people, and they have to feel it immediately. Democrats are responsible for so many good things that are both slow-working and expressed through the tax code, like the child tax credit, and for which they don’t claim credit. Those things have to change.

I was in the Rio Grande Valley after 2020, doing voter registration, knocking on doors, and talking to this guy who voted for Trump. I said, “You had a front-row seat to kids in cages, to family separation, to this cruelty here. Tell me what’s going on.” And he said, “I hate all that stuff, but voting on those issues when I can’t feed my family and I may lose my home is a luxury. I don’t have that luxury.” We have to learn that lesson. You’ve got to make people’s lives better, and if you do that, you build trust and legitimacy: “Okay, these guys are really helping me. They really reflect my values and my interests. And now that they are pursuing these investigations and this accountability, I trust them, and I know that, regardless of the outcome of these investigations, my life is better because they are in power.”

If Trump felt that he or his family were under real legal threat, is there any world in which investigations become a chip to trade, say, for immigration reform? I realize this is very Trumpy thinking, but you are dealing with Trump.

No. Totally understandable, and it’s a recognition of how politics and power typically work. But part of how we got Trump in the first place was that there weren’t consequences for massive failures or crimes committed: these banks that were bailed out after they had driven so many Americans into poverty and homelessness in 2008 and 2009, these wars the Bush administration launched on false pretenses. They lied to us, they lied to the world, and it took the lives of so many Americans, Iraqis, and Afghans. Never any consequence or accountability.

This corruption has been so flagrant, it’s as though Trump and those closest to him were daring America to hold them accountable. Then there’s the open defiance of the law and the Constitution: killing people on fishing boats in the Caribbean, kidnapping a head of state, launching a war and continuing it in violation of the War Powers Act. When you allow these things to stand, they become the precedent. But if there’s accountability, then that becomes the precedent upon which future leaders will be able to act. Trump may feel he’s fighting for his life, that he’s backed into a corner. He may make it harder for Democrats to do the things that they need to do. But I don’t think we can operate in fear of him.

Some Democrats, like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, argue that the corruption and the high prices are the same story. Do you buy that?

Talarico is masterful at saying that: Their corruption is costing you and your family. So many examples in Texas. Billionaires bought off Governor Greg Abbott and persuaded him to pursue a voucher scheme that took public dollars out of local schools and sent them to private schools, decreased the quality of your school, and raised your local property taxes to make up the difference. Abbott, beholden to corporate interests, opened the door [to data centers], and our electricity prices went up and the quality of our water and air was compromised.

O'Rourke says he doesn't know if there’s an office he can imagine running for in 2028 or 2030.

The biggest one was in 2021, when we had the winter storm. In the energy capital of the world, they couldn’t keep the lights on or the power running, and pipeline operators [and others in the energy industry], among the biggest donors to Greg Abbott, began to price-gouge, bankrupting utilities and causing ratepayers to pay sky-high prices. One of the pipeline operator CEOs wrote Abbott a $1 million check at the end of that winter storm, almost as if to say thank you for not prosecuting them. It’s not corruption in an abstract way; it’s corruption that’s costing you. And yes, that corruption should be prosecuted. It’s not enough to just win the election and throw the bums out. If the bums broke the law, then they have to face the consequences.

If Democrats hold this ground, it would seem to open the door for you again. Is there an office you can imagine running for in 2028 or 2030?

I don’t know, and people would have to answer that question for me. That’s what I’ve been trying to do these last four years, just listen to people and figure out where I can be most useful. I’ve tried to remain agnostic.

I had a conversation earlier in the year with somebody who just won in Texas, and they had been one of the people to encourage me to run for governor in 2022—what the fuck was I thinking, running in Joe Biden’s midterm?—and I asked them, “Did you think I had any chance to win?” And they said, “Oh God, no.” But they knew that we needed somebody to galvanize the state, protect our gains in Harris County, and shore up the wins that we’d [earned] in 2018. Somebody had to carry us through that next stage of the relay.

Just so I’m clear, I would not have run if I didn’t think there was a chance we could win in 2022. It was an incredibly tough environment that got tougher and tougher as the race proceeded. But it did a lot of good, and in some small way it was probably helpful toward what happened in 2026.

When [my wife] Amy and I made the decision in 2016 that we had to do something, I went to everyone: Joaquin and Julián Castro, Clay Jenkins, Michael Sorrell, Wendy Davis. I asked each of them, “Will you run? If you do, I will get behind you.” Ultimately, I was like, “Okay, if you guys aren’t going to do it, I am going to do it. I know this is crazy, and I know all of you are better positioned, I’m going to do it.” So if I feel the way that I felt that time, that I’m the right person for this, then, whatever the odds, I’m going to get out there. But if running could hurt us, if there’s somebody better—and that was a conclusion I drew coming into this cycle—then please step up, and I’ll get out of the way and support you as a volunteer.

The next statewide race in Texas is 2030. One thing I’m thinking about right now is 2028, and the fact that the 40 Electoral College votes in Texas are ours to lose. I want to be part of the team getting Texas ready for that nominee to win our state. I’m happy to follow James and Gina’s lead. They’re our leaders now.

Can you imagine working in a Hinojosa administration?

I will do anything for her, and the same for James. It’s just crazy, hearing that.

What about taking Powered by People to Florida? They could use some help, evidently.

These states of the former Confederacy have worked so hard to make it hard for people, especially young people, to vote. We don’t have Election Day data yet, but through early voting, 60% of our voters, overwhelmingly 18 to 29 years old, voted through early voting. That’s about 33 points ahead of the average for that demographic in Texas. I sure wish our party had put resources behind [Angie] Nixon and [David] Jolly in Florida. We could have won those races. What was [the margin] in the governor’s race? 1.3%. Heartbreaking. If I can be useful there, I’m happy to go.

About a year after my 2019 story came out, I texted you that I hoped there were no hard feelings, and you took responsibility for your own errors. It seems like you’ve been through a process since then.

That’s just life, right? I truly feel so incredibly lucky: getting to serve in Congress, getting to run for the US Senate, being considered for the nomination in 2020, being back out on the trail for governor, and then doing this work with Powered by People. When I get depressed is when I don’t have purpose. Then I’m prone to feel sorry for myself or to wonder what if. I’m a big believer that action is the antidote to despair. So I try not to dwell too much on decisions that I’ve made. Should I have talked to Joe Hagan when he was on my front porch in 2019? I’m glad I did. I’m grateful for everything that’s happened, because look at where we are. It’s a beautiful new day in America.

Joe Rogan suggested on his podcast that Talarico should run for president. Any advice for him?

I am the last guy to give Talarico advice, because he’s just been so freaking smart and amazing. Whether he runs for president, whether he serves out his full term in the Senate, he is one of very few leaders in this country who have met the moment. I trust him to make the best decisions for, first and foremost, the country, for Texas, and then for himself.

Who excites you in the 2028 field? You’ve got Gavin Newsom on the center-left, and AOC and Ro Khanna presenting themselves as heirs to Bernie Sanders.

We could have added another 15 people to that list. There was a lot of gnashing of teeth two years ago: We don’t have a national leader; what is Democrats’ message? That was liberating for all of these candidates, and you’re going to have so many diverse perspectives in 2028. What you did these last 10 years is going to be an important consideration. Gavin Newsom was one of the first national Democrats to recognize what Trump was trying to do by redrawing these congressional maps, starting in Texas, and I was really impressed with how quickly he moved and how strong he was on offense. Pete Buttigieg has been nonstop traveling the country supporting candidates. In the wake of 2024, with this sense of total defeat, a few people just got out there, and AOC was one of them. I like the folks who never stop fighting, who are true to themselves and not susceptible to the prevailing winds. Bernie Sanders is probably the best example of that.

Ro Khanna and I, when we were in Congress together, authored the No PAC Act. We asked our legislative staffs, “Can you find out who last authored a bill like this so we can amend it and improve it and make it our own?” There was no bill. Nobody had ever done that. He’s been so consistently focused on democracy. Greg Casar, he’s from Texas. He’s the chair of the [Congressional] Progressive Caucus and also has been crisscrossing the country. There are a lot of good people out there.

O'Rourke speaks at a campaign rally at the University of Houston on October 20, 2026.

After 2016 and 2024, a lot of women I know concluded that this country won’t elect a woman president. Can a woman be elected?

Absolutely. Gina Hinojosa—here in Texas, the conventional wisdom was that if a Democrat ever wins, it’s got to be a straight white man who fits the following characteristics. And here you have the first Latina from the border. It’s fucking awesome. It’s going to sound corny, but I really believe in this country, and that faith was vindicated last Tuesday. It wasn’t the country being like, “Go Democrats!” It was the country saying, “We can do better, and we’re going to take a chance on folks who may not fit the profile.” I think that holds true for the country in 2028.

You just turned 54. If you never ran again, would you be okay with that?

I think about it sometimes. Is the prize the office—junior senator from the state of Texas, president of the United States of America? Or is the prize a much better world for my kids and this country? I always want that to be the answer, and it is. I just fucking won the lottery in life. Our kids are absolutely thriving; my oldest is about to be 20, middle kid is 18, my youngest just turned 16. I’ve been lucky with Amy and living in El Paso, getting to do this fulfilling work.

But just to be clear: Would I love to serve in office again at some point? Absolutely. The El Paso City Council may have been my most fulfilling time in politics. Loved being in Congress—what a high honor. But if it doesn’t happen, I’m more than okay. I’m the luckiest guy out there. I’m good, no matter what happens.

#3491. My Most Hated Gilded Age Villain Has Become My Favorite Season 4 Character, And I'm Not Mad About It

A new season of the HBO series The Gilded Age is currently heating up on the 2026 TV schedule with all the social climbing, relationship drama, and elaborate costumes that it’s become known for. I’ve been watching it since the beginning, when audiences were first introduced to Enid Turner, an ambitious woman serving as Bertha Russell’s lady’s maid.

Back then, the woman only known as Turner learned quickly that if you’re going to cross Bertha (Carrie Coon), you’d better have enough standing to back it up. Turner did not and became a villain to the Russell family. If you had told me then that same character would evolve into my favorite in Season 4 of the HBO series, I never would have believed you. That would also just mean that I didn’t have the same faith in Enid as she had in herself.

Played with so many layers by Kelley Curran, Enid instantly became a character that I loved to hate but always felt like there was more under the surface. Sure, she attempted to seduce Bertha Husband, George Russell (Morgan Spector), which was a no-no for his wife, ultimately leading to her downfall within the household. The fact that she knew she was better than that kept her clawing her way up the social ladder as she returned, season after season, eventually becoming the character I now can’t help but root for.

In Season 2 of The Gilded Age, Enid seemed to have finally caught a break, marrying Joshua Winterton for financial security and a more prominent place in society. Being significantly older and in ill health led to his death, but it also left his fortune in Enid’s hands, and she was very savvy when it came to using it to the fullest extent of the social-climbing ladder.

Yet somehow, that wasn’t the end of Enid’s story. It has reached even higher with the delicious fun in Season 4. Now married to the not-very-secretly gay Oscar Van Rhijn (Blake Ritson), the duo has formed a partnership with a shared goal of social domination. Together, they plot and plan with devilish schemes that I’ve found myself rooting for with delight.

As a character, Enid is a magnificent sleight-of-hand magician, creating illusions and deceptions as she rises in social ranks. She is the definition of fake it until you make it, going toe-to-toe with her one-time rival at an upcoming lavish dinner that you must stay tuned for in Episode 5, airing on November 29.

While Marian and Larry can’t seem to get on the same page in Season 4, Enid and Oscar might not have romance between them, but being similar in age and mentality means they can understand and support each other in ways neither has had before. It allows her moments to shine with the confidence needed to not only take on Bertha but finally gain the upper hand.

The Gilded Age cast is truly stacked with talent, but what Kelley Curran has been able to do over four seasons, turning a hated villain into a powerful figure that viewers can root for, has been fascinating, fun, and entirely surprising to watch. It’s early in the season for this HBO show that got the world talking, and there’s quite a bit of Enid’s journey still to go, but you can watch all the drama on Sunday nights or with an HBO Max subscription.

#3490. RHOC's Jeana Keough Is 'Cancer-Free' After Sharing Diagnosis at 70

The Real Housewives of Orange County alum Jeana Keough has a major update to share about her tongue cancer battle.

“Jeanna is cancer-free, and that called for a little puppy party. 🤍🐾,” Keough’s friend Jeannine Cecchini wrote via Instagram on Saturday, November 14, alongside a photo showing the women cuddled up to two canine companions. “So grateful to be here celebrating this with you, my friend.”

Cecchini, who added “Cancer Free” and “Jeana Is Cancer Free” hashtags to her post, further noted that she is “looking forward to more” happy days with her friend and amid her cancer update. Keough, 71, shared the upload to her account.

Jeana’s daughter, Kara Keogh, announced in July that the former Bravo personality had been diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue. (Jeana shared Kara, as well as sons Shane and Colton, with late ex-husband Matt Keough.)

“A few months ago, while visiting Shane and me in Florida, my mom mentioned a painful spot on her tongue,” Kara, 37, wrote via a GoFundMe campaign to raise money for treatment. “She assumed a tooth had been rubbing against it and had even gone to the dentist multiple times to have the tooth filed down. I asked her how long the sore had been there. She paused, thought about it, and realized it had been nearly a year.”

She continued at the time, “After surgery to remove the cancer, we were hopeful that the hardest part was behind her. But when doctors recommended a second surgery to remove lymph nodes, they discovered the cancer had spread. What we thought would be a one-time surgery became a full cancer battle. Jeana is now in her fifth week of chemotherapy, radiation, and immunotherapy. The treatments are relentless.”

As Jeana underwent chemotherapy and radiation treatment, her three children were dutifully by her side.

“She’s strong through this. She’s got a good support network,” Shane, 40, exclusively told Us in July. “Colton, our younger brother, is there, so she’s on the right path. But you know, it’s tough for everybody, and we’re just trying to make sure she stays on her program so she’s strong when this is done.”

Kara, for her part, told Us that she was hopeful about her mom’s prognosis.

“I think she’ll get cancer to bend to her will, like she does with everything else in life,” Kara joked. “We’re choosing to stay in that mindset. … She refuses to acknowledge that she’s sick, and I think that the cancer will believe her and follow suit.”

#3489. Democrats Plot (and Party) in Washington After Midterms Rout

This is the November 12, 2026 edition of Party Animals, a letter from the back rooms, barstools, and bacchanals of Washington, DC—with exclusive reporting, interviews, and analysis.

Good evening from Washington, where Party Animals is coming to grips with how the social scene in the capital will change amidst a dramatic transfer of power. Gone will be the heady days of President Donald Trump’s total control of the US government. The next two years will be defined by how his administration handles a muscular Democratic opposition.

At Crooked Con, a conference put on the weekend after the midterm elections by the media company founded by former Obama staffers and Pod Save America hosts Jon Favreau, Tommy Vietor, and Jon Lovett, I got a sense of just how confident the party is after almost two years in the wilderness.

Read Party Animals: A letter from the back rooms, barstools, and bacchanals of Washington, DC—with exclusive reporting, interviews, and analysis.

Befitting the sensibilities of the incoming Congress, Crooked week kicked off with a surprise appearance from Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who wore keffiyeh-patterned Air Force 1s to the live taping of his Pod Save America episode. The crowd went ballistic.

In this edition of Party Animals, the view from Washington’s new libbed-up social scene; what a Newsmax show says about Trump’s tumbling popularity among young Americans; and my colleague Joe Hagan’s interview with Beto O’Rourke, the original Democrat-who-might-win-Texas, about how the party finally pulled it off in the Lone Star State.

Also mentioned in this issue: Barrett Adair, Matthew Foldi, Robert Garcia, Katie Miller, Felicia Schwartz, Keith Edwards, Vaughn Hillyard, Marc Beckman, Marco Rubio, Michael Scherer, Chi Ossé, and more.

Got tips? Hit the Party Animals hotline: aidan_mclaughlin@condenast.com. Or text me—my number is 917-817-8266. Complaints will be aired on Newsmax. Praise will be debated and affirmed by a Crooked Con panel.

I doubt there were many places on earth more buoyant than Crooked Con in DC last weekend. The conference brought together a legion of newly elected Democrats, veteran members of Congress, journalists, and liberal content creators for a day of live plotting that culminated in a party at City Tap House, where Robert Garcia, the incoming emperor of Oversight, worked the room. “I was pretty optimistic going into the election, but this is beyond anything I imagined,” Favreau tells Party Animals. “The majority of the country is clearly ready to move on from the Trump show and give Democrats another chance.”

The creators were ecstatic. At an after-after-party nearby, Barrett Adair, a platinum blonde progressive with more than 200,000 TikTok followers, bounced around in a hot-pink latex dress. Pints were passed about so generously that once I had acquired three, I stopped bothering to tell which was which. Keith Edwards and Chi Ossé chatted intently in the corner. The night felt like a portent of what was to come: After nearly two years of the MAGA Huns marauding freely throughout the capital, the libs were soon to be back in charge—of Congress, at least. They celebrated accordingly.

“There's a lot to feel good about,” said Favreau. “Now we have to make it count.”

As the country grapples with the sheer magnitude of the blue wave that crashed down last week, our nation’s besuited analysts are seeking to identify the warning signs, like a postdisaster reconnaissance team examining the swell of a tsunami after it has decimated a Southeast Asian beach town. How did Trump lose the key voting blocs, like young men, that vaulted him back to power in 2024?

I’d like to propose a bellwether: The Big Beautiful Trump Show, an unsubtle program that debuted on conservative network Newsmax in October. It’s unclear whose brilliant idea it was to launch a North Korea–style propaganda show in support of a historically unpopular president weeks before he led his party into a generational election wipeout, but the show was hosted for three episodes by a DC-based influencer named Matthew Foldi. A source shared the ratings: The show debuted to 1,000 viewers in the younger demographic, the 25–54 age group coveted by advertisers. “Insanely low,” the source explained. A Newsmax spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

Pour one out (a pint of raw milk, perhaps) for Katie Miller’s podcast, which is going on hiatus. I was a loyal listener—she booked pretty much every Trump Cabinet member, even the shy ones, and the friendly setting elicited more insight than you’d typically get out of a guarded pol like Marco Rubio. In a post on X, Miller said she would be pausing the show due to her husband’s new role as Trump’s chief of staff, writing that “the time commitment is too great and now is the time to step away.” The next day, The Atlantic’s Michael Scherer reported that Miller had signed a contract with Paramount for a future podcast deal, but that she had ended that as well. Paramount spokesperson Melissa Zukerman told Party Animals, “I don’t see she has anything with us.” When asked if Miller ever had a contract with Paramount, Zukerman did not respond.

Huang Out: The Economist does the important math and estimates that Jensen Huang’s Chinese affair “could go down as the most expensive shag in history.”

The Mayflower Millers: Read Kevin D. Williamson, of The Dispatch, on Stephen Miller and the incomprehensible case of the “heritage American.”

Dems in Vogue: Model Caroline Trentini reflects on her photo shoot with Iowa governor-elect Rob Sand, shot by Steven Meisel for a 2004 issue of Vogue Italia. I’m reliably told that these photos went quadruple platinum on Tumblr.

Cyberyuck: Read my colleague Nate Freeman’s soaring eulogy for the Cybertruck, Elon Musk’s grand experiment in bad taste.

The next two years: Vanity Fair’s Chris Whipple examines how Stephen Miller—who once told him Trump’s powers “will not be questioned”—will operate as chief of staff. In a previously unreported part of a past interview, Whipple asked Miller: “Would you agree, though, that it’s also the chief of staff’s job to tell the president what he doesn’t want to hear?” Miller replied: “No, I wouldn’t say that.”

The Shadow First Lady: MS NOW reporters Felicia Schwartz and Vaughn Hillyard profile Marc Beckman, the curious “exclusive senior adviser” to Melania Trump who has no diplomatic experience—or even security clearance—but wields mighty power over US policy in Ukraine and Russia.

#3488. ‘Rings of Power’ Stars Break Down 2 Major Deaths in Prime Video’s Lord of the Rings Series

The first batch of episodes include two major character deaths

The first batch of episodes include two major character deaths

The stakes are higher than ever in season 3 of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. Sauron (Charlie Vickers) is working on forging the One Ring that will bring all of Middle-earth under his control, recruiting powerful Ring-servants to lead his orc armies. Númenor is on the brink of civil war between the new king Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) and the Faithful loyal to the deposed queen Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson). Showrunners J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay made it clear that no one is safe this season by killing off two characters who have been part of the series from the beginning. Polygon spoke to the actors about their last moments on set and their time in Middle-earth.

This article contains major spoilers for the first four episodes of The Rings of Power season 3.

The story in Númenor has involved a lot of family drama. Captain Elendil (Lloyd Owen) is one of the leaders of the Faithful, a Númenórean group who believes in preserving the kingdom’s connection to the Elves and the Valar. His daughter Eärien (Ema Horvath) allied herself with Pharazôn and his son, Kemen (Leon Wadham), encouraging her father to renounce his faith and pledge loyalty to the new king. She participated in the arrest of the Faithful’s leaders, though she helped her father escape.

Five years pass between the season 2 finale and the start of season 3, and they haven’t been kind to Eärien.

“In season 1, I hope you get more of a sense of youth and hope,” Horvath said. “This season, you start to feel her age and shame creeping in about what she's done, what she's been involved in.”

Eärien seems to be loyal to Pharazôn, and is even called in to help interrogate a man who tried to assassinate the king. But she actually helped the Faithful plan the attack, and she kills the captive to save him from being tortured and potentially revealing her secret.

“The idea that even small actions matter is a pretty big theme in Tolkien, and even though she's done some pretty horrible things, the way she's trying to right the ship still matters in this last episode, or in the last few years that she's been helping the Faithful,” Horvath said. “I think she’s an imperfect heroine.”

Pharazôn’s chief advisor Belzagar catches Eärien sneaking into his room so she can send a message to her father, and he lays a trap that winds up with Elendil being captured by Kemen. When Pharazôn confronts her with the truth, Eärien leaps out a window to avoid being interrogated.

“That's probably my favorite day that I've ever had on this job,” Horvath said. “It's the first time I got to deliver lines to Trystan, who plays Pharazôn. He's always been the most important person in the room for her, and we've been in scenes together, but we've never gotten to really spar. I was really excited about that scene. I always knew what was coming. I knew that she was going to die on the island, and I knew what her political leanings were going to be.”

The tragic story of the Wood Elf Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) began in the first episode of The Rings of Power. A soldier guarding a village of men who are descended from allies of the Dark Lord Morgoth, Arondir fell in love with the human healer Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi). Bronwyn’s own son Theo (Nazanin Boniadi) was partially responsible for the destruction of their home after he discovered a magic sword hilt that led to the creation of Mordor. Bronwyn died offscreen from poison delivered by an Orc arrow, which prompted Arondir to dedicate himself to fighting the Orcs alongside Galadriel (Morfydd Clark).

In season 3, Arondir wants to leave the fight to take care of Theo, who took refuge in the Númenórean colony of Pelargir. He puts off their reconciliation to go on a dangerous mission with Galadriel to infiltrate the infamous prison of Gundabad. In the meantime, Theo responds to Sauron’s call for Ring-servants and becomes a Nazgnagôl. The two finally meet again at Gundabad, where Arondir tries to persuade Theo to take off his ring and leave with him. Theo seems to be on the brink of accepting the help, but when Sauron appears and compels him to kill Arondir.

“He's appealing to the last bit of hope of his son, knowing that he's been quite corrupted,” Córdova said. “Sauron is extremely powerful, and once he corrupts anything, it's very hard to fight against it. It's a testament to Arondir. He's like, ‘I'm still going to face you. I'm still not going to let my light be taken by the shadow, by the darkness.’ I think he's a badass. Until the last second, he's going to try to lead with love.”

The dramatic scene was shot over the course of a week, though Córdova said he’d been preparing for it for months.

“It was very emotional, but I felt quite supported by my castmates and by the crew,” he said. “I was going through a personal loss of a very dear loved one that same week, so the whole thing was quite charged, but I felt like I was in great hands. I knew what our director Sanaa Hamri had in store, and I trust her blindly, so I knew that the character was going to be honored in the way that he needed.”

Arondir leaves behind his surrogate son, Theo, and his pet dog, who stayed in Rivendell.

“He's just the most beautiful dog,” Córdova said. “He was a pain in the ass, but he was such a lovely dog to shoot with. Elves love and revere nature and all living things, so I think he'll be very well taken care of.”

Córdova loved shooting with the dog so much that he went to some extreme lengths to get him in more shots.

“He did not want to stay still,” he said. “He did not want to do what he needed to do. But I really wanted him to be there so I said, ‘Bring the tube of chicken paste we're using, and I'll just make it work. Just shoot me from this side.’ They did and I smeared my entire face and my neck on that side with the paste that he loved. He was a little pain in the butt, but I loved him. He was such a cutie.”

In an age of prequels, sequels and reboots, I kind of expect most successful films to get at least one of those things. Weirdly, Tangled hasn’t. Yes, it is getting a live-action adaptation, and there was the animated series Rapunzel’s Tangled Adventure. However, it has not gotten an animated sequel to go along with the 2010 hit. Now, someone asked a Disney exec if there are any plans to ever make a Tangled 2.

Not long after the live-action Tangled wrapped production, and in the lead-up to the release of Disney’s newest animated project on the 2026 movie schedule, Hexed, Disney Animation’s chief creative officer, Jared Bush, was asked if there have been any discussions about Tangled 2. Here’s how he responded to Collider’s question:

We discuss all kinds of things all the time. I think people would be kind of surprised by the number of discussions we have around, ‘Do we want to return to a world with characters that we really care about?’ It's all the time for many, many different things. I think it always comes down to: Is there a filmmaker who is passionate and has a story that's undeniable that we must tell? That usually is how we approach any new story.

While Bush didn’t confirm or deny whether there have been talks about a Tangled sequel, it does seem like, to get one made, it would need to have a director leading the charge who cares deeply about it and a story that has to be seen on the big screen. Makes sense to me. I wouldn’t want to see a sequel to one of the best princess movies ever if it didn’t have those two things either.

Adding to that, the exec explained that Tangled is what drew him to the world of Disney. He also recalled how it revived the musical for them too, saying:

The world of Tangled is one of the things that drew me to Disney Animation. I think when that movie came out, there was this resurgence of the Disney musical. That's no easy feat. You may remember that when that movie came out, we weren't sure whether Disney musicals were something that people wanted to watch, and that said, ‘Yes, it's something that people want to watch — a new version of what that could be.’ So, it has a very special place in my heart. And Byron, my good friend, was one of the directors.

Overall, it sounds like the bar is very high for a Tangled sequel (as it should be), and maybe that’s why we’ve never seen one. However, considering we’ve gotten two Frozens and now they’ve gotten a third one off the ground, I will never totally give up on Tangled 2.

Plus, while we wait to see if that ever happens, we will not be devoid of Tangled content. In fact, we’ll get to see Teagan Croft and Milo Manheim take over as Rapunzel and Flynn Rider, respectively, in the live-action version in 2028. Seriously, the casting alone has me so stoked to see this take on the animated classic, and I’m sure it’ll be well worth the wait.

Now, as we continue to anticipate the live-action Tangled and dream about an animated Tangled 2, you can stream the original Tangled with a Disney+ subscription.

#3486. The Nintendo Switch 2 Is Actually on Sale Ahead of Black Friday

If you've been patiently waiting for the right moment to pull the trigger on the Nintendo Switch 2 after the recent release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, this might be a good time to do so. Woot is selling a Nintendo Switch 2 for $469 (originally $499). The discount comes as the first major discount since the Sept. 1 price hike.

The new console is an upgrade in every way, as you can read in our full review of the Nintendo Switch 2. The ergonomics and design have improved, making it much better to hold and look at. The battery life has also improved, now with about 180 minutes of handheld playtime before the juice runs out.

A big plus is that the Switch 2 is backwards-compatible: You can play your old Switch games on it. Some Switch games have the ability to upgrade to the Switch 2 Edition by buying that game's upgrade pack. This is especially worth it for games like The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, which will look better on the Switch 2.

There are a lot more games out for the Switch 2 now than there were at the beginning of the year. Nintendo has hinted that they're prioritizing making more classic remakes, with many more on the pipeline, so there are plenty of games to keep you busy for a while, like Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, and Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment, which are already out. If you already own a Switch 2, check out our Top 10 Hacks to get the most out of your device.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.
