When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I love Jackie Chan. You love Jackie Chan. We ALL love Jackie Chan. However, I think we sometimes forget when we started loving Jackie Chan.

It's kind of crazy to think, but some people's introduction to Jackie was in the 2010 Karate Kid movie starring Jaden Smith (which I love, by the way). For others, they might have discovered him with Rush Hour (which even Chan himself seemed to not have completely understood). For me though, it all started with 1995’s Rumble in the Bronx, which I just rewatched the other day.

I’ve always loved this film, but honestly, after a rewatch, I don’t think most people remember just what an absolute gem this movie is. So, today, I’m here to remind you.

As a Black dude, I love martial arts movies (honestly, who DOESN’T?). The thing is, I’m usually into SERIOUS martial arts films, like stuff from the Shaw Brothers, JCVD classics like Time Cop, and old Bruce Lee joints. Then, in 1995, a movie came along that had everything I love about martial arts, but it was also funny as hell.

Enter Rumble in the Bronx, which basically changed the whole concept of what a martial arts movie could be for me. Here was a film that wasn’t just martial arts, but was a comedy. It was a film that had a lively cast of characters, such as Uncle Bill Ma (Bill Tung), Elaine (Anita Mui), the wheelchair bound, Danny (Morgan Lam) - who could play a Game Gear with no game inside, and Jackie Chan himself as Keung, a police officer who just wants to attend his uncle’s wedding until trouble arrives.

The fight choreography in this movie is SO GOOD (especially the warehouse fight!), and its humor also lands with the same impact. Rumble in the Bronx wasn’t the first movie I'd seen that mixed martial arts with humor - I did grow up in the age of Turtle Power, mind you - but it was the first that wasn’t based on a comic book that still had this sense of humor. Seriously, watch it again. It's probably funnier than you even remember it being.

I first watched Rumble in the Bronx when I was just a kid, and I seriously hated the villains back then. Well, I'm 43 now, and I STILL hate the villains, which is a true testament to just how awful they are to poor Keung in this film. Yes, the late Marc Akerstream as Tony is the main antagonist, and he's a pretty good villain, but even better is his underling, Angelo, played by stuntman Garvin Cross.

Angelo is a true scumbag who is always getting his ass whooped, but also finds ways to mess with Keung. The “best” scene is when Angelo and others corner Keung in an alley and hit glass bottles at him with a baseball bat, cutting Keung severely. I hated Tony’s henchmen when I was a kid, but this really infuriated me as an adult. It made their ultimate beatdown later on that much sweeter.

Lastly, can I just talk about how great the stunt work is in this film? It's not the craziest stuff in the world (we would see WAY crazier stuff from Chan in earlier films of his, many of which came stateside following the success of RitB), but when I saw his death-defying stunts in RitB - like a huge jump between buildings! - I was hooked.

And I wasn't alone. With the humor, action, and crazy stunt work in Rumble in the Bronx, it's little wonder why this film made Jackie Chan a household name - especially since it's set in “America” (Even though it was filmed in Canada).

However, I think people may have forgotten just how all of it - the humor, the action, the stunts - are just perfect in this movie, and I think you need to rewatch it for yourself just to remember. It's still really that good!

Rich is a Jersey boy, through and through. He graduated from Rutgers University (Go, R.U.!), and thinks the Garden State is the best state in the country. That said, he’ll take Chicago Deep Dish pizza over a New York slice any day of the week. Don’t hate. When he’s not watching his two kids, he’s usually working on a novel, watching vintage movies, or reading some obscure book.

#3447. Brad Pitt Helped This Underrated Prime Video Comic Book Adaptation Get Made

If you see Brad Pitt's name in the credits for a movie he doesn't star in, it's probably because the film was produced by Plan B Entertainment, which was founded in 2001 by Pitt, his then-wife Jennifer Aniston, the late Brad Grey, and Kristin Hahn. The production company has many Pitt vehicles on its resume ("Ad Astra," "F1") but that's not all. For instance, Plan B recently co-produced the meta horror magnum opus "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma."

Plan B first ventured into TV with the failed Ryan Murphy pilot "Pretty/Handsome" in 2008, which was not picked up to series at FX. The company has since returned to TV and produced shows across different streaming platforms and networks, with its biggest recent hits including "3 Body Problem" and "Adolescence" for Netflix. But it hasn't had success across the board, as the Plan B co-produced Prime Video time travel series "Paper Girls" was canceled after one season in 2022.

"Paper Girls" adapts a 2015-2019 Image Comic series by writer Brian K. Vaughan and artist Cliff Chiang. The morning after Halloween 1988 in fictional Cleveland, Ohio, suburb Sony Stream, four preteen paper girls — "new girl" Erin Tieng (Riley Lai Nelet), Tiff Quilkin (Camryn Jones) Mackenzie "Mac" Doyle (Sofia Rosinsky), and KJ Brandman (Fina Strazza) — discover a time machine in an abandoned basement. The comic follows them across different time periods. At first, they're just sent to their immediate future in 2016, where they meet a grown up Erin (Ali Wong in the show). But later trips swing back and forth from prehistoric times to the far future.

With its eight episode run, Prime Video's "Paper Girls" merely scratched that surface. Its short life sadly mirrors Vaughan's acclaimed comic "Y: The Last Man" being turned into a single-season show as well.

"Paper Girls" features four kids in 1980s Midwest suburbia, riding on bicycles and communicating with walkie-talkies, who stumble onto a science fiction story. There are undeniable similarities to "Stranger Things," and while they're coincidental (the "Paper Girls" comic was already running when the former premiered in 2016), the story's parallels to the Duffer Brothers' Netflix phenomenon probably helped the TV show adaptation get greenlit.

But compared to the 1980s nostalgia in "Stranger Things," "Paper Girls" takes a harder look at the decade. The very first time we meet Mac in the comic, she insults some local bullies with homophobic slurs — and she's one of the heroes! But that hatred turns out to be internalized. Across the story, Mac and KJ realize their feelings for each other. (That bumpy ride is another thing the "Paper Girls" TV series didn't get a chance to realize.) Compare that to "Stranger Things" Season 3, in which one character (Maya Hawke's Robin) admits she's a lesbian to another (Joe Keery's Steve), and he's totally accepting of it. It's a nice sentiment about what things should have been like, but it's also completely ahistorical.

Another story that hits the same mood as "Paper Girls" is the 2026 time travel Amblin throwback "The End of Oak Street" — for one, both have time-displaced dinosaurs. "Paper Girls" doesn't have as wide a mean streak as "Oak Street," though, making it a happy medium between that and how saccharine "Stranger Things" can get. If you love the "Paper Girls" TV series and crave more, I'd highly recommend the comic as the next best thing. It's a quick read at only 30 issues, and it's got the ending the TV show deserved to adapt.

#3446. Zara Tindall Shows Cheltenham Why She's The Queen of Race Day Dressing

Zara Tindall didn’t let the cold snap stop her from enjoying a day at the races on Friday. Accompanied by her close friend Dolly Maude and country-set favorite fashion designer Jade Holland Cooper, the daughter of Princess Anne and granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II brought a dash of regal glamour to the proceedings following a glitzy night out in support of Prince William.

And while the sun may have been out, the Olympic equestrian still needed to wrap up against the chill. Tindall opted for a long plaid coat from L'Agence, a Purdey roll-neck jumper in brown, and a fascinator from Sally-Ann Provan. She accessorized with a new pair of Hector Lion earrings, a new Fairfax & Favor handbag, and completed the look with leather boots, also from Fairfax & Favor.

Zara Tindall joined in the action at Cheltenham Racecourse on Friday

Dolly, on the other hand, wore an avant-garde feather coat with knee-high boots and what looked to be a pair of emerald tights.

The pair were last spotted together in October, when they attended the William Hill Showcase Meeting at Cheltenham, but their friendship goes way back. Long considered Zara’s best friend, Dolly became Princess Anne’s lady-in-waiting in 2024. A former NHS midwife, she helped to deliver Zara’s third child, Lucas Tindall, on the floor of Zara’s bathroom at Gatcombe Park after the plan for the birth went awry in 2021.

Jade Holland Cooper and Zara Tindall on day one of The November Meeting at Cheltenham racecourse

But Dolly’s bond with the niece of King Charles III goes back long before that. (Not for nothing did Zara’s husband, Mike Tindall, joke that the 53-year-old is “more important than I am.”) Dolly was Zara’s maid of honor when the pair tied the knot, and when Zara split from her then-fiancé, jockey Richard Johnson, in 2003, the pair moved in together—they still live close by in the Cotswolds.

Having worked as a maternity practitioner in the NHS in Gloucestershire for 13 years, Dolly also did some philanthropic work using her maternity expertise, working in the unit of a hospital in Kambia, Sierra Leone for a month in 2013. At Kambia, she taught staff basic nursing skills. Before qualifying as a nurse, Dolly studied fashion and Cordon Bleu cookery at Eastbourne College of Food and Fashion, graduating in 1989.

Zara Tindall also braved the stormy weather for a day at Cheltenham with Dolly in October

Dolly Maude is known for her love of horses—a passion she shares with Zara and Princess Anne—and is often seen in Ascot’s royal box alongside the Princess Royal. In March 2024, she made her first official appearance as the Princess Royal’s lady-in-waiting, a momentous occasion that marked a new phase of her enduring bond with the royal family.

The royal confidant has four children with her husband Chris: Billy, who studied at Swansea University; Nell, who trained at the Central School of Ballet; a keen skier, Ted; and Mary.

Princess Anne's daughter wrapped up in a warm plaid coat and roll-neck jumper

Concerning Dolly’s appointment, another friend of Mrs. Maude's told The Telegraph, “She’s such a great girl. For the Princess Royal, it’s a perfect fit because of their shared love of dogs and horses. She’s not only extremely close to Zara, she also gets on brilliantly with the Princess. She’s fiercely loyal and discreet. It’s a great match.”

While much of Zara Tindall’s time this season has been spent touring the country’s most prestigious racing meets, she still found time to support her cousin, Prince William, at one of his treasured annual traditions. The Prince of Wales helped to put together the Tusk Conservation Awards at Raffles on Wednesday night and invited Zara to the celebration of conservation, alongside Lady Amelia and Lady Eliza Spencer and the Marchioness of Bath.

Dolly Maud made her debut as lady-in-waiting for the Princess Royal at the 2024 Commonwealth Day Service in March

Zara showcased her characteristically elegant style, donning a sapphire-blue Rebecca Vallance short-sleeved midi number, aptly named the “Crown Jewel” dress, which she paired with Kiki McDonough earrings. It is not the first time that the royal has lent her support to Prince William’s second-longest patronage: she also joined the crowd at the Tusk Awards in 2025, donning Rebecca Vallance again, and tearing up at the Prince of Wales’ speech in honor of those who gave their lives as rangers.

Zara Tindall and the Marchioness of Bath at the Tusk Awards

Last night amid the 2026 TV schedule, the 39th Annual Kids' Choice Awards dropped and proved to be quite entertaining. Nominees like Stranger Things, The Thundermans: Undercover, and Spider-Man: Brand New Day triumphantly led the wins this year. And, of course, plenty of people got slimed as is tradition. However, we need to talk about one particular fashion choice that involved an influencer showing up dressed as slime. And I must say, her neon dress is completely bonkers in the best way!

We’ve seen costume fashion before at red carpet events that is incredibly eye-popping. Whether Lady Gaga dressed as meat at the 2010 MTV Video Music Awards or Katy Perry appearing as a hamburger at the 2019 Met Gala, outfits like these certainly keep viewers talking. Speaking of talking, we need to have a chat about influencer Haley Kalil (also known as Haley Baylee) showing up at this year's Kids’ Choice Awards in this slime-colored ensemble:

Now, that’s what you call an eye-popping dress! Although with this one, I'd be afraid to pop anything. The Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue winner was sporting a bright green gown with balloons of many different sizes spread throughout. It looks as if the balloons are floating right above her, and this almost feels like a piece someone from Nickelodeon could've curated.

And icing on the cake? Haley Kalil is holding a balloon-like green purse to go with it that says “Win the Mall!”, referencing her upcoming 2026 Netflix competition series. The Miss Minnesota 2014 winner was clearly paying tribute to Nick's history with her unique dress, with the kids' network known for their love of ooey-gooey green slime.

I’m not the only curious mind who needs to know more about this green neon dress. When ET wanted the juice on the creativity that went into making this dress, Kalil gave the credit to a 20-year-old fashion design student named Finn Thompson. She made sure to explain what this unique dress was made of and the secret to putting it together:

[Finn] tied each of these by hand. And the only thing I have on is a bodysuit under this. It’s all made of balloon. Even the back. Even the corset in the back. It’s balloon.

That’s real dedication on the fashion student’s part. It must have taken hours to sew so many balloons onto that bodysuit. The question on my mind is—how does she not pop any of those balloons when she’s sitting down? Fortunately, the Forbes top creator recipient answered that question as well. Here was her response:

I can actually sit because I’m wearing that bodysuit. I just lift up the back, pop a squat. I’m just very wide, you know? So, whoever my chair mate is might have to spare some room on the chairs. Sorry!

So then it’s just a matter of lifting the back of the dress to make sure she’s sitting on the bodysuit. That’s a very smart feature for Thompson to design, to say the least. Otherwise, that would be another way to make heads turn if a loud pop occurred with every squat.

As incredibly bonkers as Haley Kalil’s neon dress is, it’s still a fashion moment that I’m proud to say will live in my mind rent-free. With method dressing being so in right now, there’s no better way to show up at a Nickelodeon event than to make slime look so chic. You can see your favorite movies, TV, and music win big at the 39th Kids’ Choice Awards by streaming now the show with a Paramount+ subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3444. This '60s Sketch Show Became One Of The Biggest Flops In TV History

Networks tried all sorts of wild and outlandish ideas in the 1960s as they attempted to wrestle audiences' attention away from their rivals. This was the decade that gave us "My Mother the Car," the show for which Jerry Van Dyke turned down "Gilligan's Island" and which had him talking to his deceased mother via a car radio. The '60s also gave us Sally Field as a flying nun and sitcoms such as "The Hathaways" which featured a trio of trained chimpanzees who were treated like human children by their suburban "parents."

It was during this era that ABC decided to debut its surreal sketch comedy series "Turn-On," and when I say "series," I mean single episode. The show was so poorly received that it was yanked off the air after its debut installment in 1969, and rumors have since emerged that it became the only series in TV history to be canceled while it was airing. That might be a slight exaggeration, but not by much.

1969 was the year the world watched Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin land on the moon, "Star Trek" aired its final episode, and a man who actually did say yes to "Gilligan's Island," Alan Hale Jr. paid a visit to Sally Field's aforementioned airborne nun. But the year got off to a rocky start for ABC when it debuted one of the most notorious flops in TV history.

"Turn-On" was created by Digby Wolfe and George Schlatter, with the latter having created the hugely popular NBC series "Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In," aka "Laugh In," and the former having written for that same series. Their attempt to recreate the magic at ABC was a more lewd, surreal affair that aired once on Wednesday, February 5, 1969, and was never seen again.

Forgotten sketch comedy show "Weird TV" might be the weirdest series of all time, but "Turn-On" isn't far off. For one thing, its concept seemingly had little to do with comedy. As one of two computer engineers explains during its opening moments, "Turn-On" is "the first computerized TV show." What does that mean? Well, in a practical sense, it means every sketch unfolds in a vast all-white vacuum, where the supercomputer supposedly responsible for the show manifests sets and characters. Essentially, the whole thing takes place within the Construct from "The Matrix."

The opening sequence is a bewildering and surreal experience, featuring an array of diverse performers who appear within the Construct in quick succession, including puppets and a woman who plays a sousaphone before bursting into laughter — all scored by an electronic rhythm and synth hits that apparently have little to do with what's happening on-screen. It's the kind of thing that wouldn't be out of place on Adult Swim in the 2000s. In the late-1960s? Let's just say network affiliates were concerned about their ratings.

Things get a bit more blue as the debut episode of "Turn-On" continues. While "Laugh In" pushed boundaries, its ABC counterpart contained more sexual humor. And by "humor," I mean the word "Sex" flashing on-screen above guest host Tim Conway and Bonnie Boland and a "sketch" in which a woman tries desperately to get a box marked "The Pill" out of a vending machine. Meanwhile the show's credits continue to appear throughout the episode as suggestive cartoons pop up from time to time. This mixed media approach sort of calls to mind "Monty Python's Flying Circus," which also debuted in 1969. Unlike that now legendary series, however, "Turn-On" was cancelled almost immediately.

A stub in the February 7, 1969 edition of The Oregonian (via Newspapers.com) noted how local ABC affiliate KATU-TV did not air the "Turn-On" premiere at the behest of its management, who were evidently put off by a preview screening. "The station's management decided certain portions of the program 'are not in good taste and that these portions would be objectionable to a substantial and responsible part of the community,'" reads the report, which also noted that the Associated Press critic Cynthia Lowry had highlighted the "frankly blue jokes" that offended the Oregon affiliate management.

ABC seemed to agree, and it pulled the plug after the first episode went out. According to co-creator George Schlatter, though, the show's swift cancellation came down to a station manager in Cleveland who wanted to keep "Peyton Place," the show that would have run in the "Turn-On" time-slot, on the air. "He started calling the stations as it came across the country telling them they had to cancel this show," Schlatter stated. "[...] He convinced them to cancel the show, so by the time it got to California, the show was off the air, and some of it has never been seen." It's this recollection of events that seems to have birthed the "canceled while it was on the air" urban legend.

The attempts at transgressive humor and surrealism in "Turn-On" feel too try-hard, and the overall experience of sitting through the premiere episode is actually quite unpleasant. That said, it's not impossible to admire Schlatter and Digby Wolfe's attempt to do something different. What's more, we've gotten plenty of awful TV shows with 0% Rotten Tomatoes scores, and I'd much rather watch "Turn-On" than an episode of "Real Rob."

#3443. As Hollywood Battles AI, Pedro Pascal Says Making Behemoth! Filled Him with “a Tremendous Amount of Hope”

Pedro Pascal says that the character he plays in Behemoth!, his first leading film role, is the “closest thing to me that I’ve ever done.” And because of this, “the experience on set felt surreal in a sort of physically tangible way,” Pascal told the audience during a Q&A at Vanity Fair’s Screening Room at LACMA on Saturday.

Directed by Tony Gilroy, Behemoth! tells the story of Alex, a prodigal cellist who returns to Los Angeles and the world of Hollywood film scoring after decades performing symphonic work around the country.

“The mixing of my own life and this person's life, I've lived a very nomadic one. Don't ask me where home is. And so that felt like it was crossing personal lines for me in a way,” he continued during a post-screening discussion about the film, which featured Pascal and writer-director Tony Gilroy, moderated by VF's West Coast Editor John Ross.

Tony Gilroy and Pedro Pascal  at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

But according to Gilroy, their collaboration on the film almost didn't happen, thanks to an alleged missed connection at a Star Wars event.

“We went to a Star Wars convention in Tokyo where we took Andor,” recalled Gilroy. “There was this big Disney dinner so all the Star Wars people are there and [Pascal] was kind of busy and flighty.”

“I had the flu! I flew from London to Tokyo!” Pascal countered.

Gilroy continued: “He seemed like he was so hip that he didn't come to the dinner. I thought, 'Oh he's got such a great thing going on he's going to some better party; he's not going to a boring dinner.'”

As the audience laughed, Pascal was quick to set the record straight: “I cannot believe that you thought that I ditched that dinner. I was doing re-shoots of Fantastic Four!” he said. “They flew me to Tokyo that night and flew me back and I was on a set. [Turns toward the audience] Can you believe this?”

“Oh my God. I'm calling Kathy Kennedy [the President of Lucasfilm] right away,” Gilroy joked.

Luckily, the moviemaking stars (and schedules) aligned and the pair was able to make their personal, moving film with Pascal serving as Gilroy's “exclamation point. He has all the sadness and all the covering that this character needs to have and the nomadic life.”

Pedro Pascal, Tony Gilroy and John Ross at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Pascal and Gilroy formed a genuine bond and are very comfortable making playful jabs at each other, keeping things light but also expressing their gratitude for being able to make Behemoth! their way, in Los Angeles, where the film and television industry has been struggling to regain a foothold. Despite the challenges, past and present, they are holding out hope for human-made storytelling to foster further human connection.

“People's natural resistance to the robot takeover is clear,” said Gilroy when asked about the rise of AI. “I don't know what's going to happen. I really don't. The music scene out here is the coral reef of what's happened. It's been dying out here for the last 15 years… It's grooving a little bit now. I think people want humans. I don't know what's going to come back, but this is this incredibly humanizing element of movies that's happened. Can it be replaced by AI? Probably, quite shockingly, simply. There's probably an emotional amplitude knob on some f—ing algorithm, but this movie is organic.”

Pedro Pascal and Tony Gilroy  at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Pascal walked away from Behemoth! feeling optimistic. “The experience of shooting this movie definitely injected me with a tremendous amount of hope,” he said. “We weren't making money on this movie. Nobody was. And you had the most expensive people involved in this film because of their talent and their experience. So there was just this purity of love in the work from every single department, and that was incredibly contagious. And it was primarily locations, and so Los Angeles was just constantly revealing itself in all of these magical ways because we were so location-based. I had shot a series in Colombia for three seasons, and I would argue that the primary character of that series, Narcos, was shooting it in the country of Colombia because there was only one way of capturing that energy and that physical story. And LA did that as well. And then it's so tender. I think the story is incredibly tender. Would you ever expect it from this guy [gestures to Gilroy]?”

“Oh my God. What a cold, weird thing to say,” the director joked.

“There are other movies this year that I think in their own way, movies that I've seen this year that I love so much, that fight for humanity and the storytelling,” Pascal continued. “So I think that there is a sort of pushback that could be really, really thrilling as far as [creativity] is concerned, as far as politics is concerned. We want to be human beings and we want to be connected to one another and we want to tell each other's stories and witness each other's stories and we want to look after each other and all that shit. That's my hope.”

Tony Gilroy at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Gilroy had another suggestion: “Blow up the AI centers, man," he joked. “I don't mean to blow them up. I mean blow them up at the voting box. Go and vote and blow them up. Go see the Musk documentary, man. Go see that, watch the whole four hours. I'm pitching my movie [here], but watch that movie.”

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3442. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3441. She-Hulk's Tatiana Maslany Starred In A Must-Watch 2026 Apple TV Series

Tatiana Maslany's career exploded in the mid-2010s with her virtuoso multi-character work on BBC America's brainy sci-fi thriller series "Orphan Black." It was a very good show, but the deeper Maslany got into her roles, the more you wondered what she could do in a film or series where her performance prowess could be concentrated on one specific part. Indeed, she proved to be unsettlingly fierce as the vengeful Sister Alice on HBO's dark reinvention of "Perry Mason" and brought all the charm she could muster to Marvel Studios' irreverent "She-Hulk: Attorney at Law." Her talent was undeniable, but the projects weren't proper showcases of her astonishing ability.

This changed in 2026 with the premiere of Apple TV's comedy-thriller series "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed." The show stars Maslany as Paula Saunders, a fact checker (the noblest and most under-appreciated of journalistic professions) who's fighting for custody of her child while looking into the kidnapping and apparent death of a webcam model named Trevor (Brandon Flynn). No less an authority than Stephen King has effused that "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed" is "like Hitchcock came back to do it one more time." Its first season is streaming in its entirety on Apple TV, and it's officially coming back for more. So, now is the time to get caught up before you're 20 episodes deep down a binge hole.

The tone-setting pilot of "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed" was directed by David Gordon Green, who was once a Terrence Malick-ian stylist (see: early triumphs like "George Washington" and "All the Real Girls") before he segued to mainstream movies via broad stoner comedies like "Pineapple Express" and "Your Highness." But while "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed" possesses a bit of visual sophistication, it's the writing by series creator David J. Rosen and his staff that puts it over the top.

The casting is also key. Jake Johnson is deliciously antagonistic as Paula's ex-husband Karl, who's seeking sole custody of their child while she nurses her anguish with wine and digs into the fate of her newfound internet companion. Rosen and the show's writers pile the complications on with inventive abandon, and Tatiana Maslany surprises every step of the way as a protagonist we simply can't figure out.

"Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed," as mentioned, has been renewed for a second season, so Maslany will get another 10 episodes to explore possibly the best character she's ever been given to play. In the meantime, you should get out to see Noah Segan's "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York," where she is dynamite as John Turturro's daughter. The Maslany-ssiance is upon us.

Jeopardy! has been one of the best games shows on TV for quite a long time, but I’m rapidly learning it really does take a genius to spell out the show title. The other day, Ken Jennings spoke out about who he feels might be a good fit to step in and take over Jeopardy. The story was pretty widely read on CinemaBlend, and I was honestly kind of appalled to see some of the things people were typing in to get to our page.

In many careers, AI can sometimes be a helpful tool. Other times, it just highlights how bad people are at spelling the word Jeopardy. Thanks to Jeopardy’s current run on the 2026 TV schedule and a little help from AI, I now know the answer is: What is people are awful at it?

Here’s some of the MANY words people type in when it comes to Jeopardy! stories on CinemaBlend, as I saw when I looked in my summary that compiled the search terms people used. Please also note that, yes, all of these were in the Top 20 words people searched when looking for Jeopardy stories on site.

The only thing that gives me a little hope in this world is that the most popular search phrase for Jeopardy on CinemaBlend was in fact “jeopardy.” Yeah, that seems to be lowercase, but who cares? So, thank you to those who, like me, have firmly embedded the correct letter order into their brains. Whether or not you choose to use the exclamation mark feels like a personal choice, and not one to play out in this article.

I do think it’s also worth noting far fewer people type in the more outlandish spellings like “jeperty” than they do “Jeapardy.” The former spelling comes off like, “What accent are we speaking in?” The latter I really feel is people spelling out the show title exactly as it sounds. Regardless, again I’d like to point out these are all Top 20 search terms, so many people still search "jeperty" when looking into what Alex Trebek and co. are up to each week. Let that sit with you for a bit.

Listen, even with Google being significantly more unreliable with search than it has ever been in the company’s history, if you type in “jeperty” (I just did), it will ask if you were intending to search “Jeopardy,” so I see how there’s no real incentive to learn to spell the title of the excellent game show if you haven’t already. You’ll get what you are looking for either way.

I’m just saying though, if you’re invested in a game show series that prides itself on getting trivia facts right (even with the occasional poorly worded clue), maybe as a fan you should invest some time into learning how to spell the show's title?

Jeopardy!’s made some changes over the years, but changing the show’s spelling is probably never going to be one of them. Particularly, if you’re someone who has always wanted to compete on the game show, learning to spell it correctly is a cool thing to do.

#3438. Grey's Anatomy's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

"Grey's Anatomy" has been on the air since 2005, which is to say that it's experienced a handful of high highs and very low lows. Shonda Rhimes' medical drama, which premiered as a humble mid-season replacement and became one of the longest-running shows in the history of its medium, stars Ellen Pompeo as surgical intern turned award-winning general surgery attending and hospital owner Dr. Meredith Grey, who lives, loves, and learns alongside her colleagues and who has a knack for picking up cases that connect to her personal life in some way (as all of the doctors do, honestly).

(I say it "stars" Pompeo, but there's a technicality here; Pompeo technically left "Grey's Anatomy" as a series regular in Season 19 in 2022, but still provides voiceover and appears on the show often enough that she's still the main character for all intents and purposes.)

There are, if I'm being honest, many parts of "Grey's Anatomy" that one could identify as a major series downfall, like the time Dr. Isobel "Izzie" Stevens (Katherine Heigl) has ghostly physical intimacy with her dead fiancé before figuring out it's a brain tumor, the time a plane crash kills most of the show's surgeons, or every time a wedding is interrupted by a dramatic, ridiculous problem. The issue? Many of those lows are followed by highs (as Heigl's Izzie leaves the series, there's a hospital merger followed by a two-part finale in Season 6 that's a legitimate series highlight). That's why I'm pointing to a true point of no return for "Grey's Anatomy," and I am truly sorry to say that, despite my respect for the show's commitment to "realism" during a terrifying time for the entire world, the 17th season of the medical drama, also known as the "COVID season," is its downfall.

At face value, it makes total sense for a show like "Grey's Anatomy" to address the very real COVID-19 pandemic head-on; because the characters also dressed in protective medical gear, there was an air of practicality to the whole thing to boot. Here's the problem: the way they addressed it was straight-up bonkers. Partway through Season 17, Meredith develops a pretty serious case of COVID-19, which sidelines her (and, to an extent, Ellen Pompeo) for the remainder of the season's run, giving her a truly bizarre storyline where she sees dead loved ones in dreams in a random seaside location that fans like me simply refer to as the "coma beach."

Instead, fans of the series couldn't escape the pandemic surrounding them, and to make things worse, the show's best quality — its genuinely funny and smart dialogue — fell by the wayside in the process. Meredith may have eventually recovered from her severe case of COVID-19 and left the coma beach behind after Season 17, but the show wasn't able to pull off the same feat ... and as it continues, you can feel the slip in quality with each passing season.

I know better than most people that "Grey's Anatomy" has its fair share of detractors; I've been watching this damn show since it premiered, and it's one of the longest relationships of my life without comparison. I'll be among the first to admit that a lot of it is heightened and silly — and I got the chance to interview a friend who's a real doctor for this very site, who confirmed that it's the least realistic televised medical drama by a country mile.

Still, I'll go to the mat for a lot of seasons and episodes of "Grey's Anatomy." Shonda Rhimes, while she was still hands-on with the series, was a masterful dialogue writer and gave actors like Sandra Oh (who left the series after the Season 10 finale) unbelievably sharp monologues with regularity. The chemistry between most of the original actors was undeniably great, its jokes often hit their mark beautifully, and remember that two-part Season 6 finale I mentioned? "Sanctuary" and "Death and All His Friends," which chronicles a devastating mass shooting within the walls of the central hospital, is one of my favorite TV episodes ever ... and I'd stack it against plenty of prestige dramas any day.

That's what makes the fall of "Grey's Anatomy" particularly painful for me. I'm committed to the proverbial bit by still watching it, but it's painful. Instead of quippy dialogue that feels like a tennis match, characters over-explain everything in the preachiest way possible (like a female doctor explaining to a male counterpart that women get Brazilian butt lifts because society influences them into it). "Grey's Anatomy" is a pale shadow of what it once was, and it all started in Season 17.

#3437. Kate Middleton Announces First Major Trip Since Her Cancer Diagnosis

In unexpected news, Kensington Palace has just announced that Kate Middleton will accompany Prince William on his upcoming three-day official visit to Mumbai, India. The trip, which commences on Monday, will mark their first joint tour outside the United Kingdom in the past four years and represents a new milestone in Kate Middleton’s gradual return to public duties since she was diagnosed with cancer in early 2024 and began scaling back her official engagements.

Last May, the princess made a brief solo trip to Italy to learn about early childhood development, but this trip to India (a nine-hour flight from London) represents her first long-distance journey and her highest-profile diplomatic engagement since the Caribbean tour she undertook in 2022 and the Earthshot Awards gala she attended in Boston that same year.

"So proud, I'm very, very proud. She's been amazing. She's been through so much in the last couple of years, particularly," William shared on UK radio show Heart Breakfast in May, pleased to see that Kate was “gradually resuming” her travels. Still, the heir to the throne wanted to be cautious and warned that these visits are very taxing. "Away trips like that take a lot out of you," he explained. "So we have to balance that, make sure she's, she's OK and rested, but she's in good form."

The royal couple at the 2022 Earthshot Prize ceremony in Boston, their most recent joint trip abroad to date

The reason for the visit is the sixth edition of the Earthshot Prize, an initiative spearheaded by the heir to the British throne that each year awards one million pounds (about $1,323,249) to five innovative environmental projects and which, after making stops in other cities abroad such as Singapore, Cape Town, and Rio de Janeiro, is now taking place in the country that has produced the most finalists and winners in the competition’s history.

Standout finalists this year include Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, for its fleet of electric motorcycle taxis designed to reduce urban pollution, and Mahila Housing Trust, which installs reflective roofs capable of lowering the temperature inside homes by up to five degrees during extreme heat. The awards ceremony will be held this Tuesday evening at the Jio World Centre in Mumbai and will feature a performance by the band Take That and be attended by celebrities such as actor Rami Malek.

William and Kate during their 2016 visit to the Taj Mahal

Hours before the main event, the Prince and Princess of Wales will also preside over the first edition of the Earthshot Children’s Awards, a competition in which 15,000 schools from 24 Indian states have participated with environmental proposals designed by young people aged 9 to 17. The itinerary also includes a solo appearance by Kate Middleton, meetings with the Bollywood film industry, cricket-related celebrations, and a possible meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

In addition to being a positive sign regarding the princess’s health, this return to India holds strong symbolic significance for the couple, who last visited the country in April 2016. On that occasion, the then-Duke and Duchess of Cambridge visited the Taj Mahal and posed on the same white marble bench where Princess Diana was photographed alone in 1992—an image that has gone down in history as a reflection of the breakdown of her marriage to the now-King Charles III.

For the first time in eight years, Johnny Depp is back on top of the box office. Ebenezer is set to easily earn the most in theater grosses this weekend, and in doing so, it leads us all to a pretty obvious question. Is Johnny Depp back?

The Pirates Of The Caribbean lead was arguably the biggest movie star in the entire world for an extended period of time in the 2000s and 2010s before the fallout from his relationship with Amber Heard devolved into lawsuits, abuse allegations and tabloid headlines. Apart from the occasional artsy project here or there, he’s basically disappeared from theaters since Covid, but now, thanks to Ebenezer, he’s reminding everyone in Hollywood that he’s one of the most bankable stars on the planet.

You can take a look at the box office chart below, which has strong estimates thanks to some fine work over at The Numbers…

So, does this mean Johnny Depp is back? Well, the short answer is probably sort of, as some are predicting. The long answer is a little more complicated. Hollywood studios care about success more than any other metric, and there’s a lot of success here for Depp. Ebenezer was reportedly made for less than forty million dollars, and while critic reviews are middling, fan response has been terrific with an A- CinemaScore. The Hollywood Reporter claims half of the people who saw the movie this weekend cited Deep and his make-up heavy role as the primary reason they went, and Deadline further claims that the movie is putting people in seats across the entire country, not just in certain theaters that cater to certain demographics.

Add the positive word of mouth to the fact that it’s a holiday movie, and there’s every reason to believe Ebenezer will have a nice little extended run here in theaters. In short, it’s going to remind all of the executives and producers working in show business that Depp, despite his extended absence, is still one of the most bankable stars in all of Hollywood, even if we haven’t seen it since he was starring in the Fantastic Beasts franchise. He’s almost certainly going to get a few projects with elevated budgets coming out of this.

We already know one of those is for sure coming. Amazing Spider-Man director Marc Webb cast Depp in his next movie opposite Penelope Cruz called Day Drinker. That’s scheduled to hit theaters in March of 2027. I think it would be a surprise not to see him pick up commitments for a few more movies in the wake of this success too. I don’t think quite Marvel-style $250M event films, but I think they’ll be the type of projects that will get wide releases and have high upside. We’ll see though.

Outside of Depp, it was a pretty sleepy weekend at the box office. The Cat In The Hat held onto second place for its second consecutive weekend. It should continue doing solid business for at least a few more weeks as a great option for families. Godzilla Minus One fell quite a bit more, but that’s not a surprise for a foreign language film with a passionate target audience. The people who wanted to see that movie were always going to come out its first weekend, which is why it put up such a huge number en route to victory last weekend.

The story wasn’t quite as promising for some of the other new entries beyond Ebenezer. Ghost Soldier and How To Rob A Bank both struggled to find a wide audience and were barely able to top five million dollars. It’s unlikely either will be able to build off those disappointing numbers, but we’ll have to wait and see for next weekend when the latest edition of The Hunger Games looks poised to absolutely dominate in what could be a hundred million dollar money cannon.

#3435. Michael Bay And David Fincher Worked Together On An Unexpected Project That Still Holds Up Today

It's a rare thing when two equally well-known artists collaborate behind the camera. An auteur director team-up doesn't happen often, but it's certainly not unheard of. This year alone, we've seen the news that Steven Soderbergh is helping out Matt Reeves with "The Batman Part II," while Quentin Tarantino has handed the "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" character of Cliff Booth over to David Fincher for the upcoming Netflix spin-off. That latter director, as it happens, isn't a stranger to blending his creative DNA with another filmmaker. Famously, Fincher took over the troubled "Alien 3" after it had been developed for years, and inherited a script structure from director Vincent Ward that he isn't thrilled with to this day.

Around the same time, the budding film auteur (who was then still primarily known as a music video director) was approached to make a video for the rock star Meat Loaf's 1993 single "I'd Do Anything for Love (But I Won't Do That)." According to Craig Marks and Rob Tannenbaum's 2011 book "I Want My MTV: The Uncensored Story of the Music Video Revolution," Fincher and Meat Loaf's vision was pretty much what the finished video became, a Gothic riff on "Beauty and the Beast." However, Fincher's price tag caused Meat Loaf to look elsewhere for the video's director, turning to none other than an up-and-coming Michael Bay. (That's one version of the story, at least; more on that later.) Though the two didn't directly work together on it, the final video is, in its own weird way, a collaboration between the pair.

Although Michael Bay and David Fincher technically worked together at the production company Propaganda Films, their relationship was definitely more complex than just coworkers or collaborators. As various colleagues and other luminaries who worked at or with Propaganda detail in "I Want My MTV," Fincher was already a star internally given his extensive work on numerous successful music videos, and this was something that the young Bay was all too aware of. Employees told Craig Marks and Rob Tannenbaum that Bay would follow Fincher around the Propaganda offices constantly, with some people already considering him a younger version of Fincher.

This comparison came to a head when Meat Loaf approached Fincher with the gig for "I'd Do Anything for Love." According to Meat Loaf, the musician pitched Fincher with a "Beauty and the Beast" premise for the video, which Fincher allegedly loved. However, Fincher supposedly gave Meat Loaf a quote of $2.3 million, which Loaf balked at. He continued:

"So he came back a few days later and gave me a budget of $1.7 million. I said, 'David, we don't have that kind of money.' And Fincher said, 'Well then, get Michael Bay.' That's the last time Michael Bay was the cheaper option."

So, in Meat Loaf's version of the tale, the vision for the music video was the singer's idea, Fincher couldn't make the budget work, and the then-cheaper Bay got a hand-me-down project which he spun into a hit video.

In Meat Loaf's version of what happened with the "I'd Do Anything for Love (But I Won't Do That)" music video, the video was an idea had by the singer which changed hands from David Fincher to Michael Bay. However, according to Propaganda Films producer Joni Sighvatsson, it was his idea to pass the torch from Fincher to Bay, and as such, the video ended up being the one and only collaboration between the two filmmakers. As he recalled:

"Fincher was very expensive. He and the label were at an impasse over the Meat Loaf video, so I said, 'Why don't we just give this to Michael Bay?' Fincher gave it to Bay, we ended up spending $750,000, and it was a seminal video. Michael directed, and it was David's concept. That was the first and last time Fincher and Bay collaborated."

It's very possible that Sighvatsson is merely aggrandizing the story of the "I'd Do Anything for Love" video, making it sound like it's the result of two now-famous auteurs rather than just one. Or it's possible that he and Meat Loaf have hazy memories of what went down and how. All we really have to go on is the video itself, which remains one of the most visually rapturous short films of the 1990s. It's the most perfect visual encapsulation of Meat Loaf's sound, all theatricality and opera. It's got Bay's fingerprints all over it, of course, from a fetishization of hardware and sunsets to the way every woman is shot like a supermodel. Yet the video's Gothic flavor and trappings feel more Fincheresque. However it happened, the video is a gift, and we should probably thank all three men for it.

Guadagnino was joined by cast members Andrew Garfield (who plays Altman), Yura Borisov (who plays Sutskever) and Monica Barbaro (who plays Murati) for a post-screening conversation. The actors were challenged with preparing to play real people who they were not able to interact with ahead of time, instead relying on interviews, video recordings, and other research in order to get into their characters.

Andrew Garfield at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

“[Sam Altman] still is unknowable to me and I'm fascinated by him continuously and exponentially, for here until eternity," Garfield said about OpenAI's co-founder and CEO. “And it's important to try to understand because as Luca said, these are the kids that have the reins of the future and we've somehow allowed them to just hold onto them. And we've kind of given our autonomy over or it's been taken from behind our backs.”

He added: “It's a remarkable thing to have the resilience to go and sleep every night, knowing that you're really doing a lot of damage.”

Barbaro said the fact that Murati is very private helped her understand the former OpenAI CTO. “That is indicative of a kind of behavior and personality type and it pointed me in a certain direction as far as her values were concerned,” she said. “And we also had a lot of wonderful consultants, people who worked with them at OpenAI, but who were no longer with the company, kind of telling us what jokes and things that they would make.”

Yura Borisov at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

For Borisov, he hopes his portrayal does Sutskever justice and that people will want to know or understand him more. “I started to watch videos about him and looked at his social media, trying just to understand what he's talking about in his interviews,” the actor explained. "And step by step, as much as I discovered him, it was more and more scary for me because I started to respect and love him more and more."

Monica Barbaro, Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

The conversation had its own meta moment of sorts, when Barbaro posed a question to Guiducci about his decision to profile and feature Altman on the cover of Vanity Fair’s New Establishment Issue.

"You faced heat for presenting, maybe some people would say pedestalizing Sam Altman on the cover of Vanity Fair, what is your take on that?" Barbaro asked.

“I think that the magazine is an arena where these things have to play out,” Guiducci said. “It's so interesting to me to...have the [forthcoming] feature about this film in the issue that was preceded by one where I got to ask Sam about it." Guiducci continued: "Something about [taking Sam's] picture makes people feel, ‘Oh, that's the trophy.’ But photojournalism is journalism too. And I want people to be able to look back at the magazine and see a document of the time that we lived in," he said. "And also, if the photo is what helps me get the interview where we get to know more about these people, I'm going to take it.”

Monica Barbaro at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Other panel highlights included the subject of ChatGPT, which only Guadagnino admitted to using occasionally to ask about what’s ok to feed his dogs. He also addressed parting ways with the film's original studio partner Amazon and the fortuitous partnership that emerged with new distributor NEON.

“I think there is some kind of honor in the decision because they could have written off the movie and that's it,” he said about Amazon dropping the film from their slate. “And then they allowed us to find a partner and we found the best partner possible… They really believed in the movie.”

“They really made everything to get us to make the best movie we could,” he continued. "I only have good feelings toward my friends at Amazon. And in a strange way, I kind of understand the decision. Conflict of interest is a big thing.”

Luca Guadagnino at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

For years, Johnny Galecki was one of network television's biggest stars. His long-running sitcom, The Big Bang Theory was a hit, and hits bring fame and big paydays. Galecki could have taken his money and retired to a quiet life, and it turns out he wrestled with that decision between then and his latest gig as I just found out.

After seven years, Galecki is returning to acting by way of a theatrical production of Kowalski, and ahead of that, he talked to BroadwayWorld.com about why he chose this project. It's a fair question considering Big Bang spinoff series Stuart Fails to Save the Universe was part of the 2026 TV schedule, and I'm sure the creative team would've loved to have had him in Season 1. It turns out Galecki's decision to take this role was about more than just having a job, but wanting to see if he still had a passion for acting:

I knew I was in a position where I needed to learn if I still loved this work or not, honestly. I was beyond confused, I was concerned that this very first love of mine, and for a very long time my only love, seemed to have left me. And I was very content, but it was a bit of an identity crisis, I suppose. Or lack of knowing where I fit in the world, all of a sudden. I’d been doing theatre since I was seven and acting in various mediums since. And so, I just couldn’t figure it out, why I was entirely bereft of any interest in it any longer.

Galecki did indeed have options considering how much money he made from The Big Bang Theory. He reportedly makes a good deal more via reruns as well, so it's not like he needed to return to acting. And yet, as someone who has been working as an actor since childhood, it was a major part of his identity. Taking on this role was a test to see if he still loved being a performer, or if he needed to figure out what the next chapter of his life looked like.

And, with that, we now have him playing Tennessee Williams in Kowalski. It's not just a role, as Johnny Galecki pointed out, but one that will challenge his abilities as an actor:

I knew it needed to be something that would challenge me, something that I couldn’t hide behind, something that I couldn’t blame on it being underwritten, or a thankless role if it failed.

It's interesting to read that comment, and I do wonder if that's meant to be a pointed jab at what roles could've been waiting for him. It's easy to imagine that Stuart Fails to Save the Universe would love to bring in Johnny Galecki to reprise Leonard Hofstadter eventually, likely for one of the cameo roles we've seen others like Kaley Cuoco play. Is this a hint that co-creator Chuck Lorre shouldn't hold his breath about the Leonard actor reprising the role?

Should that be the case, he's not the only star with a stance on that. Sheldon Cooper actor Jim Parsons openly stated that he's done playing the character, which could put the Chuck Lorre series in a sticky situation. Stuart and friends need to find one of Leonard, Sheldon, or Howard to help set the universe right, and now it's looking like they may have to wait for a while.

All this to say, Johnny Galecki didn't openly besmirch his time working on Big Bang Theory. It's just hard not to think about that when it was the last role that he played before this big return to acting. It could be that this statement had nothing to do with his work on TBBT at all, but I can't help but wonder. Regardless of that, I'm glad he's found a role that he finds both challenging and exciting.

Catch episodes of TBBT by streaming them with an HBO Max subscription, or find them in syndication on various networks. Now that Johnny Galecki is acting again, I'll be curious to see if he starts to pick up more work! I guess it depends on how this acting stint goes.

#3432. 25 Years Later, Dumbledore's Best Sorcerer's Stone Line Is Still The Greatest Harry Potter Quote

In the wizarding world of Harry Potter, Albus Dumbledore is often referred to as one of the wisest and most powerful wizards in history ... so, it's lucky for the titular boy wizard that Dumbledore just happens to be the headmaster of his magical academy. In the original Harry Potter film franchise (which is getting a new life, in a way, with the forthcoming HBO Harry Potter TV show), Harry Potter, as played by Daniel Radcliffe (who may not watch the HBO reboot series), leaves his humdrum life with his mean non-magical relatives behind and starts attending Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, run by Dumbledore (Richard Harris in the first two movies before the legendary actor passed away in 2002, at which point Michael Gambon took over). There, he meets his best friends Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger (Rupert Grint and Emma Watson), learns how to cast magic spells, and has his first encounter, so to speak, with the Dark Lord Voldemort who tried to kill him as a baby.

Let's all be honest: Dumbledore sort of gets all the best quotes in the Harry Potter franchise. After all, his entire purpose is to dispense wisdom, so he drops a lot of stone-cold bangers. But what's his most memorable quote from the first movie, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" (which hit theaters on November 16, 2001)? We think we've pinpointed the perfect Dumbledore line from this film 25 years after its release.

During his first Christmas at Hogwarts, Harry receives the Cloak of Invisibility from an anonymous friend who leaves him a note telling Harry it belonged to his late father James. Emboldened by this gift, Harry starts exploring the halls of Hogwarts by night, and one evening, he stumbles upon a room containing a mirror that shows him not only James but his late mother, Lily, and even the extended family he never got a chance to meet. Understandably, the orphaned Harry becomes obsessed with visiting the mirror every night, and despite his confusion when Ron sees something completely different in said mirror, he returns until he finds Dumbledore waiting in the mirror's little room.

Dumbledore explains that it's called the Mirror of Erised, and it shows you your deepest desire. That's why Harry sees the family he never knew, and it's also why Dumbledore tells Harry, "It does not do to dwell on dreams, Harry, and forget to live." Dumbledore is right: Harry's devotion to seeing his family every night in the mirror is a short-term comfort that's terrible for the child's overall mental health, and even though Dumbledore tells him the mirror is moving to a different location anyway, Harry does promise not to look for it again.

Not only that, but in the third act of "Sorcerer's Stone" (as Harry looks for the titular object), we learn that the mirror is part of the defense system that keeps the Stone safe when Harry stares into it and receives the stone not to use but to have. In this way, Harry isn't dwelling on dreams, he's utilizing the mirror to achieve a vital goal.

#3431. Tallulah Willis: I Stayed Out Past My Bedtime to Celebrate My Mom at the Baby2Baby Gala

The whole endeavor began as it usually does, with a search for the perfect dress. Turns out it would be a yellow Carolina Herrera column-shaped confection (if you care), teetering on yellow satin pointed peekaboo-toe platforms, with my first press pass thudding around in my corresponding yellow duchess satin clutch.

Stylist Brad Goreski and his assistant Clarke, who work with my mother, Demi Moore, sourced the ensemble after finding Mom’s beautiful black ruffled two-piece (adorably also Carolina Herrera).

Around 6:50 p.m. on Saturday, my older sisters, Scout (in cocoa-brown beaded Elie Saab) and Rumer (in whimsical archival Vera Wang), florist Eric Buterbaugh, Brad, my mom and I are about to leave her house for the Baby2Baby Gala, an annual fundraiser for the non-profit that dedicated to providing diapers, clothing, and other basic necessities to children and families in need across the country.

Demi is taking photos against a pale brown backdrop when I hear her say, marginally worried, “Yes, the outfit is amazing, but they didn’t give me pockets.” I cannot fault her. A pocket, particularly in an evening gown, creates an entirely different architecture for one’s night.

When we make it to the Pacific Design Center in West Hollywood, Rihanna is blasting and a gorgeous electric General Motors car, part of the silent auction, is parked out front. I’m holding the bottom of my dress to avoid any “yard sales” on the carpeted floor when I hear, “Is it you? I hope it’s you!” It’s my very new, lovely friend Jackie Tohn, whom I met at a Nobody Wants This premiere party.

Inside, beautifully dressed people laugh and chat. I spot Miranda Kerr, who is both a Baby2Baby board member and major donor, and pass Nara Smith leaning over a dolled-up Elsa Hosk while “Espresso” blasts from overhead speakers.

Table 4 is front and center. Some could say the best seats in the house. Fitting, as Baby2Baby is honoring my mother with the Giving Tree Award tonight. The scene around our table is a frenzy of joyful energy. I make a beeline for Paris Hilton to thank her for the facial I received at her spa this week, while Dancing With the Stars alums Rumer and Jenna Dewan immediately pull out their phones to compare pictures of their kids.

Then I spot Sofia Richie Grainge and her husband, Atlantic Records CEO Elliot Grainge. I snake through throngs of elegant people and poke Elliot’s back twice. “Elliot, it’s Tallulah! We went to Wildwood together!” He instantly remembers me. “Tallulah was the cool girl in class,” he tells Sofia. I blush, but don’t feel the need to correct him.

Scout approaches and says, almost incredulously, “Hi, I’m Scout…you guys just signed me at Atlantic Records.” Elliot grabs her shoulders. “We’re so happy to have you. Are you happy with us?” She can’t say “yes” fast enough.

The program begins with Keke Palmer, who completely owns the stage, telling hilarious stories about her son before shifting into heartfelt candor about the gift of watching him grow. Kerry Washington thanks the sponsors and announces Baby2Baby’s new permanent headquarters, “a promise to millions of children. Not just for today, but for decades to come.”

Then Kelly Sawyer Patricof and Norah Weinstein, the organization’s CEOs, come to the stage, sharing the work—no, the magic—they have created over 15 years. Their first gala in 2012 raised $1 million. Last year’s raised $18 million. To date, they’ve distributed an astonishing 850 million essential items to people in need across all 50 states, responded to over 150 disasters, developed their own diaper production line during COVID, and expanded into mental health support for new mothers. The mission remains the same, but the scale is impossible to comprehend.

Now Rumer, Scout, and I are all crying during a short video about two families impacted by Baby2Baby. The feeling is palpable for the rest of the room.

As the live auction begins, I catch my mom discreetly reading over a printout of her speech. I don’t feel nerves coming off her, but a desire to match the elegance and integrity surrounding us.

Andrew Garfield takes the stage and speaks directly to my mom about the woman he knows. “She is a miracle,” he says.

Then it’s Demi’s turn. Holding her gleaming award in two hands, she thanks Andrew for carving out time amid his Artificial press tour. My mother adores Andrew, a feeling shared across our family.

Alone on stage in her Carolina gown (sans pockets), she asks everyone to breathe. “Inhale. Exhale.” That breath, she says, is the relief Baby2Baby provides when a mother no longer has to choose between dinner and diapers. “Your child matters, you matter, and you are not alone.” She leaves us with the idea that the essence of this work is to be remarkably human. Baby to baby, mother to mother, soul to soul.

Then Cardi B takes the stage and the atmosphere shifts with a jolt. Everyone is on their feet dancing. The official after-party begins, but I’m turning back into a pumpkin in towering satin stilettos. It was a remarkably beautiful night, and I’m left with the overwhelming desire to do more—to show up for someone who may not have the ability to show up for themselves or their precious loved ones.

But for this on-scene reporter’s inaugural correspondence, it was ultimately Baby2Baby2Bedtime.

For a number of families, the Christmas Season is all about Santa Claus and his gift-giving, but in Hollywood, Santa comes in the shape of Tom Cruise and his famous Christmas cake. Even Oprah Winfrey spends the holiday season waiting around for the legendary coconut cake to arrive on her doorstep. However, that seems to be changing this year now that Oprah has discovered the cake isn’t as exclusive as she thought.

That’s right: the Queen of Favorite Things and one of the most influential pop culture figures in the world used to wait all year for the infamous cake, just like Top Gun: Maverick co-star Glen Powell, longtime cake recipient Kristen Dunst, and, most recently, Digger scene partner Riz Ahmed. It’s hard to imagine any celebrity sitting around waiting for a cake to be delivered to them, especially Oprah, who has the ability to get whatever she wants. Yet that’s how all these stars have been spending their holiday season for several decades. Winfrey recently said:

In our house, we’d be like ‘Has the Tom Cruise cake come yet? Has the Tom Cruise cake come?’ And all these years, up until this year, I thought that Tom had the cake specially made for Tom, okay. Then I realized Tom has a bakery.

Now, I don’t think anyone thought Cruise was baking the Christmas coconut cakes himself. While he’s a talented actor and impressive stuntman, baking is time-consuming, and his schedule is usually packed. The identity of the bakery that prepares the cakes isn't a total secret, but now, Oprah has let that cat out of the bag on a grand scale.

During a podcast taping (shared on Instagram) where she had several caregivers in attendance, Winfrey revealed that Doan’s Family Bakery in Los Angeles was the one responsible for the Hollywood Christmas tradition and that anyone, including us normal people, can order the cake.

The Emmy-Award-winning host rejoiced at being able to order the cake whenever she wants. And in true Oprah fashion, her first instinct was to share the good news with those in her life:

I can get the cake! And so I started sending it to people, saying, ‘It’s the Tom Cruise cake.’

I'm wondering how Cruise will feel knowing that Winfrey has further emphasized the source of his famous gift With this, might he consider changing up his yuletide tradition and switch to something? It's hard to say, but even if he did, I'm sure he'd think of something just as special. After all, the Mission Impossible star is known for his generosity, like never forgetting to call Rosie O’Donnell for her birthday.

Winfrey shares the same generosity gene with Cruise, of course, so it’s no surprise that she instantly felt the need to share the cake with not only her friends and family, but also the caregivers in attendance for the podcast taping. Yep, everyone in the audience was promised a delicious coconut cake would be delivered to their door courtesy of Goldbelly. Check out the full clip below:

A post shared by The Oprah Podcast (@oprahpodcast)

I would be insanely jealous, but of course, the good news is that anyone can order the cake from Goldbelly right now. It’s not exactly cheap, but it might be worth it to say that I’ve tried the infamous “Tom Cruise Cake,” thanks to Oprah.

#3429. Nintendo Switch 2 Is Finally Getting Capcom’s Fastest-Selling Game Ever

Who needs GTA 6 when you can battle a dragon instead?

With the success of Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword, it's safe to say that Capcom has had a fantastic 2026. And the venerable developer's 2025 wasn't too shabby either. Last February, it released Monster Hunter Wilds for PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X. It went on to sell a whopping eight million copies in just three days, making it the company's fastest-selling game of all time. As of September 2026, Monster Hunter Wilds has sold 12.2 million copies, making it Capcom's 11th-best-selling game of all time. That number is set to go up significantly after Dec. 4, when it finally launches for Nintendo Switch 2.

Monster Hunter Wilds is the first game in the series to let players bring two weapons into the field — you can swap your loadout on the go thanks to your helpful bird friend known as a Seikret. It also adds pop-up camps to allow for a more seamless experience with less backtracking. The new wound system allows players to target a beast's weak points and dole out even bigger damage. You can play with couch co-op, or online with up to three buddies. Best of all, it doesn't matter which console they have — Monster Hunter Wilds supports cross-platform play between all versions, including Nintendo Switch 2,

Folks who pre-order the game ahead of the Dec. 4 launch, will also get a substantial discount. Through Dec. 3, Monster Hunter Wilds is on sale through the Nintendo eShop for $29.99, a 25% discount from its MSRP of $39.99. If you want to try before you buy, there's also a demo featuring the game's prologue available now on all platforms. Save data from the demo will transfer over to the full game if you decide to make a purchase.

If you're a die-hard Monster Hunter fan, the Gold Edition includes an extensive collection of more than 170 DLC cosmetics to customize your character. The Gold Edition isn't currently on sale, and retails for $79.99. That said, the DLC bundle on its own retails for a cool $59.99, so The Gold Edition is slightly cheaper than purchasing the DLC later.

Capcom also has big plans for Monster Hunter Wilds in 2027. The upcoming Ascendance DLC is billed by Capcom as a "massive expansion," which will add a new location called the Skybound Eyrie, which is a network of ancient floating island ruins. It will also introduce challenging Master Rank quests and new monster types. Back in February, series director Ryōzō Tsujimoto said Ascendance will be comparable in scope to previous paid expansions, like Monster Hunter World's massive Iceborne DLC.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

#3428. How To Rob A Bank Pays Tribute To A Bruce Willis Movie With A Clever Easter Egg

There's something of a paradox when it comes to making legitimately good crime action movies. On the one hand, most filmmakers want the action to be as accurate and based in reality as possible, whether it be robbing a bank, taking down a security truck, or whatnot. On the other hand, they don't necessarily wish to inspire criminals who would copycat a crime they happened to see in a movie, especially as that's an instance where all publicity doesn't necessarily equal good publicity. (Remember the brouhaha over a crime allegedly inspired by 1995's "Money Train," a case which only just reached a resolution a few years ago?)

The irony of the new crime action film "How to Rob a Bank" is that it intentionally wishes to exist on the edge separating these two sides. The film, written by Mark Bianculli and directed by David Leitch, concerns a group of friends who, upon becoming radicalized by the various injustices of the current U.S. wealth gap, decide to become bank robbers. Their gimmick is hiding their crimes in plain sight, filming themselves in the act and detailing exactly how they did it for their YouTube channel (all while hiding their identities, naturally).

Thus, Leitch and Bianculli have to include a bunch of real-world tactics and hardware without going too far. To help accomplish this, they have their bandits (who've dubbed themselves the Wolf Pack) borrow a technique from the sequel to the bonafide action classic that is "Die Hard," i.e. 1990's "Die Hard 2." And while the characters never mention the movie on-screen, the inclusion of a trick used by that film's villains works as both an Easter egg homage to that movie as well as a bit of real-world verisimilitude, as this particular tactic does sound like it could actually work.

In "Die Hard 2," the terrorists holding Washington Dulles International Airport hostage around Christmas are former U.S. Army soldiers who've been corrupted by a military drug lord. After Bruce Willis' John McClane their plans while getting a quip or two in, the airport brass call in a military counter-terrorism unit. Then, during the subsequent firefights between the counter-terrorism unit and the terrorists, each group makes a point of switching to clips for their machine guns labeled with blue instead of red stripes. Eventually, McClane discovers this code means blue for blank rounds and red for live rounds, revealing that both units are working together.

While the terrorists in "Die Hard 2" have devised a fairly elaborate scheme, the blank-vs-live rounds element seems fairly simple and self-explanatory. In other words, it has an authenticity about it, which is why its use in "How to Rob a Bank" feels smooth rather than belabored. The Wolf Pack want to make their robberies feel threatening to the authorities they encounter and only elect to use live rounds to save their own skins. As such, adopting the blue and red labeled gun clips makes for an easy to understand visual code, so much so that the characters in the film barely have to explain it to the audience.

For those who know "Die Hard 2," this is a cute Easter egg calling back to that film's intuitive code system. Yet, for those who don't know, the element still completely works, and its realism adds to the movie's credibility. Who knows if anyone has used it (or will) in real life, but it helps "How to Rob a Bank" exist on that edge.
