#3406. The Office's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

In 2005, two TV shows premiered as mid-season replacements, which isn't usually a great sign for said series' potential longevity. One was "Grey's Anatomy" on ABC, which became one of the longest-running TV shows in history. The other? "The Office," an adaptation of Ricky Gervais' British series of the same name that became one of the biggest hits in the entire history of NBC.

With Steve Carell leading the way as the well-meaning but unbelievably buffoonish Michael Scott (the regional manager of the Scranton branch of paper company Dunder-Mifflin), the American version of "The Office" made it past a somewhat rocky first season and became a small-screen staple, launching the careers of Carell and co-stars like John Krasinski, B.J. Novak, and Mindy Kaling. (It also, arguably, led to an uptick in small-screen mockumentaries like its successors "Modern Family," "Parks and Recreation," and "Abbott Elementary.") After running for nine massively successful seasons, "The Office" wrapped up its run in 2013 with a finale that actually stuck the landing ... but the road to the finish was rough.

You can argue all you want about how to pinpoint the downfall of "The Office," but I won't entertain any debate. The answer is that "The Office" hit a major point of no return in Season 7 when Carell left the show, which led to Michael Scott moving away from Scranton and decamping to Colorado. Despite its best efforts to continue relatively uninterrupted, the series just didn't functionally work without Michael Scott.

It's perfectly understandable that Steve Carell wanted to leave "The Office" behind after spending so long playing one character. (He's a pretty talented guy, after all.) Still, the show should have just ... ended. Even the lead-up to Michael's exit was, all things considered, sort of bleak. This is conjecture on my part, but it really felt like, in Season 6 episodes like "Scott's Tots" and "Koi Pond," the show was leaning into Michael's worst impulses and making him straight-up unlikable instead of silly but well-meaning.

The reason for Michael's departure, however, is undeniably sweet. After human resources representative Holly Flax (Amy Ryan) makes her debut appearance in the Season 4 finale "Goodbye Toby," she and Michael ultimately fall in love before she gets moved back to her original Dunder-Mifflin branch in Nashua due to higher-ups fretting about the pair's relationship. Then, in Season 7, she returns to Scranton, and while Holly and Michael have been broken up for some time when she finds herself back in northeastern Pennsylvania, they get back together ... but their happy ending is threatened when family troubles mean that Holly needs to move back to Colorado.

Thankfully, by this point in the series, Michael is back to being essentially likable again, so he does the right thing: He proposes to Holly and tells his colleagues he's moving with her. His final episode, "Goodbye Michael," is incredibly moving, especially the moment where Pam Beesly-Halpert (Jenna Fischer) says goodbye to Michael in the airport. Yet, the show loses its footing forever as he departs, and it never recovers. Why? Well, the string of potential replacements for Michael is lackluster at best and egregiously unfunny at worst.

One of the many crimes committed in the final two seasons of "The Office" is that the show managed to make English treasure and comedy legend Catherine Tate actively exhausting, but I'm getting ahead of myself. First, "The Office" pulls out the stops by bringing in Steve Carell's "Anchorman" cohort Will Ferrell (the proverbial comedic big gun) as Deangelo Vickers, a deeply confusing and unfunny new manager who's written off after getting a brain injury during a pickup basketball game. From there, Creed Bratton's erratic "Creed Bratton" briefly becomes the manager (and it goes just as well as any "Office" fan would expect), and while James Spader's unfathomably bizarre Robert California has his moments as one of Creed's successors, he doesn't work, either.

Ultimately, Tate's Nellie Bertram and Ed Helms' Andy Bernard are the people who run the Scranton branch most consistently in Michael's absence, and not only are they both terrible at the job, neither of them recreates the magic that only Carell could bring to the series. Instead, Tate's Nellie is, at varying times, exceedingly ridiculous or shrewd (it depends on the episode you're watching), whereas Andy is so expendable that "The Office" briefly writes him off. (This was done to free up Helms to go film "The Hangover Part III" at the time.) Moreover, everyone eventually gets simplified to the point of parody (i.e. Flanderized, to use a popular "Simpsons"-inspired term), so much so that Andy, himself an Ivy League graduate, becomes borderline illiterate. Put simply, it's a mess.

#3405. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3403. Robert Downey Jr.'s 90s Supernatural Fantasy Flop Is Worth Revisiting

It's no exaggeration to say that Ron Underwood's 1993 fantasy comedy film "Heart and Souls" boasts one of Robert Downey Jr.'s best performances. He wasn't nominated for an Oscar (although he surely deserved to be), but at least he won a Saturn Award for Best Actor for his work on it. Yet, because it flopped at the box office, it's rarely ranked among Downey's best movies of all time.

Downey stars in "Heart and Souls" as Thomas Reilly, an arrogant yuppie who is possessed by a pack of friendly ghosts that have been following him since birth. Thus, over the course of the movie, Downey takes on the speech patterns and affectations of his ghostly co-stars (Kyra Sedgwick, Tom Sizemore, Alfre Woodard, and Charles Grodin), and he does so with utter aplomb. The result is a film that's funny, profound, and sentimental in equal measure. It has the mood and structure of a high-concept Hollywood comedy, but with a toe rooted in the warmth of something like "It's a Wonderful Life." Plus, its view of the afterlife is pretty light and fun and makes sense in a secular way.

The world of ghosts plays by its own rules in "Heart and Souls," but it's not oblique or difficult. Here, the living and the dead are cosmically bound, like sometimes-invisible family members contracted to make wrongs right and assuage regrets. It's a positive and touching movie with its messages tucked in between hilarious bouts of Downey zaniness. Ultimately, Thomas learns to be less selfish and far more understanding to his girlfriend, Anne, played by Elisabeth Shue. See what I mean about the amazing cast?

"Heart and Souls" opens in 1959 and introduces us to our ghost characters while they're still alive, each of them boarding the same ill-fated bus. Julia (Kyra Sedgwick) is hoping to find her boyfriend, whose marriage proposal she regrets rejecting. Penny (Alfre Woodard) has to work a late shift away from her sons. Milo (Tom Sizemore) is a small-time crook who conned some valuable stamps from a local kid and regrets it. And Harrison (Charles Grodin) is a singer who just fled an audition due to overwhelming stage fright.

Sadly, their bus driver, Hal (David Paymer), gets distracted and crashes the vehicle, killing everyone on board in front of a car carrying a woman in labor. The four passengers, now ghosts, then witness a young Thomas being born. Over time, the ghosts realize they're physically bound to Thomas (meaning, they get dragged along if he walks away) and grow up with him. However, because they're invisible to everyone but him, Thomas' parents assume he's mentally unwell. So, the ghosts eventually decide to become invisible to Thomas to protect his mental health.

Fast-forward to the present, and the ghosts are unexpectedly visited by the now-deceased Hal. He tells them that Thomas is their "earthly vessel" and they should've been spending their time using him to right the wrongs in their lives so they can finally enter the afterlife. Now, they have to solve their biggest regrets in the next few days or risk oblivion.

Thomas, meanwhile, has become a heartless foreclosure banker who believes he had schizophrenia as a child, causing him to see his childhood "friends." But after the ghosts reappear to him, he eventually accepts that, yes, they are real, and he agrees to help them solve their earthly problems and ascend.

I maintain that "Heart and Souls" is one of the best films of its year. And, to reiterate, Robert Downey Jr. gives an Oscar-worthy performance in it. However, he wouldn't win his Oscar until "Oppenheimer" decades later, having only just been nominated for an Academy Award for the first time right before "Heart and Souls" came out for his turn as Charlie Chaplin in Richard Attenborough's biopic "Chaplin."

Overall, critics were mixed on "Heart and Souls." Most reviews tended to praise the performances from the movie's gaggle of stars, as seen in Michael Wilmington's review for the Los Angeles Times. He noted that "Heart and Souls" was about the spiritual crisis of modern humanity, "buried under several tons of Hollywood slick." But, he added, you should trust the film's actors. To quote him directly:

"There's one great opportunity for virtuoso fun here: the chance handed Downey to impersonate the mannerisms of his co-stars whenever one takes over his body. With [...] delicate, precise mimicry [...] he slips delightfully into [Alfre] Woodard's feline assurance, [Tom] Sizemore's swagger, [Kyra] Sedgwick's sexiness or [Charles] Grodin's repressions. The character he's playing — the same kind of languid, self-obsessed, inwardly anxious hedonist he played throughout the '80s — isn't deep, but Downey digs something comic out of his superficiality."

If that sounds fun or intriguing, it can serve as your "in" to "Heart and Souls." You may discover a new gem.

#3402. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3400. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3399. Why Walter Koenig Held His Tongue To Keep His Star Trek II: The Wrath Of Khan Role

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan" gives Pavel Chekov (the late Walter Koenig) one of his meatier arcs in any of the "Star Trek" films. In his new assignment as first officer of the USS Reliant, Chekov and his captain, Terrell (Paul Winfield), scout planets as a testing site for the Genesis device. But what they think is planet Ceti Alpha VI is actually the barren Ceti Alpha V, where the Enterprise left Khan Noonien Singh (Ricardo Montalbán), the 20th century's most infamous genetically engineered warlord, and his followers at the end of the episode "Space Seed."

Chekov and Terrell are captured and brainwashed via Ceti eels implanted in their ears. Khan and his people thus seize the Reliant, and boom, we have our movie. The sequence on Ceti Alpha V is predicated on Khan and Chekov recognizing each other. When Chekov and Terrell come across Khan and co.'s makeshift home, Chekov recognizes the name "Botany Bay" (the name of the sleeper ship where the Enterprise found Khan in "Space Seed"). Once the pair are captured, Khan recognizes Chekov and proclaims "I never forget a face."

Chekov also speaks to and of Khan as if he witnessed the events of "Space Seed." Except, technically, he didn't. "Space Seed" was made in "Star Trek" Season 1, and Koenig/Chekov only joined the cast in Season 2. Ergo, he obviously never appeared in "Space Seed" and shared no screentime with Khan. Oops!

Over 40 years later, Trekkies still note the inconsistency and rationalize it. Koenig, for his part, has said he recognized the error when he read the script, but chose to stay silent to preserve Chekov's role. Considering how often "Star Trek" overlooked Chekov, it's hard to blame him.

"Wrath of Khan" writer Harve Bennett wasn't a "Star Trek" fan when he took the job. That worked for the best. "Wrath of Khan" is widely credited for revitalizing "Star Trek" and part of that is because Bennett and director Nicholas Meyer brought fresh eyes. To that end, they couldn't expect everyone who would go see "Wrath of Khan" had previously seen "Space Seed." So, the movie doesn't rely on the episode outside of its big picture story details, which are easily explained via some dialogue in Khan's first scene. (I saw "Wrath of Khan" before "Space Seed" as a kid, and I followed the former just fine.)

But Chekov knowing Khan is the kind of detail that evidently slipped by Bennett. Koenig, who was asked to read the script and give it a "Trekkie read," had a vested interest in not pointing out the mistake. As Koenig put it when interviewed in "The Fifty-Year Mission: The First 25 Years" by Edward Gross and Mark A. Altman: "I was faced with the ethical dilemma of mentioning it to Bennett or letting it go. I chose survival as opposed to ethics."

Chekov is the only member of the "Star Trek" main cast who shares physical screentime with Khan in the movie. (Khan and Kirk only ever talk via viewscreens and communicators.) It's also Khan's first appearance in the movie, as well as the scene from "Wrath of Khan" that I rewatch the most in isolation. Montalbán's performance, savoring every line, is just spectacular. I can see why Koenig would, as an actor, want the chance to be in a scene as strong as that one, and he holds his own balancing Chekov's courage and fear.

For Koenig's part, his cheeky theory to explain away this inconsistency was that Chekov once made Khan wait an uncomfortable amount of time to use the Enterprise's restroom. "Chekov was on the Enterprise, just offscreen" has become the go-to fanon answer. The novel "To Reign in Hell: The Exile of Khan Noonien Singh" by Greg Cox legitimizes that; Chekov is said to have led a failed effort to retake the Enterprise from Khan, and is part of the detachment that helps Khan and his people get settled on Ceti Alpha V.

Despite the continuity gap with "Space Seed," Chekov was the best pick among the main characters as the one captured by Khan. Amusingly, this is precisely because he's the most ancillary one. The Enterprise can function without him in a way it wouldn't without Spock (Leonard Nimoy) or Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley).

While Koenig evidently feared that they would swap Chekov's part out in the script, the only other main character who could work would be Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), which would add some icky subtext to Khan violating her body with the Ceti eels, or Sulu (George Takei). With Sulu, you run into the same problem because he wasn't in "Space Seed" either! While Sulu/Takei was part of the show in Season 1, he was absent for that particular episode. If it had been Sulu who landed on Ceti Alpha V with Terrell and met Khan, you might be getting forum posts highlighting that inconsistency today.

Walter Koenig may have created a small problem in "Wrath of Khan" by staying silent here, but he helped fix a much bigger one, too, by suggesting moving Spock's death to the end of the film.

#3397. Prime Video's Near-Perfect Game of Thrones Replacement Officially Arrives in 2 Months

Time to start sharpening your bloodaxe...

Time to start sharpening your bloodaxe...

A weak king rules over a cobbled-together kingdom that's already coming apart at the seams. Various heroes and villains compete and scheme to claim the throne. A new challenger rises up from across the sea, full of vengeance and bloodlust... If that sounds like the premise of Game of Thrones, well, that's because it is, but it's also the set-up for Prime Video's thrilling new action drama from one of the 21st-century's most successful (and underappreciated) showrunners.

Back in October, during New York Comic Con 2026, I attended an early screening of Bloodaxe, a new series from Vikings creator Michael Hirst and his son Horatio. Based on the show's first episode, which premieres Jan. 20, 2027 on Prime Video, the streamer might just have a new Game of Thrones-level hit on its hands. Or at the very least, an entertaining show for VIkings fans.

Bloodaxe tells the real-life story of Eric Haraldsson (aka Eric Bloodaxe), who lived during the 10th century. When we first meet Eric (Xavier Molyneux), he's already a powerful warrior and a popular figure in Viking society. His father, King Harald (Jesper Christensen), is beginning to lose his grip on the Norwegian kingdom he spent his life uniting. Eric expects to be named successor, but then Harald reveals that his younger son Haakon (Levi Miller), who spent his childhood in England learning the art of diplomacy, will be king instead. Meanwhile, Eric's statuesque wife Gunnhild (Bridgerton's Jessica Madsen) has her own schemes in mind to elevate her husband to the throne, while her exiled brother Egil (Kārlis Arnolds Avots) plots his own ascension to power from nearby Iceland.

That might sound like a lot of plot to pack into one hour of television, and… it is. But Michael and Horatio Hirst deftly plunge us into this world headfirst like a Viking warrior sprinting into the frigid Norwegian Sea. Like Game of Thrones, Bloodaxe pulls out all the stops in its opening act to win over its audience. That means plenty of political intrigue, shocking deaths, stunning scenery, meticulous production design, beautiful actors, and gratuitous sex scenes.

The landscapes are particularly stunning. While much of what's meant to be Norway was filmed in Ireland, with rugged Scandinavian mountains added in digitally, Egil's scenes were shot on location in Iceland — you just can't fake those scorchingly beautiful geothermal pools and glaciers. The cast ain't bad to look at either. Molyneux resembles a lost Hemsworth brother (his breakout role was as a contestant on Australian Big Brother), while Miller bears a striking resemblance to Kit Harington's Jon Snow. Life-sized boats and massive sprawling sets complete the experience. It all makes Bloodaxe very easy on the eyes.

That helps when the plot quickly gets down into the muck. While Bloodaxe technically hinges on palace intrigue, this is a gritty and grimy world with its own morals and ethics that feel alien by 21st-century standards. The core story of multiple factions vying for power and bracing for all-out civil war also feels particularly Game of Thrones-esque. There's even a few prophecies and witchy rituals thrown in for good measure, all playing out against the backdrop of a larger theological battle between Viking paganism with its pantheon of Norse gods and the rising tide of Catholic monotheism. (An interesting wrinkle: Of the two, the Vikings were arguably more progressive for their time, with an egalitarian society that treated men and women equally.)

Perhaps most interesting of all, Bloodaxe is based on a true story. The writers are pulling directly from history (as recorded by Icelandic clerics and scholars several hundred years later). This also means that, like with Game of Thrones, if you're curious about what ultimately happens to Eric and the rest of the gang, you can always read ahead and find out. But why ruin the fun?

All eight episodes of Bloodaxe will make landfall on Jan. 20, 2027, with season 2 already in production. So while you could head to Wikipedia right now to find out whether Eric Bloodaxe becomes king or not, you may have a lot more fun watching his journey play out onscreen.

And assuming the showrunners get to tell a complete story, Bloodaxe has one big advantage over Game of Thrones. This story has been set in stone for over one thousand years, which means it will be very hard for Michael and Horatio Hirst to bungle the ending.

Bloodaxe premieres Jan. 20, 2027 on Prime Video.

#3396. Stephen King Named This Alfred Hitchcock Thriller As One Of His Favorite Scary Movies

Back in 2017, IndieWire amassed a list of Stephen King's favorite scary movies based on the titles he had either previously recommended on social media or written about in his 1981 non-fiction book "Danse Macabre." Among the many, many films included were Ridley Scott's "Alien," Mario Bava's "Black Sunday," Brian De Palma's "Carrie" (itself based on King's own litany of feminine rage), and George A. Romero's "Dawn of the Dead."

Somewhat surprisingly, Alfred Hitchcock's 1972 serial killer "Frenzy" made the cut as well. "Frenzy" was Hitchcock's penultimate film and is famously the only one of Hitchcock's movies to receive an R rating in the United States. Indeed, one might be startled to see actual on-screen nudity in a film from The Master of Suspense. The murders in "Frenzy" are notably brutal, too, and the movie, quite shockingly, contains scenes of sexual assault. This was clearly an attempt by Hitchcock to push the envelope, and one can only speculate if he was drawn to the film's twisted serial killer mentality, the sweatiness of the overall picture, or its sheer amount of on-screen violence.

"Frenzy" tells the story of Richard Blaney (John Finch), a sad-sack and impoverished London-based former military man who is accused of sexually assaulting his ex-wife, Brenda (Barbara Leigh-Hunt), and using a necktie to strangle her to death. However, the necktie is connected to a string of other murders that have been committed all over the city, as the real killer is Richard's creepy friend Bob Rusk (Barry Foster).

As with so many other Alfred Hitchcock movies, the main character in "Frenzy" becomes a falsely accused man on the run (see also: "The Wrong Man," "Stage Fright," "The 39 Steps," "Young and Innocent," "North By Northwest," "Saboteur," "I Confess"), and he has to elude capture to clear his name. Along the way, Richard ends up finding an ally and lover in his former co-worker Babs (Anna Massey) ... although, with Rusk still engaged in his murderous shenanigans, that doesn't bode well for her.

Hitchcock films excel at making audiences unwittingly root for the bad guy (see "Dial M for Murder" and "Psycho" for two better-known examples), and "Frenzy" includes a sequence where Rusk has to retrieve a personal item of his from a victim whose body he has already disposed of. Because of this, viewers are forced to watch as he struggles with the tension of having to retrieve the incriminating evidence, and while we might not feel sympathy for Rusk, we do become involved in his plight. (It's one of the most noteworthy scenes in Hitchcock's filmography.) You can see, then, why Richard turns to Rusk for help at one point, not knowing that his friend is the murderer.

The final act of "Frenzy" gets a little involved and maybe spins a little too far off with its trials and prison sentences, but know that the ultimate conclusion is very satisfying. It's a tonally unique movie as well, feeling very loose and 1970s-y. And where many of Hitchcock's previous films felt mannered and polite despite involving murder and fetishes, "Frenzy" is comparatively casual, focusing more on Rusk's overcooked murderous mindset and the sexual element of his killing spree.

What many cineastes saw as the sexual subtext of Alfred Hitchcock's previous movies becomes text in "Frenzy." By the 1970s, the filmmaker could afford to be a little more frank. The murder scenes, more so than in any other Hitchcock movie, "Psycho" included, are brutal and unsettling. There's even one particularly memorable shot in "Frenzy" of one of Rusk's victims, freshly dead, with her eyes wide and her tongue lolling out, that will remain in your nightmares for quite some time. This is not the balletic, aesthetic, obfuscated violence of Hitchcock's earlier movies. This is disturbing.

Many critics responded very positively to "Frenzy" at the time. Roger Ebert gave the film four stars (out of four), writing that it was both a departure for Hitchcock and a return to form. As he put it:

"This is the kind of thriller Hitchcock was making in the 1940s, filled with macabre details, incongruous humor, and the desperation of a man convicted of a crime he didn't commit. The only 1970s details are the violence and the nudity (both approached with a certain grisly abandon that has us imagining 'Psycho' without the shower curtain). It's almost as if Hitchcock, at seventy-three, was consciously attempting to do once again what he did better than anyone else."

Ebert added that "Frenzy" possesses a nice macabre sense of humor, another feature Hitchcock's fans appreciate from the Master. Vincent Canby, writing for the New York Times, listed "Frenzy" as one of the 10 best films of its year, and it was a hit at the box office to boot. (There's a reason we here at /Film once listed it as one of Hitchcock's 20 best movies.) Clearly, Hitchcock hadn't lost his talent for snagging audiences.

#3394. If You Liked Colleen Hoover's Verity, Watch Dakota Johnson's Acclaimed 2025 Movie Next

If you liked seeing Dakota Johnson starring in a twisted psychosexual drama like "Verity," which is based on the novel by Colleen Hoover, you might want to check out the more adult romantic drama "Materialists," Celine Song's acidic essay on modern dating from 2025. /Film's Bill Bria said in his review of "Materialists" that it was structured like a typical rom-com, but more heartfelt, full of yearning and depth.

More than anything, though, "Materialists" deals with a deeply cynical approach to romance, just as the title would lead you to believe. It's about how modern matchmaking has become a painfully specialized industry because modern adults have become all too fixated on the superficial qualities — and the earning power — of their potential mates. Johnson plays a cold-hearted matchmaker-for-the-rich named Lucy who has trouble weaning her male clients off of the idea of dating younger women exclusively. The movie itself seems to wince whenever one of Lucy's clients says they desire a woman who is "fit"; those characters might as well be yelling "no fat chicks."

Over the course of the film, Lucy finds herself torn between two potential boyfriends who have both appeared — or reappeared — in her life. On the one hand, she can pursue Harry (Pedro Pascal), an unbearably handsome, unfathomably rich, and suitably tall man who ticks all the boxes on the average dating profile requirement list. On the other hand, she has reconnected with her ex-boyfriend John (Chris Evans), a struggling actor who was always disorganized and never wealthy, but who loved her deeply. Does Lucy choose a life of poverty undergirded by true love, or does she follow her more cutthroat, materialistic instincts, and pursue the wealthy man who can give her a life of luxury?

For long portions of "Materialists," Lucy's choice seems obvious. Harry may not have the same kind of passion as John, but he is definitely interested in Lucy, and he is happy to share his wealth. There is a coldness, however, to his well-moneyed lifestyle, and something vaguely transactional about his love affair. She also becomes startled when she learns a secret about Harry that we won't spoil here. She begins to question if her attraction to him is genuine, or if it just checks the right boxes on a typical dating profile.

As "Materialists" unspools, however, it begins to skew away from the acidic nature of its opening act and begins strolling toward a drama about romantic truthfulness. Lucy is also thrown for a loop when she unwittingly matches one of her long-single clients Sophie (Zoë Winters) with a man who sexually assaults Sophie. Lucy subsequently doubts her every romantic instinct, and a portion of "Materialists" becomes about Lucy trying to reach out to Sophie to make amends. Perhaps she can mitigate her bad romantic instincts by being a genuine friend to this woman.

The ultimate answer is perhaps a little treacly, but Lucy finds herself drawn back to John. The pair had previously broken up over his incapacity for amassing wealth and her frustrations with the boring everyday financial struggles they went through. Now, however, she is beginning to appreciate the nature of human connection, and John looks more and more romantically alluring.

Of course, one could argue that Dakota Johnson, in being torn between Chris Evans and Pedro Pascal, is hardly in an unenviable place. We should all be so lucky to have two devastatingly handsome movie stars equally eager to court us.

"Materialists" was a pretty big hit, making almost $108 million worldwide on a relatively small budget of only $20 million. When the movie hit streaming, "Materialists" became a hit for HBO Max. The film isn't terribly deep in its commentary on the foibles of modern romance and the shallowness therein, but it's at least about something, and it features multiple beautiful people alternately romancing one another. It also, according to our exclusive interview with writer/director Celine Song, was modeled on a film noir, giving the film an alluring, mysterious quality. All those elements put together seemingly were what drew people out in such numbers.

Critics largely liked "Materialists," as evidenced by its 77% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 307 reviews. Angelica Jade Bastién, writing for Vulture, felt that the movie didn't delve deeply enough into its own thesis that modern romance is directly tied to capitalism. Indeed, she wrote that, in its last act, the film "pivots to a more conventional romantic narrative of the kind it had promised to upend, if not outright critique."

Stephanie Zacharek, writing for Time Magazine, was more generous, writing that Celine Song is speaking very much to the moment, analyzing what romance means in an ego-driven and money-driven world of Instagram and an easily reduced sense of personal value. "That's the world 'Materialists' takes place in," Zacharek writes, "and Song sees what's funny and what's terrible about it at once—even as she acknowledges that it's human to yearn for beautiful things, and for comfort. She's chosen the perfect actors for this enterprise."

If you want a romance that mixes acid with some thoughtfulness, check out "Materialists."

#3393. iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, details here

iOS 27.2 recently launched with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s new.

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

Without the redesigned Health app, none of the new features appeal to me all that much. But performance improvements, bug fixes, and security fixes are always welcomed. What most of really wants is faster and more reliable Siri AI, along with support for a wider range of personal data, such as PDF documents on the iCloud Drive.

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Apple’s Games app introduces some small updates in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track. Finally, the Friends tab “provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages” per Apple.

Which new iOS 27.2 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

#3392. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

#3391. Ms. Marvel Star Iman Vellani Believes This Is The Perfect X-Men Story (And She's Right)

Whatever role Kamala Khan has to play in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Marvel Studios needs to keep actress Iman Vellani on its payroll. A genuine comic book expert and enthusiast, Vellani is currently flexing her knowledge as co-host of Marvel's "Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday" podcast, running through all 15 films on the official "Doomsday" prep list. On the "X-Men" episode covering the original 2000s "X-Men" film trilogy, Vellani got into her love for the source material of "X2" — Chris Claremont and Brent Anderson's 1982 graphic novel, "X-Men: God Loves, Man Kills."

"If I had to recommend a single 'X-Men' comic that kind of encapsulates, like, it's the purest distillation of what these characters represent, it's 'God Loves, Man Kills,'" Vellani said, echoing common consensus among "X-Men" fans. The book's villain is Reverend William Stryker, a televangelist who believes mutants are demonic. When Stryker's "Purifiers" abduct Professor X in a plot for mutant genocide, the X-Men ally with Magneto against their common foe.

"Stryker's speaking for God, but he's preaching hatred and murder. It's so dark and explores how a lot of people's beliefs are often more dangerous than the people themselves," said Vellani. ("X2" left out the comic's religious themes and is a lesser story.)

Claremont wrote "X-Men" for 16 years and almost 200 issues. It's a soap opera, and it's so hard to pick a single story that stands out as ideal for new readers. Except for "God Loves, Man Kills," which, as Claremont told Vox in 2017, was the entire idea: "If you never read an issue of ['X-Men'] but wanted to know what the series, the concepts, the characters, the reality was all about — and to do so in a way that had, and sadly still has, relevance to the 'real world' — this was the story."

To this day, "God Loves, Man Kills" is one of the few books in Marvel's library that reaches true literary prestige, and which can compare to the great works of their rival publisher DC, like Frank Miller's "The Dark Knight Returns" or Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons' "Watchmen." It runs over 60 pages, three times as long as a typical "X-Men" issue. The art is also moodier and more down to earth than other Chris Claremont-written "X-Men" comics; heavier shadows and no flat coloring reflects the less fantastical tone.

The comic also adds more texture to how humans hate and fear mutants. The opening scene is Stryker's Purifiers gunning down two mutant children and stringing their bodies up. (Adding to the lynching imagery, both children are Black.) There's no robotic Sentinels hunting mutants here, only hateful human beings. "Genocide in the name of God. A story as old as the race," Magneto bitterly observes of the Purifiers.

The rest of the comic remains bracingly political. Claremont wrote "God Loves, Man Kills" in response to "the rise of the evangelical movement across the United States and their insertion into the political process" during the 1980s. Reverend Stryker would fit right in with the Moral Majority. (It's worth noting that one of the evangelical movement's casus belli in those days was opposition to school desegregation.) While "God Loves, Man Kills" remains a clear product of the 1980s, its themes are timeless; you would only have to change the allegory's specifics to set it today. Perhaps in 2026, Stryker would propagate mutant hatred with social media and podcasts instead of television.

But while "God Loves, Man Kills" remains Claremont's masterpiece to most, it's not without controversy — for one scene in particular.

Kitty Pryde gets in a brawl with a boy who calls her a "mutie lover" (unaware she is a mutant). Her Black friend Stevie Hunter tries to calm her, so an enraged Kitty asks Stevie if she'd be preaching tolerance if the slur had been the N-word instead of "mutie." In the original printing, the slur was written in full, though modern printings censor it.

I've never forgotten reading that when I was about 13-years-old: a Marvel comic was allowed to print something like that? The shock value has a point to make; it's easier to say "stick and stones" about bigotry if you're not its target. It makes the racism against mutants feel real and harmful, yet it tests allegory's limits: Mutants aren't real, but anti-Black racism is.

Chris Claremont more elegantly tied mutants' oppression to reality a year earlier in 1981 when, in "X-Men" #150, he revealed Magneto as a Holocaust survivor. (Claremont is Jewish himself.) "God Loves, Man Kills" comes off of that then-fresh reinvention and was pivotal in cementing Magneto as no longer a megalomaniac. Throughout the story, Magneto urges the X-Men to make their alliance permanent, but on his terms. When Kitty instead asks Magneto to join them, he refuses: "For all our sakes — mutant and human — I hope you [succeed]. But should you fail, it will be my turn."

Magneto and the X-Men both believe Stryker's hatred will endure even with his defeat. Stryker's claim that mutants are made in the Devil's image also hits especially hard for Nightcrawler, who does look demonic despite being a practicing Catholic. Later works, including "X-Men: The Animated Series," would explore that religious conflict inside Nightcrawler, pushing on the boundaries that "God Loves, Man Kills" tested first.

#3390. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3388. ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time

Every episode of “12 12 12” opens with the same explanation of its title: Citing the fictitious law enforcement manual, “Principles of Crime, FBI Research Center, 4th Edition,” Anthony Mackie explains, “A high asset robbery, professionally conceived, is 12 months in planning, 12 hours in execution. A bank robber who’s not caught within 12 days is not caught at all.” Then the screen splits horizontally to reveal images from the 12 months of preparation, the 12 hours of execution, and the 12 days when thief extraordinaire Paul Galvin (Jamie Dornan) does his best to elude Mackie’s obsessed FBI agent Jack Strickland. And then, we’re off to the races. Related Stories ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

The heist genre, in theory, seems ripe for this kind of temporal manipulation. A game of wits between cops and criminals typically involves plenty of twists, many of which pull the rug out by flashing back to show where, when, and how it was placed so stealthily underfoot. Also working in “12 12 12’s” favor is the genre’s familiarity: There will be “getting the team together” montages, there will be unexpected hiccups in the days and hours during the robbery, there will be chest-thumping meetings between our confident cop and the equally confident con artist. Throw in the complex heist itself and the tense escape soon after, and there appear to be enough recognizable pieces that jumbling them up shouldn’t prove too confusing.

And “12 12 12” isn’t confusing. It is, however, convoluted. Taking a serpentine route through well-trodden territory does more to undermine our enjoyment of an otherwise well-mounted chase than it does to liven things up. Heists are inherently exciting. They’re exciting in conception (when master thieves can wow us with their slick plans), they’re exciting to see carried out (when the shit hits the fan and even the most astute architects have to think on their feet), and they’re exciting to get away with (when safety is within reach, but it could be snatched away at any moment). Anticipation, suspense, and anxiety work to form a natural arc, and disrupting that arc over and over, every hour for eight hours, in service of a few extra twists — and to extend what’s obviously a movie-length story across eight hours — simply isn’t worth it.

On that note, let me get this minor but essential point out of the way now, quickly and clearly: Jamie Dornan needs more weird roles, not more conventional ones. We saw what he can do in “Barb and Star Go to Vista Del Mar” (a modern comedy classic). Let the man cook — or sing or dance or all three at once! He can do it! Honestly, I believe he can do anything. (Remember the bee movie?! No, not that bee movie — the other one.)

Anyway, here his character’s only unique attribute is his brilliant… planning. He’s got a mind for details, and he uses it to map out every possible contingency before embarking on his elaborate heists. Caught in a bind with his dumbass brother (Jack Kesy, doing his best Travis Kelce impression), Bobby lays it out in aptly blunt terms: “Paul, you’re the fucking plan guy, so plan me a plan.”

But the only plans Paul wants to make these days are for his family: He’s happy working on fishing boats off the coast of France and coming home to his wife, Severine (Agathe Rousselle), in their little apartment above a bar. He’s bonded with his father-in-law, Serge (José Garcia), who’s the Marxist papa Paul never had, and he’s got a kid on the way.

Unfortunately, Bobby can’t stop being Bobby and winds up indebted to the wrong people; people who don’t just want their money back, but who want more money to make up for the inconvenience. And since Bobby already owes more money than either brother could ever pay back, Paul has to take on one last job to free his brother — and himself — from their lives of crime.

Too bad that puts him back on Jack’s radar or, I should say, squarely on Jack’s radar, since Jack is nursing a (secret) grudge against Paul from years earlier. Ever since, he’s been obsessed with catching the one criminal who’s eluded his grasp. He wants revenge, he wants “respect,” he wants to win — “12 12 12” throws out a number of motivations for Jack early on that clearly don’t paint the full picture. They’re placeholder reasons until the show deems it time to dig into what’s really driving him to move to Zurich, hole up in a shitty police station, and wait for Paul to try to steal something.

Mackie, who’s reunited with his “Falcon and the Winter Soldier” director Kari Skogland, gives great determined face, and Dornan is the softest, sweetest guy on the FBI’s most-wanted list. Thankfully, co-creators Dudi Appleton and Jim Keeble don’t ask their lead characters to betray their core identities amid all the twists and turns, shading Jack as more of an antagonist (all-consumed and, thus, single-minded to a fault) and Paul as more of the protagonist. (He doesn’t want to steal, but now that he must, he’s going to do it the right way.) That helps keep our rooting interests in line, which goes a long way toward a satisfying emotional payoff, even when the momentum ebbs and flows with every flash-forward, -back, and -sideways.

With slick locations and clever-enough problem-solving, “12 12 12” should satisfy die-hard heist fans (but not “Die Hard’s” heist fans). It just takes a circuitous route to scratching that itch, and that’s almost as aggravating as not scratching it at all.

“12 12 12” premieres Friday, November 13 on Apple TV with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the finale (Episode 8) on December 25.

#3387. How Starship Troopers Author Robert A. Heinlein Really Felt About His Hollywood Experiences

Robert A. Heinlein wasn't fond of working as a screenwriter in Hollywood, and he definitely hated working in TV.

The famed sci-fi author loved the movies, but was always more comfortable sticking to his preferred medium of the printed page. Heinlein was quoted in a 1994 issue of Cinefantastique Magazine saying that working on a Hollywood screenplay meant a great deal of stress, but also that seeing a completed movie he had worked on was a rewarding experience. Heinlein, however, was pretty negative about his experience working on 1960s TV. That, he recalls, was totally miserable.

Movie fans may know Robert A. Heinlein's name best for writing the 1959 novel that provided the source material for Paul Verhoeven's 1997 sci-fi war satire "Starship Troopers," a movie full of disturbing details. He was also behind the short story " '—All You Zombies—' ," which was adapted into the wibby-wobbly time travel movie "Predestination." Sci-fi fans, however, know him as a giant of the genre, having written books like 1951's "The Puppet Masters," 1961's "Stranger in a Strange Land," and many others besides.

In the '50s, Heinlein was also tapped by Hollywood to write a few screenplays, and the famed author is a credited screenwriter on movies like Irving Pichel's 1950 film "Destination Moon" (which adapted elements of Heinlein's 1947 teen novel "Rocket Ship Galileo") and Richard Talmidge's 1953 film "Project Moonbase." About "Destination Moon," Heinlein noted that he was actually pleased with the results.

It was when he was approached in the 1960s to write the pilot for an unmade TV series called "XXII Century," however, that Heinlein's experience in Hollywood turned sour. That show, it seems, was a huge headache.

To give you an idea of how well "Project Moonbase" was received by the public, it was featured on an episode of the bad-movie showcase program "Mystery Science Theater 3000." Robert A. Heinlein didn't comment on that movie directly. But "Destination Moon" has been recognized by Steven Spileberg as the movie that taught him about cinematic suspense, and Cinefantastique quoted Heinlein about his rewarding experiences working on it:

"[I]t had cost me eighteen months work, my peace of mind, and almost all of my remaining hair. Nevertheless, when I saw the 'rough cut' of the picture, it seems to have been worth it."

Heinlein wrote his masterpiece, "Stranger in a Strange Land," several years after his experiences working on "Moonbase" and "Moon," so Hollywood started looking at him again. A producer named Howie Horowitz called Heinlein about making a TV pilot, and the result was a script called "XXII Century" (also called "Century XXII" various places online). The script can be purchased on the Heinlein archive website, and that edition contains pages and pages of notes, seemingly requiring that Heinlein repeatedly alter his work.

"[I]f the series is never produced, I hope I have sense enough to stay home and write books in the future, and leave the movie never-never land to those who enjoy the rat race."

It seems those pages of notes didn't leave Heinlein in a good mood. It was the last time he would be directly involved in any major Hollywood production.

The basics behind the pilot of "XXII Century" can be found on the Libertarian Futurist Society website. "XXII Century" was to take place in the year 2163, and followed the plight of a secret society of powerful superhumans who had the ability to think rationally at all times, even if it pained them. They had cordoned themselves off from the rest of society, and developed a benevolent dictatorship.

The LFS website notes that this premise was culled from Robert A. Heinlein's 1949 novella "Gulf." In the pilot episode, called "The Man Who Wasn't There," it was explained that the United States, Russia, and China engaged in a devastating war in the year 1984. Thereafter, the former two affected authoritarian governments founded moon colonies, and eventually began sending criminals and undesirables there. Fast forward a few centuries, and "XXII Century" can begin. The moon colonies were matriarchal in nature, as there were far fewer women than men, and were also meant to reflect a post-racism future, where prejudice was left behind. And all of this was written before "Star Trek" ever made it to the air in 1966.

Why did the show fall apart? The Space Review has some commentary on "XXII Century" from noted Heinlein scholar Bill Patterson, and he said that the script was way too daring for its own good, and that there was no way it could have ever made its way to the small screen. The project was abandoned, Heinlein lost interest in television, and he went back to writing hit novels. The TV show sounds great, but Heinlein was likely better off in his preferred medium.
