#3362. Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

From the misty seaports of Massachusetts seaports to the otherworldly town of Twin Peaks and even the distant shores of Troy, Ruth De Jong has spent the past twenty years transporting audiences into the unforgettable worlds created by auteur directors like Paul Thomas Anderson, Terrence Malick, Kenneth Lonergan, David Lynch, Jordan Peele, and Christopher Nolan.

“My goal in my work is to always paint the most authentic pictures,” De Jong shared with IndieWire at the Virginia Film Festival, where the production designer received the festival’s Craft Award. The town of Charlottesville has a special place in De Jong’s heart.

It’s here where legendary production designer Jack Fisk, father of De Jong’s high school friend Schuyler Fisk, suggested she forgo attending the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts for grad school in favor of working on the set of Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2007 Oscar-winning film “There Will Be Blood” instead. Recalling that fateful conversation, De Jong said that Fisk told her he saw the younger version of himself in her, sharing, “I think what the world continually needs are mentors [like Fisk] showing up.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

De Jong fell in love with filmmaking as she continued to work with Fisk on Anderson’s “The Master,” and a handful of films by Terence Malick, including his Palme d’Or winner “The Tree of Life.” Eventually she spread her wings and took on her first film as production designer: Kenneth Lonergan’s “Manchester by the Sea.” Looking back on these early days and everything she learned on those sets, De Jong said that she believes “a body of work like that is built upon itself. I think I’m constantly pulling from the past, but also pulling from the future.”

Whether designing a fishing village in modern-day Gloucester, recreating the White House Oval Office, or crafting the iconic Trojan horse, all of De Jong’s work comes in service of the characters and story being told. While crafting a film’s world, De Jong asks herself, “How do I make this tangible and alive and real and authentic?”

To capture undertones of the real working-class people in the fishing community at the center of “Manchester by the Sea,” this meant spending time with local fishermen. “We asked if we could go into their houses. We asked if we could use their fishing boats. We asked if we could use their lobster cages and rope everything, and then we would,” De Jong recalled. All of this research helped De Jong nail the subtle nuances and layers of the region. “You’re always striving to not make it cliché,” De Jong told IndieWire.

The first step involves breaking down the script. At this phase of her process, De Jong attaches an image to each scene. “It may be a piece of art. It could be a photograph. It could be a texture. It could be a piece of cloth. It could be anything,” she shared, adding, “Then from that, I add physical locations, and we start putting the whole thing together and seeing our film.”

Sometimes these images come from the director themselves. While working on “Twin Peaks: The Return,” David Lynch gave De Jong some of his own artwork for inspiration. “He would hand me some of his paintings, his drawings, his work, and say, ‘Here, this is this set. Build that,,’” De Jong revealed, adding that even if it was “a flat 2D painting, the colors were wild and it’s textural.” These came in handy for the new worlds of the series, like the landmark Episode 8 (also known as “Gotta Light?”), in which De Jong designed the radio station and other eerier riffs on the atomic age 1950s.

For the more iconic aspects of “Twin Peaks, ” De Jong also dug up the original plans for the Red Room from the 1990s. “David remembered in his mind’s eye,” De Jong said, “and I’m there to continue to be David’s conduit on the new work. It was just a beautiful, beautiful dance.”

Along with reviving iconic sets from pop culture’s past, De Jong herself has created work that has become part of the entertainment firmament. The set she created for the “Jupiter’s Claim” theme park in Jordan Peele’s “Nope” has been added to the Studio Tour at Universal Studios Hollywood, a unique feat for an aspect of filmmaking that is often binned as soon as a production wraps. On the honor of her set being preserved in such a way, De Jong said, “It’s pretty incredible, because in the act of doing it, you aren’t thinking about what this is going to turn into.”

After receiving her first Oscar nomination for her work on Christopher Nolan‘s Best Picture-winning biopic “Oppenheimer,” De Jong re-teamed with the writer-director this year for his ambitious take on Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” For this film, her process began at Nolan’s home, where she spent hours reading the script. Afterwards, De Jong asked for the parameters. “He said, ‘There are none,'” De Jong recalled.

This allowed the designer the freedom to “take the audience on the same journey that Odysseus (Matt Damon) was on,” she said. Starting with seven countries, De Jong and Nolan began searching for the film’s faraway locations, the only edict being that Nolan wanted the film to start in the Mediterranean and end in the Mediterranean. Without the barriers of realism, De Jong found inspiration in locations across the globe. “We didn’t care that we were shooting the Laestrygonians in Scotland. It didn’t matter. It just had the topography we were interested in. Same with Iceland and the same with Morocco,” De Jong said. Once the locations were determined, then came building sets that reflected the characters who inhabit them.

For the ominous stone house owned by Circe (Samantha Morton), who beguiles Odysseus’ men and turns them into pigs, De Jong shared that Nolan “was very clear about not wanting Circe’s home to be a Hansel and Gretel in the woods type cottage. She’s so peculiar and unique and bizarre and a witch.” With this in mind, the duo decided she should live on the edge of a cliff, finding the perfect craggy rocks in Scotland. Soon, a whole backstory informed the building of her dwelling. “She formed her house out of those craggy rocks,” De Jong said, adding, “We just made up all these stories and created the sets from there.”

The same attention to character informed the creation of the iconic Trojan horse, an imposing image of which opens the epic film. Nolan envisioned a rearing horse, telling De Jong that “it has to be iconic and it has to be larger than life.” For Nolan, De Jong said, the question at the center of this opening scene is, “Are the Trojans going to accept the gift?” Thinking about what kind of horse would be accepted, Nolan wanted their horse to be “the antithesis” of the one in Wolfgang Petersen’s 2004 film “Troy.” “We didn’t want the clunky wheels,” she said, adding that “these were master shipbuilders.”

“They’re master craftsmen,” De Jong insists, “If they collected all this wood, why don’t we shiplap the entire body, shiplap the tail? They hand-carved the legs and the head. That leaves the body all hollow like a ship, so all the men could all go inside and cut a trap door.” Once they agreed on the backstory for the building of the horse, the next step was figuring out how to make multiples out of fiberglass (and later out of plastic as one of the summer’s hottest collectible popcorn buckets).

As “The Odyssey” marches its way into awards season, De Jong is looking towards her future – and her next gig. With every project she takes, De Jong is looking to push herself as an artist. “It’s that space of being uncomfortable that is how you know you’re in the right place,” she said, adding, “The minute I find comfort, I realize I’m in the wrong place. So I’m always pushing to get back into that area of discomfort.”

Thinking back to her conversation with Fisk all those years ago, De Jong feels that what he taught her was “The act of physically doing and going and staying in momentum,” adding, “That’s something that Christopher Nolan has. All of these directors; They don’t stop producing work. They don’t do it in vain. They do it because that’s their language and their medium. They’re all artists at heart.”

Although De Jong looks back at her past fondly, she doesn’t regret forgoing art school to join the movie business. What she learned after all these years is that, “You need to go forward, and even if you go forward and you hit a wall, then just keep pivoting a little bit. Stay open and don’t be fearful. You can’t fear. I’d rather screw up royally and have tried than not tried at all.”

#3361. 8 Hard Sci-Fi Shows Even Better Than The Expanse

When it comes to hard sci-fi shows for the true genre aficionado, The Expanse is hard to beat. Its attention to scientific principles like gravity, acceleration, and the practical difficulties of interstellar society gives its futuristic setting a remarkably grounded foundation. However, while it’s difficult to argue against The Expanse being the definitive modern space opera series, its position as TV’s best hard sci-fi show isn’t so clear-cut.

Several hard sci-fi TV shows bring their fiction with just as much science, if not more, than The Expanse. True, they don’t all focus on life among the stars or deliver storytelling as consistently compelling as the Rocinante crew’s saga, but they definitely match and even beat Prime Video’s series when it comes to their sci-fi being cerebral, complex, and rooted in real scientific principals.

The Expanse makes space travel much more interesting because it remembers that the challenges of traversing the void last long after liftoff. The short-lived 2009 hard sci-fi series Defying Gravity leads into this even harder, making the daily struggles of its eight astronauts the central attraction. The show focuses on an international crew on an extended expedition through the solar system, with the central drama and tension all stemming from the day-to-day difficulties of simply continuing the mission. Their spacecraft, the Antares, feels genuinely claustrophobic and fraught with danger even when things are going smoothly.

For viewers who appreciated when The Expanse focused on the Rocinante as a home and shared workplace and the interpersonal difficulties this caused, Defying Gravity is ideal. As far as hard sci-fi goes, it does a fantastic job at bringing to light the practical problems of making a spacecraft habitable. Power, temperature regulation, and the crew’s ability to function belong to the same fragile system. That approach makes real-life engineering dramatically meaningful, because keeping people alive requires several things to keep working simultaneously. It’s a much more intimate account of life aboard a spacecraft than The Expanse usually has room for, accurately portraying interplanetary travel as difficult, exhausting daily work.

Dangers to humanity after first contact is the focus of many great action-heavy sci-fi TV shows, but in both The Expanse and Another Life it creates problems that firepower can’t solve. In the two-season Netflix show, Niko Breckinridge (Katee Sackhoff) commands the Salvare on a mission to investigate a civilization responsible for an alien artifact discovered on Earth. That premise already gives both series a connected scientific challenge: reaching an unknown intelligence and understanding what humanity has encountered. Just like in The Expanse, exploration in Another Life is an exercise in interpreting incomplete evidence while keeping the expedition alive.

Where Another Life beats The Expanse is that it explores concepts like extraterrestrial biology and technology with much more depth. Where The Expanse left its protomolecule and Ring Gates a mystery, Another Life explores the science behind understanding unfamiliar organisms in great detail. It takes The Expanse’s alien intrigue and turns it into a central drip-feed of discoveries that undermine the Salvare crew and the audience's existing assumptions. As a bonus, the Netflix show also handles existential questions around AI incredibly well through the ship’s on-board intelligence, William (Samuel Anderson), and his emergent emotional capabilities.

Orphan Black doesn’t look to space for its hard sci-fi, but to human cloning and the age-old debate around how much genetics and circumstances shape who we are. Thanks to Tatiana Maslany’s incredible performance as over a dozen different clones, the relationship between inherited biology and lived experience become apparent long before the show dives into scenes that discuss it in a laboratory. The mystery begins when Sarah Manning discovers another woman who looks exactly like her. From there, the series turns cutting-edge genetic science into something personal, raising fascinating debates around scientific ownership when “experiments” have been in the real world long enough to start families, have ambitions, and, most importantly, forge their own identities.

The hard sci-fi dive into biology in Orphan Black explores contemporary concerns around genetic manipulation and the ethics of the institutions controlling these areas of research. It’s this foundation that gives the central conspiracy significant weight and makes it feel much more grounded than many other TV shows and movies about cloning. Fans of The Expanse who are drawn to the exploitation surrounding protomolecule research specifically will find similar material in Orphan Black. However, this show focuses much more on the human consequences of biotechnological research than The Expanse ever did, especially when it comes to treating people as experiments.

A continued presence after death is something The Expanse explores through the protomolecule reconstruction of Miller (Thomas Jane), but in Netflix’s hard sci-fi cyberpunk series Altered Carbon it’s treated as a society-wide economic issue. Human consciousness can be stored in devices called cortical stacks and transferred into replacement bodies, creating a civilization where wealth can literally buy immortality. Former soldier Takeshi Kovacs (Joel Kinnaman, Anthony Mackie, and Will Yun Lee) enters this world’s privileged superhumanly-long-lived circles through a murder investigation. The detective story is incredibly gripping, but it’s the worldbuilding surrounding it that makes Altered Carbon so great when it comes to hard sci-fi specifically.

Altered Carbon explores the natural ramifications of technologies that allow new bodies to be purchased, identities to outlast their original appearance, and the wealthy being able to protect themselves against consequences that remain permanent for everyone else. This becomes especially harrowing and fascinating when it comes to the implications of the human mind as transferable information. Backups introduce gaps between a person’s remembered experience and what happened to their body, while replacement bodies complicate intimacy, punishment, and recognition. These consequences create an authentic-feeling picture of everyday life where the show’s speculative neuroscience technology is real.

Artificial Intelligence exists in the world of The Expanse, but it’s not a central focus. The implications of civilization-changing technologies, however, is. Another hard sci-fi show also focuses on this specific idea only with man-made AI instead of alien-created space portals. That show is Person of Interest, which starts as a straightforward crime procedural but ends over a struggle to reclaim humankind control of its own destiny from the grasp of unplanned rapid technological progress.

In the show, scientist Harold Finch (Michael Emerson) builds a system capable of identifying potential violence through surveillance data, then recruits John Reese (Jim Caviezel) to investigate the people it flags. Of course, over time this system becomes so advanced that it’s dangerous, especially when rival equally powerful artificial intelligences begin to emerge. For The Expanse fans, Person of Interest’s escalating struggle over a technology powerful enough to reorder society is incredibly satisfying, despite the specifics of both plots being worlds apart.

A huge part of the hard sci-fi appeal of The Expanse is its grounded depiction of the space technologies of the future and the political frictions facing a humanity spread out across multiple planets. Any fans who want a story that focuses more on this than it does on mysteries like the ring gates and protomolecule will find Apple TV’s For All Mankind much more satisfying. The show begins with the USSR beating NASA to the Moon Landing, then explores how this impacts technological and social progress. It especially focuses on space travel, which takes a drastically different turn. The result resembles a history that could conceivably lead to the 24th century solar system of The Expanse.

For All Mankind’s attention to spacecraft operations and the demands of maintaining distant settlements gives its ideas an intellectual weight that makes it one of the 21st century’s best hard sci-fi shows. As the series reaches humanity's attempts to colonize Mars, it moves from practical concerns to societal disputes over political authority. This should feel instantly familiar to fans of The Expanse, and it’s hard to recommend a show that feels like a better companion piece.

Interplanetary politics are complicated and detailed enough in The Expanse, but Apple TV’s Foundation expands that challenge across an entire galaxy to make it the core of one of television’s most ambitious space operas. Its hard sci-fi focuses on how a civilization spread across hundreds of stars would function, particularly when its worlds all have different priorities and relationships with the central authority of humanity’s galactic empire. Mathematician Hari Seldon (Jared Harris) approaches this society through psychohistory, a predictive science combining mathematics with the statistical behavior of vast populations. His forecast of total societal collapse across the galaxy forms the center of a narrative exploring what the forces that shape civilizations truly are, and whether humankind really will ever have control over them.

Essentially, Foundation is a much more focused dive into one of the most satisfying themes of The Expanse. Both shows understand that humanity’s expansion into space creates political problems that a unified central government alone can’t seem to solve. Foundation also stretches this exploration problems across generations too, examining how knowledge survives, political power fades, and long-term plans are never immune to chaos. Its scale makes the difficulties of governing an interplanetary society in The Expanse feel like the earliest stage of a much greater challenge.

Keeping thousands of people alive in space requires more than winning the next battle, which Battlestar Galactica understands with brutal clarity. The Expanse understands this too, but it’s Battlestar’s commitment to making problems like exhaustion, water, food, and fuel central to its survival story make it much more satisfying in this arena. After the Cylons devastate human civilization, a surviving fleet must keep moving while preserving the systems that sustain its remaining population. This fascination with realism even extends into the fleet’s technology. Computer networks create vulnerabilities and maintenance becomes harder as equipment deteriorates.

At the same time, Battlestar Galactica also focuses on its wilder elements through an incredibly hard sci-fi perspective. Through the Cylons, the series rigorously examines ideas like artificial consciousness and the relationship between memory and identity. Not only that, but it also manages to have an incredibly plausible depiction of the complex political intricacies of a humanity spread out across multiple starships too. While both shows are brilliant, Battlestar Galactica feels like it surpasses many of the hard sci-fi strengths of The Expanse, even when it veers into more fantastical or conceptual territory like Cylon prophecies or cyclical time loops.

#3360. Reddit Reviews goes against the whole philosophy of the platform, say users

Many Redditors have expressed dismay at the launch of Reddit Reviews, a new AI-powered feature which aims to summarise posts about particular products.

Reddit is positioning the feature as a way to save time and effort when researching a potential purchase, but many Redditors say that replacing human interaction with AI summaries is antithetical to the whole philosophy of the platform – and is going to make the existing spam problem massively worse …

The value of customer reviews on ecommerce platforms like Amazon is becoming increasingly questionable thanks to practices like astroturfing by brands and offering people free products in return for five-star reviews.

That’s led to Reddit becoming one of the most trusted sources of feedback and advice on potential purchases, precisely because it’s a forum in which real people are free to express their true opinions. Indeed, many use a filter in their Google searches to draw content from Reddit specifically, adding the suffix ‘site:reddit.com’.

Reddit is increasingly a cesspool of maligned moderators (human and bot) and owners looking to make a bot. Posters on the platform are simply supplying free content with nothing to gain except bans when someone/somebot disagrees with them.

Reddit certainly isn’t immune to astroturfing – that is, fake posts by brands posing as ordinary users – but moderators put a lot of work into deleting spam and other inauthentic posts.

The platform yesterday announced the launch of Reddit Reviews, in which AI summarises the posts made about particular products and product categories. It’s being pitched as a way for people to save time when seeking the product opinions of Redditors.

Across Reddit’s communities, people discuss everything from hobbies and daily life to products they’re researching. By offering perspectives grounded in real experience, these conversations provide valuable context in every purchase decision journey […]

Today, we are starting to test Reddit Reviews, a new experience that organizes product conversations from across Reddit into dedicated reviews and highlights the most important takeaways from across our communities.

However, as CNET spotted, the move has led to a backlash by many Redditors and subreddit moderators.

“I’ve already seen this in practice and it is a nightmare. It turns a basic conversation into an ad-ridden distracting mess. It’s horrible to read and had me fleeing every thread I saw it in.”

“I am a moderator on a couple of health subs and we explicitly do not allow advertisements because most of them are bullshit slop and completely predatory for vulnerable and newly diagnosed patients. We do not want, or need this, on our subs!”

“Yeah, this definitely isn’t going to lead to even more fake account stealth marketing efforts across the site.”

“This is going to make our spam fighting even worse. This is horrible.”

“Every decision made by Reddit lately encourages spam and/or abuse that will make spam.”

“Not a single person who uses Reddit wants this.”

“You are incentivising existing spammers to continue or step up their activities, now that there’s a new well they can poison.”

I find it hard to disagree with the view that almost every monetization step the platform has made has degraded the user experience. This seems almost guaranteed to be another one.

#3359. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3358. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3357. Guy Ritchie’s $50 Million James Bond Replacement Officially Begins Streaming Conquest

Guy Ritchie has been booked and busy in 2026 with several new releases, most of which have been hits among both critics and audiences. Much earlier in the year, Ritchie returned to Prime Video for the Sherlock Holmes prequel series, Young Sherlock, which was renewed for Season 2 after spending months in the global top 10.

It wasn’t until the theatrical launch of In The Grey (co-starring Henry Cavill and Jake Gyllenhaal) that Ritchie stumbled this year, but despite a woeful performance at the box office, the film has gone on to become one of the most-watched titles of the entire year on Starz. Later in the year, Ritchie also found success with gritty crime thriller streaming shows like The Gentlemen (starring Theo James) and MobLand (starring Tom Hardy), both of which have been renewed for new seasons.

Guy Ritchie is one of the most famous action directors in the world, and along with that prowess comes the ability to work with some of the most famous movie stars. Over the years, one of Ritchie’s most frequent collaborators has been Jason Statham — the two have worked together on five movies to date, and they’re set to reunite for a few projects coming to the big screen and streaming in the next few years.

Most recently, they teamed up for Operation Fortune: Ruse de Guerre, the James Bond-style spy thriller starring Statham as Orson Fortune, a high-level operative who recruits a movie star to help him stop the sale of dangerous weapons technology. Operation Fortune was recently removed from streaming in America, but the film is charting a comeback on VOD, where fans are renting it on platforms like Prime Video and Apple TV.

Guy Ritchie’s next movie, Wife and Dog, is coming to theaters on February 19, 2027. The film features a star-studded ensemble led by James Norton, Paddy Considine, Rosamund Pike, Anthony Hopkins, and Benedict Cumberbatch. Ritchie is also reuniting with Jason Statham for a new action thriller Viva La Madness, which is set for release in theaters less than one year later, on January 21, 2028. He and Statham are also teaming up for another action thriller, Dogfight, which will be released on Netflix at a currently unspecified date.

#3355. After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

With Cannes entry “Bitter Christmas,” Oscar-winning Spanish auteur Pedro Almodóvar (“Talk to Her”) is back making movies in his native language. Since his debut “Pepi, Luci, Bom and Other Girls Like Mom” in 1980, Almodóvar has written singularly identifiable, heightened, rhythmic, and mellifluous Spanish dialogue.

While Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore adeptly wrangled his translated English in Golden Lion-winner “The Room Next Door,” which deployed his usual bright Almodóvar colors and exacting mise-en-scène, the director did not enjoy dealing with the unions in New York. “In Spain everything is much more immediate, and also it is my language, it’s my culture,” he told me during the New York Film Festival. While he doesn’t rule out making another English-language movie, it would have to be small-scale. “I don’t find myself, anymore, capable of dealing with a production that is chaotic with a lot of people and a lot of characters.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Now he’s back in Spain in self-referential, meta autofiction mode in full force. The results are exhilarating. “Bitter Christmas” offers a movie within a movie, as writer-director Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia) crafts a script that lifts some key story points from his friends’ experiences. Even though Almodóvar considers the movie one of his riskiest, it’s the filmmaker’s biggest hit in Spain since “Volver.”

Almodóvar considers “Bitter Christmas” to be “twins” with Oscar-nominated “Pain and Glory,” which starred his old favorite Antonio Banderas as his alter ego. “‘Pain and Glory’ is more about the physical pain, right?,” he said. “The character [Raul] has had a lot of surgeries, and his fear is about that the fact that he’s not going to be physically able to to handle another another film shoot. Whereas in this film I deal with a different pain, which is the pain of writer’s block, of the blank page, or writing something that doesn’t quite come together for you. The character of Aitana in the film says to Raul, ‘you know we are all losers, you have lost grace.’ And by grace it means inspiration, something that is equally painful to that writer-director as the physical pain was to the writer director in ‘Pain and Glory.'”

Mostly when Almodóvar sits down to write, he’s making things up. He’s gotten into trouble in the past for raiding his friends’ stories. “There is not any law that creates the limits of the autofiction,” he said. “There is no law that’s going to define the limits of what you can appropriate and what you can’t appropriate. But if I’m inspired by the life of someone who’s close to me, who’s going through a difficult time, as a writer, you are selfish, because what propels you is the idea, even if it means going against the relationship. I don’t feel comfortable the two or three times that I did it. This is the limit: not to hurt anyone. But it’s normal that writers are influenced by everything in life you see, you talk to with others, you read, you see movies. So it’s impossible to renounce the influence of the life of others.”

And he’s passionate about making movies. As Raúl says in the film, “This is all there is to my life.” But Almodóvar has never suffered writer’s block. “I inspire myself because this is the profession that I know better than anyone, than any other,” he said. “The only thing that separates me from this alter ego is that I never lived a creative crisis. The experience I have had is more scripts that have taken me a long time to find the solution and to get them to gel together. But I’ve always succeeded ultimately.”

And he only recently discovered panic attacks, which took him by surprise. “I hadn’t previously experienced panic attacks, but now I have,” he said. “At that moment I was unconscious, and it was something awful, awful.”

Needless to say Almodóvar spends most of his days sitting at his desk at the computer. (Hence his legendary bad back.) Mostly he enjoys writing but also feels the clock ticking. “You always feel like time is lacking, right?” he said. “Especially that moment when you get that idea that’s going to become the motor of your story, you feel like there’s no time to breathe, because you want to get it all down as fast as possible. They’re quite intense days as we’re trying to get this. And then once I’ve started the story, my process is to get up in the morning and start writing. Those are some of the most pleasurable days in my life because you know where you’re going. But also, I have to pay attention to everything, because in that moment that you are possessed by the idea, you experience everything in your life filtered through the sensibility of the story that you’re writing.”

Listening to music feeds his creative beast. While he was writing “Talk to Her,” he listened to Caetano Veloso’s “Cucurrucucú Paloma,” a song that he had heard thousands of times, “but then it was like an epiphany. I discovered the song, and you feel it in a different way.” And in “Bitter Christmas,” his two actresses in the movie-within-the-movie listen to “Weeping Woman” from the filmmaker’s longtime muse, Mexican chanteuse Chavela Vargas.

Finally, the filmmaker had fun making himself the bad guy. “This was a new structure for me,” he said. “What I liked about it was that I could talk about myself as a writer-director, but mostly I also enjoyed the part of becoming the villain in a sense of that story. But the spectator does have to pay a lot of attention because if they go to the bathroom for two minutes, they’re going to miss something and be lost.”

In one scene, the filmmaker offers a close-up of the cursor on the computer screen. “Even though the cursor itself is not a very cinematic thing to see,” he said, “it’s his call to creativity, right? It’s the thing that calls him and pulls him in to have to tell his story. So it’s autofiction.”

Going forward, Almodóvar has no plans to put himself at the center of another film. “I promise not to talk about me anymore,” he said. “I was interested since the beginning of my career about the origin of creation and the relation with reality. Inspiration and life together, like the two sides of a coin. This mysterious question that so fascinates me is about not just where does creativity come from, how does it come, when does it come, how does it manifest? I have reached the end of my exploration around this.”

Up next: He’s writing, he said. “This is almost the opposite of this one. The new one will be very different.”

A Sony Pictures Classic release, “Bitter Christmas” is now playing in theaters in New York and Los Angeles. It expands nationally on November 25.

#3354. This video lets you actually see the ‘incredible’ new MacBook Pro cooling system

When Apple launched the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, the company said that it had completely redesigned the cooling system for “incredible sustained performance.”

That could sound like marketing hype, but a YouTuber has found a great way to let us actually see the new system living up to Apple’s claims …

The real-life performance of any electronic device depends not only on the power of the chip but a range of additional factors. A key one is the effectiveness of the cooling system, because when the device gets too hot, the performance will be throttled in order to avoid damage.

In the worst of cases, the theoretical maximum performance of a chip is only delivered for a very short time before it is throttled back to a much lower level. Thermal management is absolutely key in the case of a laptop like the MacBook Pro.

Apple said that the latest model has a completely new cooling system.

A completely redesigned thermal architecture enables […] incredible sustained performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, even in a lighter design, while redirecting warm air away from the display.

As Macworld spotted, a YouTuber has found a simple but clever way to enable us to actually see the difference with our own eyes.

A YouTube video by Geekerwan compared the mini-LED MacBook Pro with the new PROLED XDR model using a fog machine. With each MacBook’s fans running, you can clearly see how the internal design disperses the heat: In the old model, heat goes both out and up through the display, while the PROLED pushes the heat toward the back of the device through the hinge.

Cooling is particularly challenging when the laptop is closed while connected to an external monitor, and the results of the testing show a dramatic improvement by the latest model. You can watch the video below, which links directly to the demo – but Geekerwan’s videos are always worth watching in full, so click here to watch the whole thing.

#3353. 7 Pointless Sci-Fi Movie Remakes That Were Worse Than The Original

The science fiction genre has been particularly afflicted with movie remakes that couldn’t hold a candle to the original. Sci-fi has always been one of cinema's most imaginative genres, exploring technological breakthroughs, alien civilizations, dystopian futures, and the potential extinction of humanity. Sci-fi's greatest stories are often remarkably adaptable, with ideas that remain relevant across generations. Naturally, Hollywood has repeatedly returned to successful science-fiction movies, hoping to introduce familiar stories to new audiences with bigger budgets, modern special effects, and contemporary interpretations.

Unfortunately, updating a classic doesn't necessarily improve it. Some older science-fiction movies were products of particularly inventive film-making, using practical effects, intelligent writing, and ambitious social commentary to create worlds that audiences hadn't experienced before. Reproducing their basic premises with more sophisticated technology can leave remakes looking considerably less impressive, especially when the original's most interesting ideas are diluted in favor of generic action and spectacle.

Hollywood has produced plenty of successful sci-fi reimaginings, but there are also several examples that struggle to justify their existence. Whether they misunderstand the original's central themes, replace distinctive characters with forgettable alternatives, or simply fail to capture the same imaginative spirit, these remakes demonstrate that some classics really are better left alone.

The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951) is one of science fiction's greatest films, using an extraterrestrial visitor's warning to dissect Cold War paranoia, nuclear proliferation, and humanity's capacity for self-destruction. Scott Derrickson's 2008 remake, starring Keanu Reeves as the alien Klaatu, attempts to modernize that message by replacing the original's anxieties about nuclear warfare with environmental destruction.

Unfortunately, the updated version sacrifices much of the intelligence that made its predecessor so effective. The remake certainly has impressive visual effects, particularly when Gort unleashes a swarm of microscopic machines capable of consuming everything in their path.

However, its environmental message is surprisingly muddled, with the remake struggling to reconcile its ecological concerns with conventional disaster-movie spectacle. The original’s memorable philosophical exchanges and restrained tension are replaced by an overreliance on destruction and spectacle. As a result, it lost all its charm and was left feeling notably hollow.

Paul Verhoeven's Total Recall (1990) is gloriously excessive science fiction. It combines Arnold Schwarzenegger's unmistakable action-hero charisma with grotesque practical effects, absurd humour, and an increasingly complicated mystery surrounding Douglas Quaid's identity. Len Wiseman's 2012 Total Recall, starring Colin Farrell, is considerably more interested in looking futuristic than recreating the original's wonderfully strange personality.

Both films follow an ordinary construction worker who visits Rekall, a company promising to implant artificial memories of an exciting adventure. However, the remake abandons Mars entirely, relocating the action to a dystopian Earth divided between the wealthy United Federation of Britain and the impoverished Colony.

The production design is undeniably impressive, particularly the enormous futuristic cities and the Fall, an underground transportation system connecting the two territories. Unfortunately, Total Recall's visual similarities to Blade Runner are distracting, and its elaborate action sequences lack the personality of Verhoeven's original. There's also no equivalent to Schwarzenegger's outrageous one-liners, the bizarre Martian mutants, or the unforgettable practical effects that made the 1990 film so distinctive.

H.G. Wells' The Time Machine has inspired numerous adaptations, but George Pal's 1960 film is particularly memorable for its imaginative depiction of a distant future divided between the peaceful Eloi and the subterranean Morlocks. Simon Wells, the author's great-grandson, directed a new adaptation in 2002, starring Guy Pearce as Alexander Hartdegen.

Despite its impressive production design, the remake struggles to recreate the sense of wonder that made its predecessor so effective. The biggest change is the addition of a romantic motivation for Hartdegen's time-traveling adventures. After his fiancée Emma (Sienna Guillory) is killed during a robbery, the scientist becomes obsessed with traveling backwards through time to prevent her death. His repeated failures eventually lead him 800,000 years into the future.

The revised motivation makes the story considerably more personal, but it also reduces the intellectual curiosity that drives Wells' original novel. Instead of exploring the consequences of humanity's social and evolutionary divisions, The Time Machine resembles a conventional adventure about a man attempting to rescue a romantic interest. Jeremy Irons' sinister Uber-Morlock provides an entertaining antagonist, but the character feels more like a generic blockbuster villain than an interesting development of Wells' ideas. It lost all sense of wonder and replaced it with bland action.

Frank Oz remake of The Stepford Wives transformed an unsettling satire on technology and social conformity into an underwhelming comedy vehicle. Bryan Forbes' 1975 adaptation of Ira Levin's novel follows Joanna Eberhart (Katharine Ross), a photographer who moves with her family to a seemingly idyllic Connecticut suburb. She gradually discovers that the town's husbands are replacing their wives with obedient robotic duplicates, creating a nightmare vision of patriarchal control.

The 2004 remake, starring Nicole Kidman and Matthew Broderick, retains the basic premise but dramatically changes its tone. The light-hearted interpretation certainly features some funny jokes but completely undermines the message of the original. The critique of patriarchal control becomes a star-studded farce – cheapening its central message.

It feels a lot like the original movie itself has been replaced by a compliant robotic duplicate designed to perpetuate the status quo. The 1975 Stepford Wives presented the idea of men literally engineering their ideal wives as frightening, the modern remake decided it was funny.

Rollerball (1975) imagined a future in which multinational corporations controlled society and maintained public order through a violent spectator sport. Starring James Caan as Jonathan E, the original used its fictional competition as an allegory for corporate power, consumerism, and the suppression of individual freedom. The 2002 Rollerball remake, starring Chris Klein, largely abandons that political sophistication in favor of chaotic sporting violence.

The new version relocates the action to Central Asia, where Rollerball has become a hugely popular extreme sport. Jonathan and his friend Marcus (LL Cool J) become involved in the competition, only to discover that promoter Alexi Petrovich (Jean Reno) deliberately engineers increasingly dangerous matches to improve television ratings.

There is certainly potential in updating the original's criticism of corporate entertainment for an era dominated by reality television and sensationalist broadcasting. However, the is much more interested in showing people crashing into one another than examining why audiences enjoy watching them suffer. Furthermore, Rollerball's heavily edited matches are frequently difficult to follow, while Klein lacks the commanding presence Caan brought to the original.

Paul Verhoeven's RoboCop (1987) is a particularly effective fusion of science-fiction action, political satire, and grotesque violence. Peter Weller plays Alex Murphy, a Detroit police officer murdered by a gang of criminals before being resurrected as a technologically enhanced law-enforcement machine. His gradual rediscovery of his humanity provides the emotional foundation for a film that simultaneously ridicules corporate greed, privatized policing, and sensationalist television.

José Padilha's 2014 remake updates that premise for an era of military drones, surveillance technology, and sophisticated robotics. Consequently, it should have had so much more to play with. Indeed, there are interesting ideas here, particularly through Gary Oldman's Dr. Dennett Norton, who becomes uncomfortable with the corporation's manipulation of Murphy's memories and emotions. However, the remake's more restrained approach to violence removes an essential ingredient of Verhoeven's satire.

The original Robocop's exaggerated corporate advertisements, grotesque news broadcasts, and outrageous action sequences made its criticism of 1980s capitalism considerably more effective. Padilha's version is slicker and more technologically sophisticated, but its conventional action-movie structure simply cannot match the original's personality.

The original Death Race, directed by Paul Bartel and produced by Roger Corman, starred David Carradine as Frankenstein, a masked driver competing in a cross-country race where contestants earned points for running down pedestrians. Its deliberately outrageous premise provided the foundation for a gleefully tasteless satire of authoritarian entertainment and America's obsession with violence.

Paul W.S. Anderson's version replaces the original's bizarre road-racing competition with a prison-based televised spectacle. Generic muscle man Jason Statham plays Jensen Ames, a former racing driver framed for murder and imprisoned in a privately operated facility run by the calculating Warden Hennessey (Joan Allen). She offers him a chance to regain his freedom by taking the place of the masked racer Frankenstein, competing in heavily armed vehicles against other prisoners.

The remake delivers plenty of entertaining automotive carnage, with its armored cars, mounted machine guns, and elaborate stunt driving providing some impressive action. However, Death Race loses much of the original's darkly comic premise. The 1975 film's scoring system, which rewarded drivers for killing pedestrians, was an absurd extension of its dystopian satire; Anderson instead turns the concept into a fairly conventional prison-break adventure. It’s not a remake in the conventional sense, but a reimagining based on the least important parts of the iconic sci-fi original.

With the end of ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026, the world’s premier annual celebration of cinematography has come to a close. #3351. I feel a little nostalgic about the Apple Support Community forums, but it was time

Yesterday brought a surprise move by Apple when it abruptly ceased write access to the Apple Support Community and announced that it would be permanently closing in just over a week.

While the news does make me a little nostalgic, I do have to say that I think its time had long since come and gone …

As we noted yesterday, the community has a fairly long history. It started in 1998 as the Apple Tech Exchange before being renamed Apple Discussions and finally relaunching as Apple Support Communities in 2011. There were some paid community specialists working for Apple on the forum, while the majority of the responses came from volunteers.

The company’s statement was brief and didn’t give any official explanation for the shutdown.

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

Interestingly, Verizon did exactly the same thing with its own Community Forum earlier this year, with an immediate switch to read-only access, followed shortly afterwards by closing it altogether. That too had a reasonably long history, having first launched back in 2008.

I suspect in both cases this was mostly about streamlining operations and reducing costs. CEO John Ternus does seem to be aiming to improve efficiency and eliminate what he views as unnecessary expenses. Additionally, community forums always run the risk of reputational damage when customers criticize decisions made by the company.

I’m old enough to remember the times when the forum was one of the first places I’d turn when troubleshooting an issue with an Apple product, but in all honesty, that hasn’t been the case for a very long time now. A lot of the suggestions were very basic steps any experienced user would already have tried.

There was sometimes also a snarky tone to some of the responses, essentially amounting to “Apple doesn’t promise you should be able to do X, so why are you expecting to do this?” or “Apple already provides a better way to do Y so use it.”

If you were very new to Apple devices and needed very basic help, then I’m sure it could sometimes prove useful, but I have to say that for a very long time now my own starting point has always been Reddit. I don’t think too many people are going to mourn the passing of ASC.

#3350. Taylor Sheridan’s Hit Western Series Officially Dominates Streaming Worldwide

From Mayor of Kingstown and The Madison to Lioness and Landman, Taylor Sheridan's impact on modern television through his pantheon of shows cannot be overstated. Currently, the fourth season of Tulsa King is the latest to dominate the streaming charts, as viewers remain gripped by Sylvester Stallone's Dwight "The General" Manfredi and his fight "to legitimize his empire while facing corrupt politicians and new enemies."

As Season 4 continues weekly, Season 5 of Tulsa King remains in production in New York. Erik Palladino, Glenn Fleshler, Anthony Skordi, and Nickola Shreli have already been added to regular series roles, with it confirmed that Girls and Ironheart star Manny Montana has also joined the growing ensemble as "Gilberto Torres, a gangster with a strong presence, though he doesn’t have to advertise it." The good news continues for Sheridan fans, as the most important series in his catalog has returned to the global streaming stage.

At the time of writing, Yellowstone is one of the ten most-watched shows on Paramount+ in the world, a list featuring the aforementioned Tulsa King in second place. Sheridan's flagship series ran for six years, five seasons, and 53 episodes, rarely missing a beat as it helped pioneer a Western renaissance on the small screen. The show's impact cannot be overvalued, as the current landscape of 21st-century streaming simply wouldn't have been the same without its major pop culture impact.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

#3349. WhatsApp may soon replace the Communities tab on iOS

Some WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are seeing a new option in the app’s bottom navigation bar that replaces the Communities tab. Here are the details.

Over the past few years, WhatsApp has increasingly focused on Communities as more people have turned to messaging platforms to interact in smaller, more private groups rather than through traditional social networks.

At the same time, WhatsApp has been testing several features that make it easier for users to see which of their contacts are online and available to chat.

Back in May, WABetaInfo found that WhatsApp was developing a new Contacts hub that would bring together users’ favorite contacts, as well as those who were currently online or had recently been active.

A few weeks later, WhatsApp began testing a new green dot indicator on iOS to make it easier to identify contacts who were online.

Now, WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is rolling out the new Contacts hub to some iOS beta testers, replacing the Communities tab in the app’s bottom navigation bar.

The new tab includes a section with favorite contacts and a full contact list. Users can see their favorite contacts at the top of the screen, making it easier to start a conversation with them. They can also sort the full contact list by activity, alphabetical, and birthdays. With alphabetical, the app organizes contacts by name. With activity, WhatsApp shows who is currently online at the top of the list. WhatsApp marks these contacts with a green dot, so users can easily distinguish them from offline contacts. WhatsApp also sorts recently active contacts by last seen, so users can quickly identify who was active most recently. With birthdays, WhatsApp sorts contacts by their upcoming birthday, so users can see who has a birthday coming up soon.

The site notes that the new tab also allows users to add contacts directly, with the option to sync them to their iPhone’s address book.

As for Communities, the feature itself isn’t going away, but rather being moved to a dedicated filter in the Chats tab.

WABetaInfo also notes that WhatsApp is experimenting with potentially replacing the Updates tab, rather than Communities, with the Contacts tab in a future configuration.

For now, the new Contacts tab is available to a limited number of beta testers running the latest WhatsApp beta for iOS via TestFlight, with a broader rollout expected over the coming weeks.

#3348. Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

If Johnny Depp was hoping that “Ebenezer” would mark a glorious return to mainstream movies, he may need to hold out for another vehicle. The Christmas fable, released long before Thanksgiving, let alone the holidays, topped the box office this weekend with $19 million domestically and $42 million globally, a solid but unremarkable debut. It shows that enough moviegoers are able to look past the scandals that led Hollywood to remove Depp from their call sheets for the better part of a decade, but also exposed the limitations of his popular appeal.

The fact is that Depp was always something of a dicey commercial proposition. Put him in a “Pirates of the Caribbean” movie and you were guaranteed to earn $1 billion even if the script sucked and the plot seemed designed at the end of a wine bottle. Team him with Tim Burton, as he was quite successfully with “Sweeney Todd” ($153 million gross, $50 million budget), “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” ($475.8 million gross, $150 million budget), and “Alice in Wonderland” ($1 billion gross, $200 million budget), and you were likely to have a big hit. Well, unless they were looking to reboot “Dark Shadows.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

But the rest of Depp’s track record was spotty. “Public Enemies” ($214.1 million gross, $100 million budget) and “Black Mass” ($100 million gross, $53 million budget) did well considering they were R-rated adult dramas, but struggled to break even because they cost too much to make and Depp commanded his full $20 million salary. Then there were the costly bombs, a litany of duds that includes “Mortdecai” ($47.3 million gross, $60 million budget), “The Lone Ranger” ($260.5 million gross, $250 million budget), “Transcendence” ($103 million gross, $150 million budget), and “Alice Through the Looking Glass” ($300 million gross, $170 million budget), the latter a return to Wonderland sans Burton. Many of these seemed like paycheck gigs rather than an attempt to burnish Depp’s star power. There was a private island to pay for and a pirate-themed wine cave to keep stocked on Depp’s sprawling French estate. But the promise of another Jack Sparrow adventure meant that Hollywood was able to look the other way, confident that there was more plunder to be found by allowing the actor to follow his idiosyncratic muse.

Depp could have kept going like this, but his messy personal life interceded. Depp’s reputation took a hit in 2020 when he became embroiled in a costly, two-continent legal battle against ex-wife Amber Heard, in which he was accused of domestic abuse. He denied the allegations, and later lost a U.K. libel suit against The Sun, when the court found an article calling Depp a “wife beater” was “substantially true.” Depp would go on to defamation trial against Heard in the U.S., after she wrote an op-ed in the Washington Post, calling herself a domestic abuse survivor. By that time, he’d been fired from the “Fantastic Beasts” franchise (it would be canceled after a non-Depp-led installment bombed), and was consigned to appearing in straight-to-streaming schlock or barely seen indies. But it wasn’t just the reputational damage that made major studios skittish about Depp. They had grown tired of his antics. There were reports he would show up late and unprepared, even as his salary demands and requests for perks escalated. That’s fine when your movies are making lots of money, it’s less charming when they are losing it.

So a lot is riding on “Ebenezer.” Depp looked a little uneasy on red carpets promoting the movie and Paramount, which is backing the film, wisely kept him from doing profiles with harder-hitting journalists who might ask him a probing question. He also cut his salary, reportedly receiving a $5 million paycheck to play one of his dream roles — Ebenezer Scrooge, and with it a chance to wear fright makeup and talk in a weird voice. But unlike most of Depp’s recent films, “Ebenezer” is poised to be a modest financial success. The film skewed older, with 59% of its domestic audience over the age of 30, and was slightly more female, as only 48% of ticket buyers were men. Paramount said it over-indexed in the South. One warning sign is that family crowds didn’t turn out in force for the PG-13 movie, comprising just 9% of opening weekend crowds.

However, the $38 million budget is low enough that if the film continues to draw crowds through the holidays and performs well overseas, where it has earned $23 million, it will turn a profit. But that points to a new reality — Depp is a sound bet, for the right price. Maybe that was a lesson that studios should have taken long ago. Depp’s taste is rococo, but Hollywood kept treating every one of his outings like potential blockbusters when a little more caution was warranted.

Next up for Depp is “Day Drinker,” an action thriller that seems to play into the star’s libertine image. Lionsgate will release the film in March. Will it be the vehicle that puts the 63-year-old Depp back on top, or will it, like “Ebenezer,” confirm that there’s still a smaller, but committed audience for his antics? Budget accordingly.

#3346. HomeKit Weekly: SwitchBot’s Curtain Track 4 is the easiest smart curtain retrofit yet

The worst part of owning smart curtain motors is charging them, because it usually means taking the whole motor down from the track or running a really long USB cord to charge it. Today, SwitchBot has released the SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 aimed at solving that problem with a battery module that detaches on its own, so the motor stays in place, and you only take down the part that needs to charge.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is a retrofit motor for curtains that hang on a U-rail track. You hang it on the track between the curtain hooks, run a one-tap calibration in the SwitchBot app, and your existing curtains can then be motorized and used in your smart home. There’s no drilling, no rewiring, and no need to position magnets to stick to the rail, as earlier SwitchBot curtain motors required. SwitchBot claims the whole setup takes about 30 seconds.

One thing to check first: this version is for U-rail tracks only, not curtain rods.

The Battery+ version pairs a small built-in battery with a detachable 5,000mAh module for a total of 6,400mAh. SwitchBot rates it at up to 12 months of use for each charge, depending on curtain weight and movement frequency. When it needs charging, you pull the module off, charge it via USB-C, and clip it back on. SwitchBot also sells a Solar version that uses a small panel to keep the battery topped off if the window gets enough sun.

The motor itself connects via Bluetooth, so getting it into Apple Home requires a compatible SwitchBot Hub, which brings it there via Matter. Once it’s there, the curtains work like any other window covering in your Home app. You can add them to scenes, control them with Siri, and include multiple windows in a single automation. It’s always nice to time smart curtains/shades with dusk/dawn as well.

SwitchBot’s built-in QuietDrift mode opens the curtains slowly in the morning, at about half a centimeter per second, so the room fills with daylight gradually rather than all at once. SwitchBot says it runs at around 25 dB in that mode. You can also give the curtain a gentle tug by hand and the motor takes over, which is great if you don’t have your iPhone with you or someone doesn’t have access to your Apple Home setup.

SwitchBot built it in a way to correct drift over time, so you shouldn’t need to recalibrate it if it gets off.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 turns the U-rail curtains you already have into Apple Home window coverings without replacing anything. The detachable battery is the best feature here, as it lets you charge it without a long cord.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is available now on Amazon and directly from SwitchBot.

#3345. Black Clover Won’t Get A Season 3, But Season 2 Might Not Be The End

Black Clover is having the time of its life with its long-awaited season 2 comeback. Nine years after its October 2017 debut, and five years after episode #170 went off the air in March 2021, Studio Pierrot’s seasonal overhaul is finally giving Yuki Tabata’s shonen epic the universal acclaim it always deserved.

That newfound respect is showing up across every major metric. Black Clover currently sits at #6 on IMDb’s global Most Popular TV Shows chart, standing completely alone near the top while the next closest anime, Attack on Titan, trails way back at #50. On top of dominating viewership on Crunchyroll, season 2 also delivered the highest-rated anime episode of 2026 after episode #5, “The Highest vs. the Lowest,” scored a near-perfect 9.9/10 on IMDb.

However, the anime is burning through the manga so quickly that a traditional season 3 might not make sense. Tabata’s eleven-year manga run officially ended in May 2026 in Jump GIGA with chapter #392, leaving just 122 chapters between the end of season 1 (chapter #270) and the finale.

With season 2 reportedly planned for 24 to 26 episodes across two cours, the first cour is already adapting the 61-chapter Spade Kingdom Raid arc. By its end, the anime will be ready to enter the final 61-chapter Ultimate Wizard King saga. Whether Cour 2 covers the Land of the Sun and Judgment Day battles in 2027 or reaches the showdown against its next major threat, Asta's journey may wrap up in a completely different format rather than a traditional season 3.

On paper, Black Clover season 2 adapting four to five manga chapters per episode makes it look like Studio Pierrot is racing through the remaining story. However, that breakneck pace has more to do with how Yuki Tabata structured the Spade Kingdom Raid arc. Most of those chapters are packed with massive double-page spreads, fast fights, sparse dialogue, and shorter 13-to-15-page counts. Five chapters of nonstop action might sound like a lot, but they don't necessarily translate into five times the usual amount of animation.

That should change as the anime moves into the final Ultimate Wizard King saga, which begins with chapter #332. The story shifts towards heavier lore, character development, and longer conversations, especially during the Land of the Sun training arc with Ryuya Ryudo and the Ryuzen Seven.

Black Clover also moved to Jump GIGA in late 2023, where chapters became longer, often reaching 20 to 25 pages. With all that in mind, the adaptation rate could naturally drop to two or three chapters per episode. If Cour 2 follows that pattern, season 2 could end around the peak of the Judgment Day invasion, leaving the final stretch for a separate finale.

Even then, there won't be enough chapters left to fill a traditional 12- or 24-episode season 3. A canon theatrical movie could be one way to finish Asta's story. With Demon Slayer: Infinity Castle, Jujutsu Kaisen 0, and Chainsaw Man – The Movie: Reze Arc showing the box-office potential of anime films, Studio Pierrot has plenty of reason to consider it.

The studio also has experience with the format. Its 2023 film, Black Clover: Sword of the Wizard King, was directed by current season 2 director Ayataka Tanemura and became a hit on Netflix. A theatrical finale could give the series the grand send-off its long-awaited return deserves.

A theatrical movie isn't the only way Studio Pierrot could wrap up Asta's story. If the studio wants to keep the finale on television, it already has the perfect blueprint in Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War. Pierrot worked with Tite Kubo to expand the manga's rushed final arc with new fights, extended backstories, and never-before-seen Bankai reveals. Yuki Tabata could take a similar approach with an expanded final cour for Black Clover.

With the manga officially ending, the final war against Lucius has finally revealed the absolute strongest mages.

Tabata struggled with health issues towards the end of his Weekly Shonen Jump run and had to condense several side battles during the Judgment Day war. An anime adaptation could finally give those moments the time they deserve, whether by extending the Magic Knight Captains' fights against upcoming threats or adding more material after chapter #392. So, while Black Clover might not get a traditional season 3, that doesn't mean Asta's story is ending with season 2. Between a theatrical finale and an expanded final television event, the series still has plenty of ways to give its fans the ending they've waited years for.

Asta and Yuno, orphans with a shared dream of becoming the Wizard King, follow distinct paths: Yuno with natural magic abilities, and Asta through determination despite his lack of powers.

#3344. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.
